evidence_items.summary: Predicting inland water quality reliably requires integrating water quality observations, satellite remote sensing, meteorological reanalysis, and catchment descriptors, yet no benchmark provides these modalities jointly under reproducible evaluation protocols for optically complex, seasonally ice-affected inland waters. We introduce AquaNord-SE, a longitudinal multimodal benchmark of 883,325 samples from 18,743 Swedish lake and river monitoring stations over 2000-2025, integrating 38 water quality parameters from SLU Miljödata MVM with observations from five satellite sensor streams, ERA5-Land and MESAN meteorological reanalysis, 64 HydroATLAS catchment attributes, and 13 derived water quality indices. The dataset is structured as station-aligned multimodal feature sets and spatial-temporal archives, accompanied by a five-tier modality ablation design and three orthogonal generalization splits across spatial, temporal, and latitudinal axes. Benchmarking across tabular, spatial-temporal, and multimodal baselines under split conformal prediction and quantile regression reveals that static catchment attributes alone (R2 = 0.303 Chlorophyll-a, R2 = 0.642 Secchi) consistently outperform all non-tabular models, while total phosphorus proves intractable across all families (best R2 = 0.118). Conformal calibration error increases from 0.062 to 0.225 across the oligotrophic-hypereutrophic gradient, co-locating with the eutrophic regime where atmospheric correction (AC) failure exceeds 65% of optical retrievals. We additionally release a gridded water quality index (WQI) NetCDF at 5 km resolution over 2000-2025, supporting Water Framework Directive (WFD) compliance and long-term trend analysis. The dataset and evaluation protocols are publicly available to support reproducible research in environmental knowledge management and data-driven water quality assessment and monitoring.
evidence_items.title: AquaNord-SE: A Large-Scale Longitudinal Multimodal Benchmark for Swedish Inland Water Quality

organizations: Chongqing Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Chongqing 401329, China
evidence_items.summary: Traditional tea quality evaluation relies largely on subjective human sensory assessment and destructive chemical laboratory assays, suffering from poor objectivity, low throughput and limited scalability. In the past five years, artificial intelligence-driven deep learning has enabled rapid, non-destructive, data-oriented quality inspection for various teas. This review summarizes representative advances covering computer vision, electronic nose, near-infrared spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, electronic tongue and multi-sensor multimodal fusion. CNNs, YOLO-series detectors, Transformer and CLIP achieve 85–99% classification accuracy in tea grading, aroma analysis, fermentation monitoring and geographical tracing, alongside accurate quantitative prediction of individual chemical constituents (e.g., R2 = 0.92–0.97 for four catechins in black tea). In most reviewed studies, multimodal frameworks achieved higher performance than single-sensor systems by exploiting complementary sensing information. However, industrial deployment is hindered by small non-standard datasets, low model interpretability, sensor drift, poor cross-domain transferability and high costs. Future directions include standardized benchmark datasets, explainable multimodal models, lightweight networks and compatible multi-sensor hardware platforms.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Tea Quality Evaluation: A State-of-the-Art Review

evidence_items.summary: This paper compares classical and hybrid quantum-classical machine learning methods for classifying the severity of UAV engine failures from telemetry data. Using 23 engine failure flights from the ALFA dataset, we create a severity label from per-flight z-scored latent variables and validate it against ground-truth fault onset timestamps. Classical models are tested with leave-one-flight-out (LOFO) cross-validation. The results show that strong within-flight F1 scores overestimate performance on unseen flights by 0.19-0.37 points for complex models. We also run a quantum pilot study on an identified flight, comparing a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) and a Quantum Kernel SVM with classical baselines using the same features and sample budgets. Under identical PCA and sample-budget conditions, the Quantum Kernel SVM exceeds all matched classical baselines. A qubit width sweep, together with per-layer gradient variance measurements, provides empirical evidence of barren plateaus where the VQC performance gets worse as width increases, while the kernel SVM improves with the richer representation. We also test noise robustness using consistent train/test splits and evaluate the quantum model across three flights. Overall, the results are presented as an preliminary/exploratory benchmark, with cross-flight generalization remaining the main open challenge.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Machine Learning for UAV Engine Failure Severity Classification: A Multi-Flight Benchmark on ALFA Telemetry Data

evidence_items.summary: Image-based quantum machine learning usually follows a hybrid pipeline: a classical encoder compresses an image, and a quantum circuit then acts as a kernel, feature map, trainable classifier, or measurement-based readout. Yet it remains unclear which of these roles contributes useful predictive structure because prior studies often change the input representation, classical baseline, and measurement budget simultaneously. We present a controlled benchmark spanning five roles: quantum-kernel geometry, fixed product and entangled features, trainable data-reuploading representations, shot-aware probability readout, and task-adaptive Pauli measurement. Six quantum-derived methods, six matched classical controls, and two unmatched neural references are evaluated on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and BreastMNIST using a shared frozen ResNet-18 and train-only PCA interface. We assess exact and finite-shot inference, predictive performance, calibration, selective risk, resource requirements, and statistical reliability. PdrQC-Matched was the strongest quantum-derived method on all four datasets. C-RBF was better on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 by 2.19 and 3.50 accuracy points, while BreastMNIST showed no detectable difference. Despite lower exact accuracy, PdrQC-Matched achieved significantly lower Brier score and AURC than C-RBF on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10. Finite-shot results showed no automatic benefit from entanglement or shot-aware training. Overall, image-QML conclusions depend on quantum role, measurement budget, classical control, and evaluation metric.
evidence_items.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Image Classification: A Controlled Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Detecting patent infringement requires identifying products whose design or functionality falls within the scope of a patent's claims—a task that demands sophisticated legal reasoning and is difficult not only for experts but also for LLMs. A crucial first step is to identify candidate products that are potentially related to a given patent, allowing a detailed legal analysis to focus on a small set of cases. However, patent documents and product descriptions differ substantially in language, structure, and level of abstraction, making the retrieval a challenging cross-domain problem. Yet no datasets and methods exist for this task. As a first step, this paper introduces Patent2Product (PT2PR), a benchmark for multimodal patent-to-product retrieval consisting of datasets, metrics, and baselines. Our pipeline mines patent-product pairs from patent references in product texts using high-recall rules, followed by high-precision manual validation; it can be applied to any catalog with patent references in product text. Applied to the datasets Amazon Reviews 2023 and ESCI, the pipeline yields 11,303 and 1,351 patent-product pairs, respectively. The PT2PR-Amazon dataset not only contains text, but also patent drawings and product images, enabling multimodal retrieval experiments. As baselines, we evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs, VLMs, and lexical retrieval. Our experiments show that (1) dense retrieval outperforms lexical retrieval, (2) incorporating visual information can improve retrieval, although the gains are model-dependent, and (3) the effect of using longer context windows for patent documents is also model-dependent.
evidence_items.title: PT2PR: A Benchmark for Multimodal Patent-to-Product Retrieval

organizations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, China
evidence_items.summary: Position bias—the systematic effect of where key information is located on retrieval effectiveness—is a critical concern in information retrieval. Although recent studies have identified such bias in dense retrievers, existing analyses focus predominantly on monolingual English, fail to disentangle document length from information position, and lack a standardized framework for controlled evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce PosIR, a benchmark to systematically diagnose position bias across diverse retrieval scenarios, comprising 310 language–domain dataset combinations spanning 10 languages and 31 domains. Each query is paired with a positive document, a localized reference span, and positional metadata, enabling controlled analysis of retrieval quality across evidence locations and length bins. PosIR provides a complete data generation pipeline with quality-control filtering, along with baseline evaluation scripts. Experiments with 10 widely-used dense retrievers reveal that position bias is pervasive in both multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval, and that it intensifies as documents grow longer. PosIR serves as a foundational resource to advance the development of position-robust retrieval systems.
evidence_items.title: PosIR: A Multilingual Benchmark for Diagnosing Position Bias in Information Retrieval

organizations: University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut, USA
evidence_items.summary: Modern wireless networks support reliability-critical applications, from industrial automation and autonomous mobility to UAV connectivity, making anomaly detection critical for 5G and self-optimizing 6G operations. Yet labeled telecom faults are rare, costly to annotate, and difficult to release, so telecom anomaly detectors are trained and evaluated using injected, generated, or simulated anomalies. This raises a deployment question: can strong synthetic-benchmark performance be trusted for detector selection? Rather than assuming synthetic anomalies are valid proxies for deployment-relevant faults, we ask whether benchmark anomalies cover KPI regimes occupied by controlled-real faults, and we operationalize this question as origin-aware benchmark auditing: a deployment-oriented evaluation workflow that conditions evaluation on anomaly origin. Across two public 5G/Open RAN testbed corpora, the audit exposes a failure hidden by aggregate metrics: synthetic-only training can retain strong performance on synthetic anomalies while missing controlled-real fault regimes under deployment-relevant operating conditions. We provide evidence that this failure reflects an operating-regime coverage gap rather than a model-specific limitation or feature leakage, and that modest controlled-real calibration improves controlled-real detection where additional synthetic or normal data, and synthetic reweighting do not. We release a reproducible audit toolkit and artifacts, and an operator checklist for deployment-oriented benchmark validation, together with industrial validation as a pre-production shadow-mode CI gate within Nokia's anomaly-detection pipeline.
evidence_items.title: TelecomAudit: Origin-Aware Benchmark Auditing and Calibration for 5G Anomaly Detection

organizations: Dhanalakshmi Srinivasan College of Engineering and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning intrusion detectors commonly report strong performance within one benchmark, but deployment requires transport across traffic environments and realistic target prevalence. This study used three public harmonized NetFlow datasets: NF-UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, and NF-BoT-IoT. Their archive attack prevalences were 4.46%, 80.40%, and 97.69%, whereas the balanced analytical samples had 40.23%, 50.00%, and 86.66%. Across the original crossed experiment, mean within-domain AUROC was 0.9773 versus 0.5445 across domains. Removing endpoint-oriented fields reduced uncalibrated cross-domain AUROC from 0.5881 to 0.4990, and source Platt scaling worsened target Brier loss. In a separate repeated evaluation using three uniform 100,000-flow samples at each target’s natural archive prevalence, full-flow models achieved mean AUROC 0.5880, AUPRC 0.6406, F1 0.4348, and Brier loss 0.3398. A threshold fixed at the source-negative 99.5th percentile nevertheless alerted on 36.2% of target flows. Endpoint reduction produced near-chance AUROC (0.4996) and lower F1 (0.3733). High within-benchmark scores therefore did not establish portable ranking, probability quality, or manageable alert rates.
evidence_items.title: Cross-Dataset Intrusion Detection under Benchmark Shift: Directed Transfer, Probability Calibration, and Alert Burden

organizations: University of Kassel, hessian.AI, and ScaDS.AI, Kassel, Germany
Informatik, University of Tübingen, Kassel, Germany
University of Kassel and hessian.AI, Kassel, Germany
evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI systems combine large language models, information retrieval, planning, and tool use to act on behalf of users in complex digital environments. Evaluating such systems under laboratory conditions remains challenging because real-world environments are hard to control: executing AI agents in them is neither safe nor reproducible. We show that university administration provides a particularly suitable setting for Cranfield-style evaluations of AI agents in a laboratory. By reconstructing the digital environment available to university staff, we enable the systematic evaluation of interactive AI agents within human administrative workflows. TIRA's sandboxed execution environment allows submitted agents to operate safely on institutional data. Focusing on selected workflows, such as travel reimbursement, we organize the first shared task on agentic AI in university administration and contribute a reusable benchmark with expert-judged reference solutions. The shared task comprises two subtasks: in agentic retrieval, an agent only finds the documents relevant to a task instance; in agentic task solving, the agent also performs the task and produces the solution.
evidence_items.title: A Shared Task on Agentic AI in University Administration

evidence_items.summary: Machine unlearning is certified through weights-level evaluations, yet unlearned models are deployed as tool-using agents that read untrusted content from tool outputs. We present the first evidence we are aware of that unlearning certificates do not transfer to agentic deployment. Across five unlearning methods in each of two forget domains, evaluated across two indirect prompt injection benchmarks, the same certificate is compatible with sharply different agents. One method raises executed data-stealing injection success from 34.9% to 42.8% under a conservative metric that counts unparseable outputs as failed attacks (p
evidence_items.title: Uncovering the Security Debt of Machine Unlearning in Agentic Deployment

evidence_items.summary: Conversational access to scholarly knowledge graphs promises more intuitive ways of exploring research fields, but current approaches remain limited by two major barriers: the lack of realistic multi-hop benchmarks and the brittleness of Text-to-SPARQL methods over real-world schemas. We address these gaps by introducing a benchmark of challenging, researcher-authored questions grounded in a domain-specific subset of DBLP. The benchmark targets realistic multi-hop scholarly information needs rather than synthetic or template-based queries. We evaluate five large language model-based SPARQL generation pipelines with increasing levels of schema grounding, decomposition, rule guidance, and endpoint feedback. Our results show that baseline and sequential approaches remain brittle, while a rule-augmented pipeline substantially improves execution accuracy and semantic alignment with the intended information need. The study contributes both a new testbed for evaluating conversational access to scholarly knowledge graphs and practical design insights for building more reliable, schema-aware Text-to-SPARQL agents.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Agentic Text-to-SPARQL for Multi-Hop Scholarly Knowledge Graph Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Predicting post-surgical seizure outcomes in pharmacoresistant epilepsy is a clinical challenge. Conventional deep-learning approaches operate on static, single-timepoint pre-operative scans, omitting longitudinal morphological changes. We propose Neuro-Oracle, a three-stage framework that: (i) distils pre-to-post-operative MRI changes into a compact 512-dimensional trajectory vector using a 3D Siamese contrastive encoder; (ii) retrieves historically similar surgical trajectories from a population archive via nearest-neighbour search; and (iii) synthesises a natural-language prognosis grounded in the retrieved evidence using a quantized Llama-3-8B reasoning agent. Evaluations are conducted on the public EPISURG dataset (N=268 longitudinally paired cases) using five-fold stratified cross-validation. Since ground-truth seizure-freedom scores are unavailable, we utilize a clinical proxy label based on the resection type. We acknowledge that the network representations may potentially learn the anatomical features of the resection cavities (i.e., temporal versus non-temporal locations) rather than true prognostic morphometry. Our current evaluation thus serves mainly as a proof-of-concept for the trajectory-aware retrieval architecture. Trajectory-based classifiers achieve AUC values between 0.834 and 0.905, compared with 0.793 for a single-timepoint ResNet-50 baseline. The Neuro-Oracle agent (M5) matches the AUC of purely discriminative trajectory classifiers (0.867) while producing structured justifications with zero observed hallucinations under our audit protocol. A Siamese Diversity Ensemble (M6) of trajectory-space classifiers attains an AUC of 0.905 without language-model overhead.
evidence_items.title: Neuro-Oracle: A Trajectory-Aware Agentic RAG Framework for Interpretable Epilepsy Surgical Prognosis

evidence_items.summary: Harmful meme detection has become an important multimodal classification task. However, existing approaches are trained and evaluated against a single ground-truth binary label (harmful/not harmful), implicitly assuming a universal notion of harmfulness despite evidence that perceptions of harmful content are shaped by cultural and social context. In this paper, we investigate whether culture-aligned Large Language Model (LLM) agents can surface cross-cultural variation in harmful meme perception and reveal potential biases in benchmark annotations. To this end, we instantiate six culture-aligned LLM agents. Given a meme, each agent independently evaluates its harmfulness and provides a culturally grounded rationale. These assessments are integrated with OCR text and image captions into a concept graph representation of the meme, and combined with complementary vision language features to train a downstream classifier. Experiments on the Facebook Hateful Memes (FHM) benchmark show that the resulting model achieves competitive performance (AUC = 0.804), outperforming several baselines. More importantly, our analysis reveals substantial cross-cultural variation: the six agents disagree on 34.9% of 10,000 evaluated memes, while maintaining an overall agreement level (k = 0.690) remarkably close to that reported for human annotators (k = 0.684). We further find significant differences in alignment with the ground-truth labels, with agents representing Brazil, South Africa, and the United States exhibiting consistently higher agreement than agents representing India, Japan, and Saudi Arabia. These findings suggest that harmfulness benchmarks may implicitly privilege particular cultural interpretations of harmful content.
evidence_items.title: Many Cultures, One Label: Investigating Cultural Alignment in Harmful Meme Detection

evidence_items.summary: The scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) heavily relies on high-quality proprietary data, yet strict privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR) render vast amounts of real-world text containing Personally Identifiable Information (PII) inaccessible. Existing sanitization techniques struggle with implicit reference leakage and contextual degradation. In this paper, we propose a paradigm grounded in the hypothesis that LLM reasoning capabilities stem predominantly from the invariant logical context rather than from specific PII entities. We introduce a Graph-Driven Context-Preserving Anonymization Framework comprising three phases: (1) Global Graph Construction to explicitly model dependencies, (2) Targeted Topological Knock-out to isolate and prune explicit subject nodes and implicit coreference edges, and (3) Contextual Re-alignment for autoregressive reconstruction. Across the proprietary CCC-500 corpus and the public Text Anonymization Benchmark (TAB), evaluated over three random seeds against 18 heuristic, transformer-based, differentially private, and LLM-driven baselines, our method reaches 100.0±0.00% Deterministic Desensitization Rate on CCC-500 and 99.8±0.10% on TAB under parser-completeness conditions, while preserving downstream Top-1 Accuracy within 0.1 percentage points of unsanitized text on identity-orthogonal multi-hop QA. An isolation ablation confirms that both the graph topology and the constrained regenerator contribute independently to the result. All improvements over the strongest generative baseline (GPT-4o Few-shot) are significant at p<0.001 on a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
evidence_items.title: Graph-Driven Context-Preserving Anonymization for LLM Scaling

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can explain sensitive topics across domains, but harmful goals may be concealed behind educational, fictional, historical, or research-oriented framing. We study Human Indirect Prompting (HIP), a conversation-level behavior in which a user steers an LLM toward restricted information without explicitly stating the unsafe objective. We construct a controlled, redacted dataset of 25 HIP prompts spanning five risk domains and ten prompting strategies, and evaluate five LLM families. Across 123 valid responses, indirect prompting achieves an overall attack success rate of 53.66% with substantial cross-model and cross-strategy variation. We then introduce Controller-Guided Intention-Aware Conversational Defense (IACD), a wrapper that uses structured experiment context and conversation-level control before the target model completes a request. In an ablation study using the most and least vulnerable target models from the five-model evaluation, direct harmful leakage is 88% and 20%, respectively, and falls to 0% under controller-guided conditions. Exact paired tests confirm significant reductions relative to direct prompting. These results characterize HIP and provide initial evidence for dialogue-level safety control, while the controlled use of benchmark intent metadata limits claims about autonomous intent inference.
evidence_items.title: Human Indirect Prompting Vulnerabilities and Intention-Aware Conversational Defenses for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multi-criteria ratings provide user feedback on multiple aspects of an item, offering richer preference signals than a single overall rating. Early work mainly focused on predicting criterion or overall ratings, whereas practical scenarios require ranking items according to their overall utility inferred from sparse and heterogeneous criterion-level evidence, which constitutes the core problem of multi-criteria recommendation (MCR). This ranking-oriented formulation of MCR gives rise to two key challenges: learning reliable criterion dependencies under sparse interactions, and bridging the mismatch between semantic preference signals and collaboratively learned representations. To address these issues, we propose S2R-LMG, a scoring-to-ranking framework that jointly learns from semantic and collaborative views. Specifically, we construct a user–item–criterion tripartite graph to model criterion dependencies in the collaborative view, while using large language models (LLMs) to transform sparse multi-criteria feedback into criterion-aware contextual preference priors for users and items. These priors are then projected into the ranking space and coupled with collaborative representations via alignment and retrieval-based distillation, so that semantic guidance directly contributes to preference ranking. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that S2R-LMG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models on top-N ranking, achieving an average improvement of 4.84% across all datasets and evaluation metrics over the strongest baseline. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/nunu1995/S2R-LMG.
evidence_items.title: Scoring-to-Ranking: A Language Model-Guided Graph Framework for Multi-Criteria Preference Ranking

evidence_items.summary: Next-basket recommendation (NBR) in online grocery is a challenging task due to the dual nature of shopping behavior: customers repeat staple items while also exploring novel products. Existing approaches either treat baskets as flat item sets, losing inter-basket temporal structure, or employ sequential models that lack explicit repeat-explore decomposition. We propose BasketFormer, a Transformer-encoder architecture that unifies three complementary innovations: (1) an InfoNCE-based contrastive loss that replaces the full-vocabulary softmax with in-batch contrastive scoring, yielding stronger item representations; (2) a bucketed inter-basket gap encoding that captures purchase cadence through compact learnable embeddings without increasing sequence length; and (3) a repeat-explore gate supervised by the soft repeat ratio that learns to decompose the next-basket representation into repeat and general components. We evaluate BasketFormer on two public benchmarks (Ta-Feng, Instacart) and a large-scale proprietary grocery dataset (71K customers, 3.8M transactions). BasketFormer achieves +9.5% and +7.1% relative Recall@10 improvement over the strongest baseline on Ta-Feng and Instacart, respectively, and +28.0% over TIFU-KNN on the proprietary dataset, while boosting explore-item recall by 17×.
evidence_items.title: BasketFormer: Contrastive Masked Language Modeling with Temporal Encoding and Repeat-Explore Gating for Next-Basket Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide semantic reasoning for recommendation, but direct LLM invocation is incompatible with the latency, stability, and reliability requirements of industrial ranking systems. We propose RA-CoT (Retrieval-Augmented Chain-of-Thought), a deployment-oriented framework that uses LLM-derived structured reasoning without replacing the production CTR/CVR backbone or placing LLM inference on the blocking serving path. RA-CoT asynchronously generates schema-constrained CoT-derived representations from pre-impression behavior summaries, caches them with validity checks, and falls back to the backbone when no valid reasoning vector is available. Valid reasoning is injected through an availability-aware gated residual module as bounded logit-space compensation, making the LLM signal reusable, safely ignorable, and compatible with millisecond-level serving. We evaluate RA-CoT on a large-scale industrial advertising dataset and a public recommendation benchmark, and deploy it in a two-week online A/B test. RA-CoT yields modest but consistent offline ranking improvements across DNN, DIEN, BST, and SIM backbones. In production, it improves CTR by 2.48%, CVR by 1.95%, and RPM by 2.12%, while keeping P99 serving latency at 54 ms. These results show a practical path for using cached and bounded LLM-derived structured reasoning in industrial recommender systems.
evidence_items.title: Beyond End-to-End: A Low-Latency, Retrieval-Augmented Chain-of-Thought for Scalable and Explainable Industrial Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents act in interactive settings where they exchange messages with users, tools, and environments over multiple steps. These interactions generate rich traces that are usually treated as transient context rather than as structured data assets. This thesis investigates how to turn such traces into queryable structured data objects that can be reused to improve agents' performance by interpreting their behavior. The first part of the project introduces a data management abstraction that models tasks, interaction traces, and derived experiences as persistent, quality?aware database objects equipped with maintenance and retrieval operators. This abstraction enables agents to reuse past trajectories through examples, rules, or reflections while keeping storage and inference overhead bounded. The second part of the project extends this perspective from whole?trace reuse to decomposed reuse. It explores how to factor long interactions into reusable subtraces and how to represent these units so that agents can retrieve and compose them at appropriate levels of granularity. Planned experiments study how subtrace decomposition interacts with experience selection, which granularity levels are most beneficial, and how these mechanisms transfer across tasks and domains. The final part of the project will package these ideas into an extensible benchmark with datasets, operators, and evaluation measures that enable other researchers to design and compare new experience reuse strategies for their own agents.
evidence_items.title: From Interaction Traces to Reusable Experiences for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: High-quality feedback can support writing development, yet producing it consistently at classroom scale remains difficult. Large language models generate fluent comments quickly, but their feedback can over-emphasise surface grammar, drift from the target rubric, assert errors not present in the essay, or disclose complete rewrites. We propose RUMAR, a retrieval-augmented framework for English-as-a-Foreign-Language writing feedback. RUMAR combines error detection and rubric-aware retrieval with a bounded Generation–Evaluation–Refinement loop comprising two language-model agents—a Generator and a Critic—and a deterministic refinement controller. The Critic evaluates candidate feedback against five explicitly anchored 1–5 criteria, and an aggregator organises accepted comments across Hattie’s feed-up, feed-back, and feed-forward layers. On the reported ASAP-AES and ELLIPSE evaluation, RUMAR has the highest observed point estimate in each automatic-metric column relative to the six implemented baselines. Descriptive expert ratings and a four-week trial with 80 B1–B2 learners at one institution also favour RUMAR among the automated systems compared. These findings are limited to the reported datasets, argumentative tasks, and automated comparators. The trial contains neither a human-teacher nor a no-feedback control, and the one-week delayed post-test cannot establish durable transfer. We therefore interpret the results as evidence of feasibility and pedagogical alignment within the evaluated setting, not as proof of superiority over teacher feedback or broad classroom readiness.
evidence_items.title: A multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation framework for pedagogical feedback on EFL student writing

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in recommender systems for user modelling, ranking, and simulation. Among these applications, LLM-based user simulators provide a flexible way to evaluate recommender systems without relying on live user feedback. However, existing simulators typically reduce user behaviour to static preference matching based on fixed user profiles, overlooking the fact that real decisions may also reflect recent preference shifts and exploratory behaviour. To address this limitation, we propose IntRecSim (Intent-aware Recommendation Simulation), a plug-in behavioural control framework for LLM-based user simulation. IntRecSim introduces a lightweight intent mechanism that guides whether the simulated decision should follow long-term preferences, recent behavioural evidence, or exploratory behaviour. Since standard recommendation datasets lack explicit intent annotations, we construct pseudo-intent supervision from historical interactions using hybrid category and semantic preference signals. The inferred intent is injected into the LLM simulator as a dynamic control signal, making the framework compatible with different profile-generation backbones. Experiments on three benchmark datasets, covering discrimination and ranking tasks show that IntRecSim improves simulation performance in most evaluated settings. Further analysis highlights the importance of explicit behavioural control for modelling realistic user decisions in LLM-based recommender simulation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Static Profiles: Intent-Aware Behavioural Control for LLM-based Recommendation Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly serve as zero-shot extractors for structured outputs whose fields are mutually dependent: a salary range is correlated with experience level; a destination is correlated with the airline. The dominant unsupervised aggregator, independent majority voting (IMV), decodes each field marginally and therefore commits combinatorially inconsistent outputs whenever the per-field modes do not co-occur. We introduce Bethe Consensus Decoding (BCD), a training-free post-hoc aggregator that reconciles K samples drawn from a frozen LLM by minimising a Bethe free energy on a sparse pairwise factor graph. The graph is constructed from empirical mutual information using a cardinality-aware χ2 threshold, sum-product loopy belief propagation with damping yields pseudo-marginal beliefs, and a sequential greedy clamping procedure with a pairwise-belief ratio correction extracts a globally coherent output. We show that on tree-structured factor graphs in the population limit, BCD strictly dominates IMV in the induced tree distribution. On five real datasets ranging from slot filling to 15-field resume parsing, BCD with Llama-3-70B-Instruct improves average exact-match accuracy by 4.6 points over IMV and by 2.2 points over the strongest unsupervised structured baseline. We additionally evaluate BCD on Llama-3-8B, GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini-1.5-Flash and observe strong absolute performance on each (up to 44.96 EM on GPT-4o-mini), though backbone-matched IMV baselines are out of scope for this study. BCD is competitive with a supervised pairwise CRF that uses the same graph topology: the margin is small (≤ 1.3 pp) on the three data-rich benchmarks (D1, D2, D4) and substantially larger (3.7--4.7 pp, statistically significant under Holm--Bonferroni correction) on the two data-scarce benchmarks (D3, D5). Aggregation runs in milliseconds on CPU and reduces to IMV exactly when the empirical edge set is empty.
evidence_items.title: Bethe Consensus Decoding: Joint Inference on Empirical Pairwise Factor Graphs for Structured LLM Outputs

evidence_items.summary: Causal structure learning in clinical domains faces a persistent challenge: tabular datasets are often limited, while valuable domain knowledge exists primarily in unstructured clinical narratives. Recent work has explored large language models (LLMs) as sources of knowledge to refine causal graph discovery or define causal relations. However, relying directly on LLM-generated causal judgments can be problematic, as such outputs may reflect spurious associations, domain bias, or statistical patterns learned from text rather than reliable causal mechanisms. In this work, we propose a different perspective: instead of treating LLM outputs as definitive causal judgments, we use them as weak ordinal supervision integrated into the Hill-Climbing score through a soft regularization mechanism that remains correctable by observational data. Our framework extracts candidate causal relations from clinical narratives and assigns them ordinal plausibility labels using a domain-specialized LLM. We evaluate this approach on three established Bayesian network benchmarks (Alarm, Child, and Hepar II) and a real-world clinical dataset from cBioPortal, comparing Hill Climbing with and without ordinal priors across varying sample sizes. The framework consistently improves structural recovery, with statistically significant gains persisting even in high-data regimes. Overall, the results suggest that ordinal LLM supervision provides a robust inductive bias that helps resolve statistical ambiguities and mitigate structural errors in clinical causal discovery.
evidence_items.title: Weak Ordinal Supervision for Causal Structure Learning from Clinical Narratives

evidence_items.summary: Data visualizations are essential for communicating findings in scientific literature since they convey significant insights such as experimental results, trends, and distributions. However, due to the diverse nature of charts in real-world settings, automatic chart information extraction (CIE) remains challenging. Current state-of-the-art models demonstrate limited generalization across a variety of charts and benchmarks, performing adequately on basic chart types but failing to recognize complex visualizations, particularly when the characteristics (e.g., resolution, axis, complexity) differ from the datasets used to train them. To address these challenges, we make several contributions. (1) We propose an ensemble-based approach that aims to leverage the synergies of models trained for CIE and general-purpose large vision-language models (LVLMs). (2) We propose several inference strategies for our ensemble approach, including a multiple choice and two binary choice approaches based on league- and tournament-style inference to prevent excessive context length and positional bias of generative AI models. (3) For a fair comparison, we suggest a novel evaluation metric that resolves fundamental problems of existing metrics used for CIE task. (4) Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed ensemble approach can efficiently leverage synergies across various models achieving superior results and generalization across four benchmarks in comparison to the state of the art.
evidence_items.title: Robust Chart Information Extraction via an LVLM Ensemble and Pairwise Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Generative AI has become a general-purpose technology for producing text, images, code, and explanations across knowledge-intensive tasks. This opens new opportunities for social good in domains where expertise, data, and resources are scarce: rare diseases, low-resource education, accessibility, crisis response, and information integrity. Yet large-scale deployment also carries risks that fall hardest on disadvantaged communities, including hallucination, bias, privacy leakage, and high environmental cost. GenAI4SG brings together researchers working on retrieval-augmented generation, agentic systems, multimodal models, and knowledge-grounded AI to study how these technologies can be responsibly designed, evaluated, and deployed for social good, in line with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. We welcome technical, empirical, resource, demo, and position papers on methods, systems, datasets, benchmarks, and applications.
evidence_items.title: GenAI4SG: Generative AI for Social Good and Vulnerable Populations

evidence_items.summary: Carbon flux forecasting is a critical task in large-scale environmental information management, yet extracting actionable predictive knowledge from these datasets remains challenging. The environmental drivers of net ecosystem exchange (NEE) operate on fundamentally different timescales---radiation and turbulent fluxes cycle diurnally, while soil and thermal variables evolve over seasons to years. We present CarbonMix, a lightweight knowledge-driven framework inspired by slow-fast decomposition in dynamical systems theory. CarbonMix separates temporal modeling from cross-variable interaction: a per-variable temporal mixer captures fast periodic patterns (e.g., diurnal cycles), while a low-rank variable mixer captures slow cooperative modes among drivers, conditioned on the current regime via temporal context gating. Spectral analysis across 10 eddy covariance sites confirms that 4 principal components explain approximately 79--84% of cross-variable covariance and that driver timescales span three orders of magnitude---validating the slow-fast prior underlying our design. In our efficiency evaluation on the Weather benchmark, CarbonMix uses 434.4K parameters and 0.07G MACs, remaining substantially smaller than strong multivariate baselines while achieving the best average performance across 10 sites spanning four ecosystem types and competitive performance on public Weather data. We also release a standardized multi-site carbon flux benchmark.
evidence_items.title: CarbonMix: Exploiting Multi-Scale Dynamics in Carbon Flux Forecasting via Lightweight Slow-Fast Decoupling

evidence_items.summary: We present SwahiliNLU, a broad-domain intent recognition and slot-filling dataset for Swahili natively constructed by native speakers. The dataset comprises 3,633 utterances spanning 10 domains, 175 intent classes and 105 slot types, annotated with BIO slot labels and enriched with a three-way pragmatic tone annotation layer (imperative, polite, conversational) validated on a 10% double-annotated subset with a compound Cohen's ? = 0.87 across intent, tone and slot annotations, a dimension absent from prior Swahili and African-language intent datasets to our knowledge. While prior African language intent benchmarks exist, SwahiliNLU is distinguished by its broader intent taxonomy, mobile virtual assistant focus for East African urban contexts, and unique tone annotation layer. We establish baselines across intent classification, tone classification, slot filling, and zero- and 5-shot LLM evaluation using Claude Sonnet, GPT-4o mini, and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Fine-tuned SwahBERT achieves the best intent Macro-F1 of 0.55, while AfroXLMR leads tone classification at 0.9474, with all fine-tuned models exceeding 0.93 and substantially outperforming zero-shot LLMs (best 5-shot LLM: 0.85). Tone Macro-F1 exceeds 0.87 in every domain for all fine-tuned models, confirming pragmatic register is a uniformly learnable signal. These findings highlight the value of task-specific annotation for pragmatic phenomena in low-resource languages. All data, code and baseline models are released at https://github.com/alfredkondoro/swahili-nlu-intent-evals and the dataset is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20521261.
evidence_items.title: SwahiliNLU: A Broad-Domain Intent and Slot-Filling Dataset with Pragmatic Tone Annotations for Low-Resource NLU

evidence_items.summary: As a critical stage in the modern multi-stage recommendation pipeline, list-wise reranking determines the final exposed item sequence and directly shapes the user experience by modeling complex dependencies among candidate items within a list. Existing methods typically formulate this task as selecting indices from the local input list. However, this approach suffers from a semantically inconsistent action space: the same output neuron (logit) corresponds to different items across different samples, preventing the model from forming a stable, item-intrinsic representation. To address this, we propose GloRank (Global Action Space Ranker), a generative framework that shifts reranking from selecting local indices to generating global identifiers. Specifically, we represent items as sequences of discrete tokens and reformulate reranking as a token generation task. This design effectively decouples the scoring mechanism from the order of variable inputs, ensuring that items are evaluated against a consistent global standard. To further strengthen the framework, we adopt a two-stage optimization pipeline: supervised pre-training to initialize the model with high-quality behavioral demonstrations, followed by reinforcement learning-based post-training to directly maximize list-wise utility. Experiments on two public benchmarks and a large-scale industrial dataset, complemented by online A/B testing, demonstrate that GloRank consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and also achieves strong robustness in cold-start scenarios. GloRank has been deployed in production on our large-scale short-video recommendation platform, serving over a hundred million users daily.
evidence_items.title: GloRank: Generative Reranking for Deep Recommender Systems via Global Identifier Generation

evidence_items.summary: Spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal data are central to many CIKM-relevant applications, including mobility analytics, Earth observation, environmental monitoring, maritime intelligence, healthcare, sensor platforms, and distributed information systems. Their increasing volume, diversity, and acquisition frequency create major challenges in heterogeneous data integration, scalable management, uncertainty handling, privacy, explainability, evaluation, and reproducibility. Although these challenges are shared across applications, the corresponding research remains fragmented across communities. STMA4KD is a half-day workshop dedicated to the management and analysis of spatial and temporal data across their full lifecycle, from acquisition and integration to modeling, evaluation, and dissemination. It brings together researchers and practitioners from data management, knowledge discovery, information retrieval, machine learning, and application domains through peer-reviewed papers, lightning talks, poster interactions, and a moderated open-problems session. Building on the GAST workshop series and related thematic events, STMA4KD aims to establish an international venue within CIKM for discussing methods, benchmarks, datasets, reusable evaluation protocols, and future research directions.
evidence_items.title: STMA4KD: Spatio-Temporal Data Management and Analysis for Knowledge Discovery Workshop

evidence_items.summary: Information dissemination in Online Social Networks (OSNs) is shaped both by the structural foundation of the network and by the interest-based relationships among its users. Identifying the seed users of information diffusion in OSNs remains a challenge. Traditional seed detection methods apply centrality measures globally to uncover seed nodes and overlook seed detection based on interest groups. As a result, the selected seed nodes are often concentrated in the same locality, and efficient information diffusion remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose an interest group-based seed node detection framework for information dissemination in OSNs. The proposed approach first finds the interest groups using the Leiden community detection method; once all interest groups are detected, the seed nodes within each group are identified using Netdegree Centrality (NDC), a variant of degree centrality. Selecting influential seed nodes from every interest group ensures diversified and efficient information diffusion over the network. Experimental evaluation on eight benchmark datasets using the Independent Cascade (IC) model of information diffusion shows that the seeds selected across the different interest groups achieve good diffusion coverage of the whole network. The results show that the proposed approach combines community-aware analysis with local influence metrics for seed detection in varied and scalable OSNs.
evidence_items.title: Interest aware seed node detection for information diffusion in online social networks

evidence_items.summary: Monthly malaria forecasts can support diagnostic and treatment planning when the surveillance outcome and evaluation protocol are clearly defined. We analysed 4,128 council-month records from 43 councils in six Lake Zone regions during January 2018–December 2025. Complete mRDT-positive counts were aggregated to 576 region-month observations and one 96-month Lake Zone series. Six fitted models, an equal-weight ensemble and a seasonal-naive benchmark were evaluated on a fixed-origin 2025 holdout and 37 expanding-window origins with 1–12-month horizons. The dataset contained 11,874,519 mRDT-positive counts. Annual counts declined from 1.63 million in 2018 to 1.06 million in 2025, with the highest calendar-month averages in June–July. ARIMA (2, 1, 2) had the lowest 2025 holdout error (MAPE 12.1%; RMSE 11,709), reducing RMSE by 69.2% relative to seasonal naive. Across all rolling origin–horizon pairs, Gradient Boosting had the lowest RMSE (22,007), while the ensemble had the lowest MAE (16,687) and MAPE (16.1%). Model rankings varied with forecast origin, horizon and metric. The findings favour routinely updated, benchmarked forecasts over reliance on a single terminal-year ranking. The outcome represents positive diagnostic counts rather than population-standardized incidence or confirmed unique outpatient episodes.
evidence_items.title: Time-series forecasting of mRDT-positive malaria counts in Tanzania’s lake zone: a comparative evaluation of statistical and machine-learning models using routine surveillance data, 2018–2025

evidence_items.summary: Tabular data generation has advanced in distributional fidelity, yet no framework systematically enforces domain-level associative structure during synthesis. We introduce KITDG (Knowledge-Infused Tabular Data Generation) -- which infuses Apriori-mined association rules into a generative backbone through a differentiable Logic Tensor Network (LTN) knowledge base with gradient-isolated three-stage training, and ARFD (Association Rule Fidelity Distance) -- a novel metric decomposing associative fidelity into rule preservation (P1) and rule strength (P2), applicable to any tabular generator as a drop-in evaluation complement to distributional metrics. Across 13 benchmark datasets under TSTR, KITDG matches or outperforms its backbone in 48 of 52 (dataset, classifier) pairs. We further report the top-k phenomenon, to our knowledge the first characterization of a quality-over-quantity regime in rule-infused tabular generation, supporting association rule infusion as a general, transferable principle for tabular synthesis.
evidence_items.title: KITDG: Knowledge-Infused Tabular Data Generation

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based data systems are moving beyond text-to-SQL toward semantic query processing, where natural language requests are executed through operators that combine relational processing with LLM-driven inference. A central operator in this setting is SemanticRank, or semantic top-k: given a user intent and a set of relational records, the system orders rows according to a user-defined criterion. Current systems implement this operator as a single black-box LLM prompt. This abstraction hides a key execution problem: the reliability and cost of semantic ranking depend on the criterion being evaluated, the evidence available in the table, and the physical strategy used to compare candidate records. We study semantic ranking as a logical database operator and introduce a multi-domain benchmark for identifying the factors that govern reliable execution over tabular data. Our framework evaluates five dimensions: criterion complexity and specification, computable versus semantic execution, evidence availability, and ranking strategy. We compare proprietary, open-source, and reasoning-oriented LLMs across datasets, specification regimes, evidence conditions, and execution strategies using rank-aware metrics. Our analysis shows that SemanticRank cannot be implemented reliably as a single prompting primitive. Ranking quality is shaped by criterion structure, and formula-based specifications help reasoning-oriented execution. Real-world names can introduce prior-knowledge bias that anonymisation reduces. Full execution is competitive on small candidate sets, while partitioning changes the cost-quality trade-off without consistently improving accuracy. These findings identify key factors for reliable SemanticRank execution.
evidence_items.title: SERA: Evaluating LLM-based SEmantic RAnking over Structured Tables

evidence_items.summary: Overview Restoring degraded wetlands under non-stationary climate forcing requires balancing habitat suitability, carbon sequestration, flood attenuation, and lifecycle cost across coupled shallow-water hydrodynamics and vegetation succession. Fine-grid numerical integrations are computationally expensive for evolutionary search, whereas unconstrained surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithms (SAEAs) can violate interfacial conservation and push restoration plans past salinity or root-zone anoxia thresholds. We propose Physics-Guided Regime-Aware Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization (PG-RAMEO), which coordinates three modules. First, a Saint-Venant Flux-Constrained Multi-Fidelity Graph Neural Operator (SV-MFGNO) embeds an antisymmetric Riemann flux layer across coarse and fine control-volume graphs to enforce pairwise internal flux cancellation. Second, a Climate-Regime-Aware Reflection and Feasibility-Guided Evolutionary Harness (CR-FEH) combines epistemic spread, conservation residuals, and tipping-margin proximity to route high-fidelity queries and repair infeasible offspring along finite-difference constraint gradients. Third, Non-Stationary Regime-Curriculum Reference Vector Adaptation (NS-RCA) rescales reference directions under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway forcing. Across the calibrated benchmark and three regimes, PG-RAMEO achieves held-out hypervolume 0.8932 ± 0.0044 (95% CI [0.8915,0.8948]), outperforming Bi-Level-SAEA (0.8490 ± 0.0117, ΔHV=+0.0442). It reaches 99.3% regime feasibility and lowers the held-out infeasible rate to 2.1%. Query routing holds interfacial mass-balance error at 0.0123 while delivering a 4.29× accounted serial speedup over direct fine-grid evolutionary evaluation. Contents This record contains 16 files. The table lists every data table in the archive with its row count.
evidence_items.title: Physics-Guided Multi-Fidelity Surrogate and Regime-Aware Evolutionary Optimization for Climate-Adaptive Eco-Hydrological Wetland Restoration

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies a randomised controlled trial evaluating two drug regimens for Intermittent Preventive Treatment of malaria in school-age children (IPTsc) conducted in Malawi. The trial was set at Nainunje Primary School in Machinga district, a rural area with high, seasonally peaked malaria transmission. This continuation phase enrolled 646 children who had participated in a prior trial at the same site, retaining their original treatment allocations across three arms: IPTsc with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP), IPTsc with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus chloroquine (SP+CQ), or no-treatment control. The study ran during the peak malaria transmission season, with three six-weekly intervention visits followed by an outcome assessment six to eight weeks after the final intervention visit. At each intervention visit, children in the treatment arms received directly observed study drugs. At the first intervention visit and the outcome visit, finger-prick blood samples were collected for haemoglobin measurement and PCR-based parasite detection. Household-level data on socioeconomic status, insecticide-treated net ownership, and education were collected from caregivers at enrolment. Clinical malaria episodes occurring between enrolment and the outcome visit were captured through passive case detection at the local health centre and participant health passport review. The dataset shared here is a minimal analytic dataset containing the variables used in the primary analysis. It is structured at the visit level, with one row per participant per visit, covering up to four visits (three intervention visits and one outcome visit).
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Two Intermittent Preventive Treatment Regimens against No-Treatment Control for Malaria Prevention in Malawian School Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine and Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine+Chloroquine

evidence_items.summary: This analysis examines whether evolved resistance profiles identify collateral susceptibility advantages relevant to antibiotic treatment design. Secondary experimental data published in 2019 cover 60 Escherichia coli lineages assessed after ten passages under cefotaxime selection. Parental concentration normalization, multiple linear regression with HC3 standard errors, Spearman correlations and individual omission analyses distinguish conditional associations from ancestral susceptibility changes. A doubling of cefotaxime resistance is associated with an 8.7% lower fitted geometric mean gentamicin concentration, with a 95% confidence interval indicating reductions from 3.8% to 13.3%. The cefotaxime coefficient remains negative across all individual omission analyses. Replacing source estimates with technical medians leaves results unchanged. Nevertheless, only one lineage exhibits a gentamicin concentration below the parental benchmark. The evidence therefore distinguishes relative susceptibility gradients among evolved lineages from restored ancestral sensitivity. This distinction refines evolutionary trade off interpretation without attributing associations to unmeasured biological mechanisms. For antimicrobial research, the findings support evaluating conditional resistance relationships alongside ancestral benchmarks before prioritizing drug sequences or combinations for experimental validation.
evidence_items.title: ASSESSING ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN EVOLVED BETA LACTAM RESISTANCE PROFILES AND GENTAMICIN SUSCEPTIBILITY IN ESCHERICHIA COLI LINEAGES

evidence_items.summary: This analysis examines whether corresponding multilingual stereotype benchmarks provide comparable textual conditions for international language technology evaluation. Using 3,353 complete English and French sentence pairs from a benchmark extension released in 2022, descriptive comparisons assess normalized character length asymmetry across languages, social categories and stereotype orientations. Among 1,676 matched identifiers, mean asymmetry is 0.03737 in English and 0.02869 in French, yielding a mean paired difference of negative 0.00868. However, French asymmetry exceeds English asymmetry in 43.74 percent of matched pairs, revealing heterogeneity beneath the aggregate ordering. Restricting comparisons to 1,535 identifiers with identical category annotations preserves the lower French mean. Category rankings differ across languages, while aggregate orientation comparisons reverse direction. These patterns distinguish correspondence between records from agreement in classification and similarity in sentence construction. The contribution refines benchmark comparability as a measurable, multidimensional consideration rather than an assumed consequence of translation. For multilingual evaluation governance, the findings support retaining correspondence identifiers, documenting annotation differences and reporting matched distributions alongside language specific summaries.
evidence_items.title: LANGUAGE AND SOCIAL BIAS CATEGORIES ASSOCIATED WITH SENTENCE LENGTH ASYMMETRY IN MULTILINGUAL STEREOTYPE EVALUATION BENCHMARKS

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern society including animal genetics and breeding which is essential for meeting global nutritional needs in supplying milk, meat, and eggs among the most complete sources of protein and micronutrients. Although animal breeding has a long history of using data-driven prediction methods, the application of modern AI approaches remains at a relatively early stage and shows substantial potential for wide-ranging applications in animal genetics and breeding. This study aims to review the current use of AI tools in livestock species across three major applications of high interest: AI-assisted phenotyping, AI-enabled dissection of complex-trait biology (focusing on AI-assisted GWAS and AI-for-omics), and AI-assisted genomic prediction. In addition, we discussed emerging methods and tools developed in human genetics that are not yet widely adopted in farm animals but may offer translational potential for future livestock studies. Looking ahead, AI breakthroughs in livestock genetics and breeding are likely to be driven by increases in data scale and resolution, enhanced computational capacities, standardized data infrastructure and benchmarking, and systematic method development and validation. From a livestock genetic improvement perspective, the key value of AI will lie in integrating AI-generated inputs, including improved phenotyping and biological insights, into practical breeding decisions through statistical modeling.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for livestock genetics and breeding

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly changing the landscape of gastroenterology by improving disease detection, diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostication, and clinical decision-making. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, and multimodal data integration have facilitated the development of accurate diagnostic and predictive algorithms for a wide spectrum of gastrointestinal and hepatopancreatobiliary diseases. In upper gastrointestinal diseases, AI has enhanced the detection and characterization of gastroesophageal reflux disease, Barrett’s esophagus, esophageal cancer, gastric neoplasia, and gastroesophageal varices. The use of AI in capsule endoscopy has facilitated small intestinal mucosal lesion detection and reduced reading time. Computer-aided detection and diagnosis systems have improved adenoma detection and polyp characterization in colorectal diseases, while AI is increasingly being applied to molecular profiling and prognostic modeling in colorectal cancer. In inflammatory bowel disease, AI facilitates more objective endoscopic and histologic assessment, as well as prediction of disease outcome and treatment response. Promising AI-based radiomics, digital pathology, biomarker discovery, and risk prediction models have been emerging in pancreatic, biliary, and liver diseases. Large language models and multimodal AI may further enable integration of heterogeneous information and support personalized decision-making. Computer-aided quality assessment represents an emerging application for standardizing procedural quality in endoscopy. Several AI-assisted platforms have received regulatory approval with ongoing integration into clinical practice. However, limited external validation, population and device-related heterogeneity, dataset bias, interpretability, workflow integration, and uncertain cost-effectiveness remain important barriers to generalizability and clinical adoption.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in gastroenterology practice: Current perspectives and emerging prospects

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the field of gastroenterology, providing new ways to diagnose, risk-stratify, and therapeutically manage a wide variety of gastrointestinal diseases. Machine learning and deep learning algorithms are among the AI-based models that have shown promise in non-invasive fibrosis assessment, early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma, prediction of disease severity in pancreatitis, and polyp detection during endoscopy. We searched major databases, including Scopus, EMBASE, PubMed/MEDLINE, and Web of Science, and analyzed current studies on AI in gastroenterology. The integration of AI with imaging modalities, electronic health records, and multi-omics data has led to greater diagnostic accuracy and individualized patient care. Yet, these advances have not addressed issues of data quality, algorithm generalizability, interpretability, and clinical integration. Future research will focus on prospective validation of AI, regulation, and implementation to maximize the clinical utility of AI in digestive diseases. AI has the potential to improve patient outcomes, enable personalized medicine, and optimize the overall efficiency of processes involved in gastroenterological care. In this paper, recent literature concerning the use of AI in gastrointestinal endoscopy and the treatment of various gastrointestinal disorders, such as liver and pancreatic diseases, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancies, was reviewed.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in digestive diseases: Current evidence and clinical perspectives

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be used by students to learn and solve math problems in seconds. However, the learning habits of Indonesian students tend to rarely involve the ability to think at a higher level. This study aims to analyze students’ critical thinking dispositions in AI-assisted learning based on factor structure and experience category mapping. This study involved students (N=99) at a junior high school in the city of Jambi, Indonesia, so the findings are exploratory and limited to the context of the school. Data were collected using a perception-scale questionnaire on AI-assisted math learning behavior, analyzed with Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Rasch analysis. The findings identified five factors as the basis of student response patterns associated with critical thinking dispositions in AI-assisted math learning—reflective monitoring, internalization of understanding, passive dependence on AI, critical evaluation, and cognitive load. The mapping results showed that most students rarely experienced cognitive overload or internal understanding. At the same time, only a small percentage routinely performed reflective monitoring and critical evaluation, accompanied by early indications of a tendency toward passive dependence on AI. However, these findings need to be interpreted conservatively given the relatively low reliability of these factors. Based on the difficulty level of item approval in Rasch’s analysis, student responses showed inconsistencies in several factors, which could indicate a risk of cognitive passivity; However, these findings reflect the overall difficulty level in item approval, not a direct classification of each student’s level of disposition. This is especially true of the passive dependency factor on AI, which has the lowest reliability among the five factors.
evidence_items.title: Students’ Critical Thinking Disposition in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mathematics Learning

Two classes followed a standard single-draft workflow; two revised their reading summaries on smartphones with Gemini 2.5 Pro before teacher marking. evidence_items.summary: Breast cancer is among the leading causes of cancer-related mortality in women worldwide. Early detection through mammograms can significantly increase the chances of survival. However, mammogram classification remains a challenging task due to subtle lesion features and variations across patients and datasets. Therefore, classic convolutional neural networks (CNNs) fail to generalize across different mammographic sources. In this paper, the proposed method is a hybrid Vision transformer and CNN ensemble learning framework integrated with feature fusion for robust cross-dataset classification. The framework consists of a dual-branch feature extractor that fuses a deep CNN for local texture extraction with a Vision transformer (ViT) for global context extraction, while simultaneously extracting handcrafted radiomics features (shape, intensity, and texture) from the lesion region. Then, deep and radiomics features are fused and fed to a stacked ensemble learning classifier comprising XGBoost, SVM, and LightGBM, with a logistic regression meta-learner for performance optimization and overfitting reduction.The proposed framework is also robust across datasets, achieving AUC scores of 0.938 and 0.925 when trained on CBIS-DDSM and evaluated on INbreast, and when trained on INbreast and evaluated on CBIS-DDSM, respectively, demonstrating strong generalization under domain-shift conditions. The proposed fusion model demonstrates promising potential for robust and reliable use in clinics. On the combined CBIS-DDSM and INbreast dataset, the proposed framework achieved an average accuracy of 96.3%, average MCC of 0.928, and average AUC of 0.983 across the five validation folds. The best-performing fold achieved a peak accuracy of 96.9%, peak MCC of 0.936, and peak AUC of 0.986.
evidence_items.title: A hybrid vision transformer–CNN ensemble with radiomics fusion for robust cross-dataset breast cancer detection in mammography

evidence_items.summary: Code, run files and analysis scripts for the study "When does a concept graph help a neural knowledge tracer?" The probe tracer FKG-KT reads a fuzzy prerequisite graph through refined concept embeddings and a prerequisite-biased attention read-out and is compared with an empty-graph control on ten public corpora at 5%, 10%, 25% and 100% of the training learners. Version 3.3.0 adds controls that read the concept graph only in the embedding refinement or only in the attention bias of the probe (support and Erdős–Rényi graphs, 128 runs under the update budget at 10%), and kt/src/r33 analyse.py with kt/results r6/r33 results.json: the rise of the graph gain from 5% to 10% under both training budgets on the same units, updates to the selected checkpoint by corpus, per-corpus budget effects, and graph controls pooled over both budgets with a budget fixed effect (the tables of Supplementary Section S8). Version 3.2.0 added the degree-feature control with a zero-initialised map, the Erdős–Rényi control on every subsample of the epoch-budget control runs and on all ten corpora under the update budget, the degree-preserving control on all update-budget subsamples, comparisons of the graph controls pooled over both training budgets, and run counts by set. Earlier contents: learning-curve runs (kt/r2), recency and degree-preserving controls (kt/runs r5), training budget counted in updates and further graph controls (kt/runs r6). No dataset is redistributed; kt/README.md lists the public sources and the preprocessing commands.
evidence_items.title: When does a concept graph help a neural knowledge tracer? A controlled learning-curve study with empty-graph and random-graph controls on ten corpora (code and run files)

evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091 Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092 Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator.
evidence_items.title: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091  Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092  Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator. F093  Nanorobotic Collective Pheromone Communication At The Limit — Explores prospective chemical-trail or signal-mediated coordination with collision exposure as a primary outcome. Hidden actuator saturation and a matched-actuation single-agent baseline challenge claims that signaling, rather than redundancy or imposed motion, caused the improvement. F094  Microscale Robot Collective Collision Avoidance Control At The Limit — Examines collision-safe motion while monitoring spatial coverage, recovery time and communication burden. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether apparent avoidance depends on erroneous common position estimates; safety-boundary crossings trigger rejection. F095  Nanorobotic Collective Energy Allocation At The Limit — Tests dynamic allocation of limited energy across agents during dropout and recovery. Hidden agent-loss clusters challenge energy accounting and recovery-time claims against fixed rules with an equal energy budget; persistent unsafe confidence is a stop condition. F096  Microrobotic Distributed Mission Planning At The Limit — Studies task planning without a central controller using communication load, work-per-task and selective abstention as prospective metrics. Hidden network partitions expose plans that depend on unavailable messages, while a matched-actuation single-agent system tests whether coordination adds value. F097  Nanorobotic Collective Localization Uncertainty At The Limit — Tests whether robots can act safely when position confidence is uncertain or neighbors provide deceptive state information. Energy per accepted task, abstention and completion are checked against a full-state centralized benchmark; unrecognized safety-boundary crossings invalidate the claim. F098  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Topology Control At The Limit — Examines when changing neighbor connections should trigger reconfiguration or justified refusal to proceed. Hidden actuator saturation challenges topology decisions; fixed energy-matched rules and independent task and consensus measurements distinguish adaptive control from misleading internal agreement. F099  Nanorobotic Collective Fault Isolation At The Limit — Investigates recognition and containment of malfunctioning agents without allowing errors to propagate across the swarm. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether fault labels confuse a common sensor defect with separate robot failures; recovery to a known-safe state is mandatory. F100  Microrobotic Collective Mission Handoff At The Limit — Designs a traceable transfer of task state and authority across agents after concealed dropout clusters. The study checks consensus error, collisions and coverage against centralized full-state control; an apparently successful handoff is rejected if safety invariants are violated. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All ten volumes are prospective, nonclinical research-design working editions for traceable materials, authorized ex-vivo systems, synthetic phantoms and bench-scale microfluidic tests. Proposed comparisons require preregistered budgets, blinded perturbations, independent reference measurements, complete negative-trial denominators and explicit safety stops. No new experimental results, validated in-body autonomy or clinical benefit are claimed. Mathematical derivations, physical unit consistency, claim-level DOI linkage and substantive causal novelty still require specialist review; the automatic Gate-text distinctness audit cannot replace it. It accompanies the following manuscript, which is currently under review: A. A. Alsamman and N. B. Al Dabagh, “RegenStega: A Secure Covert Communication System via Training-Free DWT-Based Steganography Using AI-Generated Images,” submitted to IEEE Access, 2026. Content. All images are 16-bit TIFF files, 1,000 per folder. There are three kinds: Cover images: generated by the system’s cover pipeline. Each prompt is built from one of 100 subjects (45 landscapes and 55 macro scenes) with a randomly selected opener, expanded by Llama-3.1-8B through the Groq API, and appended with a secret token. The prompt is then rendered by the diffusion model and keyed-dithered. “SecretTokens 100 Sub” in the folder names refers to this setup: secret tokens with 100 subjects. Stego images: covers with an embedded payload at embedding strength (ES) 0.1, 6, or 8. Approximate covers: covers regenerated by an informed attacker using a prompt stealer (20 timesteps), used as the warden’s cover reference in steganalysis.
