evidence_items.summary: This analysis examines whether assessments of language model resilience depend on decoding configuration and measurement scale, addressing international debates on recursive synthetic training. A descriptive reanalysis uses 24 published WikiText 2 perplexity endpoints from 2025, forming 12 matched configurations across GPT 2, SmolLM2, and six decoding strategies at generations zero and nine. Paired absolute changes, percentage changes, ratios, means, and medians reveal deterioration in every configuration, with percentage increases ranging from 10.24% to 513.83%. SmolLM2 records a smaller mean absolute increase than GPT 2, but a larger mean percentage increase, while its median deterioration remains lower on both scales. Different baseline denominators and concentrated deterioration under greedy decoding and beam search explain this aggregation reversal. Sampling strategy rankings also differ between models, and temperature sampling reverses their comparison across measurement scales. These findings qualify interpretations of resilience as an intrinsic model property by demonstrating configuration and measurement dependence. International benchmarking should report matched baselines, absolute and proportional changes, and distributional summaries to support transparent configuration selection.

evidence_items.summary: Recommender systems are increasingly expected to combine interaction histories with language. In many cases, a user's next choice may depend on a temporary situation---such as their current mood, plans, or constraints---that is not visible in past behavior. Existing benchmarks, however, mostly evaluate average next-item accuracy, broad instruction following, or content understanding; they do not isolate recommendation episodes in which external situation context is plausibly needed. We introduce e OffTrail, a benchmark built on MovieLens for situation-aware recommendation beyond interaction histories. It contains two complementary families of episodes: observed off-trail choices that are real user transitions but hard to infer from prior behavior, and neighbor-supported alternative continuations that represent plausible futures for similar recent histories. Each episode packages a user history, target item, item metadata, and generated life-situation context. The contexts are treated as plausible external circumstances rather than ground-truth user intentions. OffTrail supports controlled evaluation across sequential models, LLM-based recommenders, and hybrid systems by keeping the recommendation episode fixed while exposing or withholding the situation context. By releasing the artifacts, construction pipeline, and evaluation protocol, OffTrail provides a reproducible testbed for studying whether natural-language context improves ranking when interaction history is weak or ambiguous. Benchmark: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20560655.

evidence_items.summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are evaluated on increasingly large and diverse benchmark suites, running an LLM on the entire benchmark incurs substantial costs. We study efficient LLM evaluation, where the goal is to accurately estimate full-benchmark performance by adaptively querying only a small subset of prompts. The key challenge is that selected prompts should be informative for the target model while remaining representative of diverse response patterns in the benchmark. To address this, we adopt a posterior-aware Bayesian perspective: historical response data are used to characterize complex prompt--model behaviors, and the resulting posterior information guides adaptive prompt selection under a limited budget. Specifically, we develop a variational Gaussian Process Item Response Theory (VGP-IRT) model, which leverages item-specific Gaussian process response functions to flexibly capture nonlinear prompt--model interactions beyond restrictive parametric response curves. Based on prompt features and predictive information derived from the VGP-IRT posterior, we further construct group-balanced candidate pools within local routed subspaces for adaptive selection. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate improved score estimation through our method, with the strongest gains in the low-to-moderate budget regime.
evidence_items.title: Efficient LLM Benchmark Evaluation with Bayesian Item Response and Routed Subspace Selection

evidence_items.summary: Illicit account detection in blockchain-based cryptocurrencies seeks to pinpoint anomalies within large-scale, decentralized transaction networks, figuring prominently in financial risk control systems. Existing efforts typically formulate transaction networks as directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to capture topological information under limited supervision. Despite their decent performance, supervised GNN models are capped by data scarcity and structural noise, with the former arising from the lack of annotated data and the latter stemming from malicious actors forging deceptive connections. In light of these, we in this paper propose LABRA, a novel label-free graph modeling for detecting illicit accounts in blockchain transaction networks. Operating in an unsupervised manner, LABRA. The source code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/bicheng1225/LABRA. leverages a discrepancy-aware graph encoder to produce discriminative node representations, and subsequently employs an anchor-guided scoring mechanism to designate anchor nodes for anomaly detection. Furthermore, a tailor-made message-passing scheme is introduced to mitigate structural noise, which captures atypical financial flows within a transaction graph while attenuating the feature-smoothing effect caused by high-degree nodes. Extensive experiments on several cryptocurrency benchmark datasets demonstrate the feasibility and superiority of our method over several cutting-edge methods. To our knowledge, LABRA is among the first training-free frameworks for illicit account detection in cryptocurrencies, delivering robust performance without resorting to any learnable parameters or iterative model optimization.
evidence_items.title: LABRA: A Label-free Graph Neural Framework for Illicit Account Detection in Large-scale Blockchain Transaction Networks

evidence_items.summary: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) has created demand for faster responses and lower costs. Semantic caching, reusing semantically similar requests via their embeddings, addresses this need but breaks classic cache assumptions and raises new challenges. In this paper, we explore offline policies for semantic caching, proving that implementing an optimal offline policy is NP-hard, and propose several polynomial-time heuristics. We also present online semantic aware cache policies that combine recency, frequency, and locality. Evaluations on diverse datasets show that while frequency based policies are strong baselines, our novel variant improves semantic accuracy. Our findings reveal effective strategies for current systems and highlight substantial headroom for future innovation. All of our code is open source.
evidence_items.title: Semantic Caching: From Exact Hits to Close Enough

evidence_items.summary: Instruction-tuning corpora are commonly constructed by pairing fixed input--output examples with static or randomly sampled instruction templates. However, for clinical reasoning, different candidate instruction templates may emphasize different learning signals, including diagnostic conclusion, evidence synthesis, and explanation structure. This paper studies instruction-template assignment as a training-time corpus-construction problem: given fixed clinical input--output examples and a pool of candidate templates, can performance feedback guide template assignment during fine-tuning? This paper presents Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment (PAITA), a framework that uses validation feedback to assign instruction templates to fixed clinical input--output examples during fine-tuning. Unlike static assignment, which repeatedly applies one template, or random assignment, which samples templates without regard to observed performance, PAITA balances exploration of alternative templates with exploitation of templates associated with stronger validation feedback. We evaluate PAITA primarily using LLaMA-3-8B and further examine instruction-template assignment across additional model settings using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and BioMedLM-2.7B on the Clinical Reasoning task; Clinical Diagnosis and Medical QA serve as auxiliary evaluations. PAITA improves clinical reasoning conclusion accuracy over static assignment (0.397 vs. 0.372; +2.5 percentage points, p=0.001) and random template assignment (0.397 vs. 0.383; +1.4 percentage points, p=0.044), with additional gains in several reasoning-quality metrics. Auxiliary results and template-assignment analyses further suggest that performance-adaptive assignment can provide benefits beyond instruction diversity alone. These findings support instruction-template assignment as an important design variable in supervised instruction tuning of clinical LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for tabular data analysis, but their performance often does not transfer from standard Table QA benchmarks to real-world settings, where tables are typically non-relational, with hierarchical headers, merged cells, inconsistent units, noise, and implicit cross-table dependencies. We present \name, an interactive system built on top of \gradino for generating verifiable non-relational multi-table QA benchmarks and evaluating LLMs on them. Users configure domain-specific benchmark settings, inspect and refine generated instances, and compare API-based or locally deployed models through live leaderboards and error analysis views. Across procurement, failure diagnosis, and benchmark curation scenarios, \name provides an end-to-end workflow for deployment-oriented assessment of LLMs on real-world tabular data.

evidence_items.summary: Graph pre-training and prompt learning paradigm have recently achieved remarkable success by improving the adaptability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and alleviating the reliance on large task-specific datasets. However, we find that this paradigm inadvertently increases the vulnerability of GNNs to model extraction, a type of attack in which adversaries replicate a target model by observing its outputs. A particularly challenging and realistic scenario arises when attackers cannot access any target training data, known as the data-free setting. To address this, we propose GrAP3, a novel framework that enables the reconstruction of high-fidelity surrogate models under this resource-constrained condition. We first conduct a formal risk analysis to examine the impact of pre-training and prompt learning on model extractability. The analysis shows that these paradigms jointly tighten the theoretical upper bound of surrogate–target discrepancy. They are achieved by reducing representation, classification, and distribution gaps, which is the barrier to model extraction. Building on this insight, GrAP3 generates structurally coherent and label-aware query graphs using a multi-class contextual stochastic block model. It further integrates a learnable prompt subgraph whose embeddings and structural connections are jointly optimized with a pre-trained surrogate through alternating optimization. Comprehensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior model extraction performance of GrAP3 without any access to the training data.
evidence_items.title: GrAP³: A Data-free Model Extraction Attack Framework under Graph Pre-training and Prompt Learning Paradigm

evidence_items.summary: The discovery of first integrals is of profound scientific significance for understanding physical conservation laws in dynamical systems. However, existing symbolic computation systems and Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with this task due to the scarcity of high-quality training data and the reliance on mathematical intuition for finding solutions. This paper introduces FISolver, an LLM-based solver designed to bridge this gap. First, we propose a novel ''Backward Generation'' algorithm that systematically constructs large-scale datasets of (differential equations, first integrals) pairs by deriving equations from sampled integrals, effectively overcoming the data scarcity bottleneck. Second, we perform supervised fine-tuning on a compact mathematical model and further enhance its capabilities using reinforcement learning with a Levenshtein Distance-based shaped reward function. Additionally, we introduce data synthesis and blending techniques that enable effective adaptation to specific hard instances with sparse examples. Experiments demonstrate that FISolver, with significantly lower computational cost, substantially outperforms larger mathematical LLMs and commercial solvers like Mathematica on complex benchmarks, establishing a new data-driven paradigm for automated mathematical discovery.
evidence_items.title: FISolver: Data-Driven Discovery of First Integrals via Backward Generation and Guided Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract For a variety of applications, the flow of fluid that is induced by rotating disks has become a problem that is worth addressing. Nanofluids that flow over rotating disks display a complicated relationship between their behaviour, the viscosity of their fluid, and the inertia of their fluid properties. The applications including polymer-based treatment, reactive systems, accelerators, storage equipment, lubricating processes, nuclear reactors, a MHD-based generators, and microfluidics all require improvements in heat transfer and performance. These improvements are necessary. Within the scope of this investigation, an LMANN-numerical method is utilized to investigate a magnetised Boger nanofluid that undergoes heating by ohmic current while rotating. The Levenberg–Marquardt Artificial Neural Network(LMANN), in conjunction via a back propagation based artificial neural network, is utilised in order for investigating the steady, incompressible movement of a Boger nanofluid. The investigation focuses on mathematical modelling and characterization of Boger nanofluids flowing with a spinning disc. The bvp4c algorithm is utilized in order to acquire numerical solutions corresponding to the reduced equations. The bvp4c solver is then utilised in order to simulate the numerical behaviour that has been observed. The research investigates the impacts of relevant parameters on profiles of temperature, concentration, velocity, and motile microbes, as well as the Nusselt number and the Sherwood number. An artificial neural network that is driven by the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm includes the additional feature of being able to simulate and forecast flow behaviour in an extremely efficient manner. A training dataset consisting of 70 % is followed by a validation dataset consisting of 15 % and a testing dataset including 15 %. Simulations using numerical data and the Levenberg–Marquardt Artificial Neural Network(LMANN) approach are in good agreement. For the purpose of evaluating and validating Levenberg–Marquardt Artificial Neural Network (LMANN) performance with relation to variations in physical parameters, the study made use of regression techniques, training process procedure (MSE) analyzing graphs. The utilization of this hybrid framework allows for the efficient management of heat management systems in industrial applications. When it comes to developing accurate predictive models, this study will be helpful to scientists and engineers who are interested in understanding flow characteristics and how they behave. Increasing the magnetic parameter from M = 0.5 to M = 2.0 changes the skin friction coefficient by 51.7 %, reflecting the retarding Lorentz force on the flow; increasing the Brownian-motion parameter from Nb = 0.5 to Nb = 2.0 reduces the local Nusselt number by 66.4 %, as enhanced nanoparticle motion raises the near-wall fluid temperature and weakens the wall temperature gradient. These results are relevant to the design of rotating-disk contactors, MHD-based pumps and generators, and spinning-disk bioreactors, where the present LMANN surrogate offers a computationally inexpensive route to predicting heat- and mass-transfer rates across operating conditions without repeatedly re-solving the full boundary value problem.
evidence_items.title: Numerical investigation of magnetized Boger nanofluids with ohmic heating under permeable revolving disk: LMANN approach

evidence_items.summary: Certified PINN surrogate inference-latency benchmark — preregistered T4 timing dataset, audit runner, and correction note Companion dataset for the manuscript "How Fast Is a Certified PINN Surrogate? A Preregistered Latency Benchmark for Spillway Cavitation Screening" (companion manuscript, 2026). What was measured A frozen, preregistered timing protocol (1 cold start + 10 discarded warm-ups + 100 timed replications per arm, CPU-only, pinned 4-thread platform) measured the inference latency of a certified physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate, identified by SHA-256 fingerprints, on the certified 42,920-cell ogee-crested spillway mesh. The 222-call campaign ran as a single PUBLICATION-mode session on 2026-09-30 (elapsed 29.15–29.82 s; see the correction note below for the audit of the recorded second-resolution window stamps). Two inference shapes were timed: batch-1 arm — one grid point per call (per-point latency); full-grid arm — all 42,920 certified cell coordinates per call (whole-field latency). Headline frozen results (reproducible from the raw CSVs below): single-point median 0.0515 ms ; full-field median 263.4802 ms ; throughput 13,663.265 certified fields/hour at the median and 11,953.5 fields/hour under the p90 bound; vectorized batching gain 8.39x ; cold-start contrasts 4.99x (batch-1) and 0.82x (full grid); audited CFD baseline 5,838.72 s per certified field -> field-level speed-up 22,160x on three mutually consistent bases. Version 1.1 — independent audit and correction note Version 1.1 adds CORRECTION NOTE.md / CORRECTION NOTE.pdf (independent audit of 2026-11-06: checksum re-verification 8/8, recomputation of every reported statistic from the deposited CSVs, cross-checking of every fingerprint quoted by the manuscript) and MANIFEST SHA256.txt . Findings: F-T4-1 (closed). The recorded timing-window endpoints are second-resolution truncated and internally inconsistent.

evidence_items.summary: Schema matching (SM) is a critical step in data integration pipelines and serves as a foundation for tasks such as Table Search and Entity Matching. However, applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to SM is prohibitively expensive due to the task's inherent quadratic complexity, which hinders scalable and cost-efficient deployment. In this paper, we investigate two SM scenarios: the most common instance-based scenario where headers and their values are available, and the metadata-based scenario where only metadata is provided (e.g., due to privacy constraints). We propose Fermat, a unified framework designed to address both scenarios effectively. Fermat incorporates a Small Language Model (SLM)-based filtering strategy that significantly reduce the computational overhead of applying LLMs to SM. We also introduce a column synthesis workflow that enables a fully unsupervised solution, effectively mitigating the scarcity of ground-truth data. Additionally, we implement a specialized loss function with hard column mining to counteract the biases of the filter model on imbalanced data, ensuring improved recall of positive candidates. Finally, we conduct comprehensive reproduction and evaluation of recent schema matching methods on both metadata-based and instance-based datasets, providing insights into their generalizability across diverse scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Filter-then-match: Holistic Schema Matching via Small Language Model Filtering and Large Language Model Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Romanian, like most non-English languages, has no dedicated safety benchmark for large language models—existing multilingual efforts (XSafety, M-ALERT) cover 10 and 5 languages respectively, none of them Romanian, and derive their non-English prompts by translating a source set written for other languages, which leaves culturally-specific risks like anti-Roma discrimination and Romanian profanity patterns with no source to translate from. We introduce RoSafetyBench, a Romanian-first benchmark of nearly a thousand prompts across six dimensions (toxicity, bias, hallucination, jailbreak, over-refusal, cross-lingual transfer), and evaluate 17 open-weight models (0.5B–27B) plus three frontier APIs (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro). Methodologically we contribute a dual-judge refusal-scoring protocol pairing a primary LLM judge with a second-rater from a different vendor (κ = 0.79 over 1663 responses), with bootstrap intervals on every agreement statistic. Two findings follow that the keyword protocols of prior multilingual benchmarks could not have produced: over-refusal of benign Romanian prompts spanning 0–53% and largely missed by keyword detection (κ = 0.11 over all 2000 judgments); and a positive size–safety association within Gemma 3, Qwen 3, and Qwen 2.5 (with a small 14B dip), reversing an apparent inverse-scaling artefact. Independently of the scoring protocol, Romanian factual accuracy stays below 32% across the entire open-weight range. Comparing English and Romanian within prompt pairs rather than between marginal rates, the transfer gap reverses sign by category—English refuses more on harmful intent, Romanian more on bias probes—so the near-zero aggregate reported by unpaired analyses averages two opposite panel-level differences away. A scoped comparison with a 40-prompt machine-translated HarmBench control finds none of our prespecified Romanian-specific risk markers and much higher refusal than on the separate native-toxicity set; because the sets are not content-matched, this is descriptive rather than a causal translation effect. We release the benchmark, harness, all model responses, and the complete categorical judge-label table on Zenodo and Hugging Face (Section 9).
evidence_items.title: RoSafetyBench: A Culturally-Native Safety Benchmark for Romanian Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have been introduced into recommender systems to enhance semantic understanding. However, LLM-generated user interests often consist of discrete phrases containing noise, redundancy, and structural instability. Moreover, the semantic gap between generated interests and collaborative recommendation objectives limits effective user--item matching. To address these challenges, we propose LLM-GRec, a robust graph-based recommendation framework enhanced by granular-ball computing. First, historical interactions and collaborative candidate items guide LLMs to generate recommendation-oriented user interests. Second, granular-ball computing organizes fine-grained interests into stable, multi-granularity interest anchors. Third, a unified graph integrates users, items, knowledge entities, and interest anchors for graph representation learning. An anchor alignment constraint encourages semantic consistency between user and item representations in the shared interest space. Furthermore, a quality-aware interest masking and reconstruction mechanism reduces the influence of noisy interests during graph propagation and recommendation learning. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that LLM-GRec outperforms existing recommendation methods on most evaluation metrics, with particularly notable improvements in sparse scenarios. The proposed framework effectively integrates semantic interest modeling, structured representation learning, and robust graph recommendation. Source code is available at https://github.com/shenjiale534/LLM-GRec.
evidence_items.title: LLM-GRec: Large Language Model Enhanced Graph Recommendation via Granular-Ball Computing

evidence_items.summary: High-quality data is essential for effective decision-making, data analytics, and training machine learning models. Numerous data cleaning tools and systems have been proposed in both academia and industry. Several recent tools utilize Large Language Models (LLMs), but most rely entirely on their unverified reasoning capabilities, struggling to effectively handle dirty datasets with heterogeneous error types. In this demo, we describe MADClean, a tabular data cleaning system that uses statistical profiling and a multi-agent architecture to achieve strong performance in several data cleaning tasks. MADClean uses dedicated LLM agents to recommend cleaning operations, generate executable source code, and iteratively verify and improve its outputs. We show that MADClean reliably handles dirty data across three real-world data cleaning scenarios, and scales to datasets with hundreds of thousands of rows in our evaluation.
evidence_items.title: MADClean: Statistical Profiling and Multi-Agent Large Language Model Reasoning for Automatic Data Cleaning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs), especially recent reasoning-oriented models trained with reinforcement learning, achieve near-saturating accuracy on many reasoning benchmarks. However, it remains unclear whether these models truly reason over semantic structure or rely on superficial symbol patterns and familiar language forms. This issue is increasingly critical in the agent era, where reasoning systems must remain reliable under changing representations. We introduce FLoRE, a controllable evaluation benchmark for diagnosing LLM reasoning robustness and effectiveness using formal languages. By isolating reasoning from world knowledge, formal languages enable direct evaluation of structural reasoning with machine-verifiable ground truth. We defines two tasks: Formal Language Recognition and Grammar Induction and construct 25.5k data instances. Evaluating diverse reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs, we identify two universal failure modes. First, models exhibit severe symbol-binding fragility: changing symbolic representations while preserving semantics causes large drops on positive instances but increases accuracy on negative instances, revealing a strong default rejection bias under unfamiliar symbols. Second, many reasoning-oriented local LLMs show negation non-termination during grammar induction, failing to terminate reasoning on negative instances and instead exhausting large portions of the context window. Our results show that current LLM reasoning remains strongly dependent on surface symbol priors and lacks robust semantic invariance and termination stability. FLoRE provides a unified framework for systematically evaluating these properties in controllable formal-language settings. Code and data files are available at https://github.com/HoganZinger/FLoRE
evidence_items.title: FLoRE: A Formal Language Benchmark for Robustness and Effectiveness Evaluation of LLM Reasoning

organizations: Kyung Hee University, Yongin, Republic of Korea
evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models achieve remarkable results on various visual question-answering benchmarks. However, they struggle with ambiguous questions where the target entity is unclear. To address this issue, it is essential to construct a benchmark dataset that pairs ambiguous questions with entity-grounded clarifying sub-questions. This paper presents GQA-Q2Q, a large-scale dataset for resolving entity ambiguity in visual question answering via entity-grounded clarifying sub-questions. GQA-Q2Q is constructed through a template-assisted human annotation pipeline. The pipeline generates candidate sub-questions from attribute, relation, and position templates and asks human annotators to verify, select, or revise them. As a result, GQA-Q2Q contains 46,554 human-verified clarifying sub-questions with target-instance grounding. This paper also presents a proposed ambiguity-resolving VQA model that leverages the generated sub-questions before producing final answers. The experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms zero-shot and ambiguity-resolving vision-language baselines. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/gminipark/GQA-Q2Q.git.
evidence_items.title: GQA-Q2Q: A Large-scale Benchmark for Entity Ambiguity Resolution in Visual Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show exceptional skills in a wide range of tasks, with their ability in lateral thinking standing out as a particularly intriguing area. Lateral thinking in LLMs allows them to understand deeper or suggested meanings from the context, which is essential for making sense of complex scenarios, especially in puzzle-solving games. To delve deeper into and improve the lateral thinking capabilities of LLMs in the realm of puzzle-solving, we introduce the ''Lateral Thinking Puzzles'' and construct the accompanying dataset. Our novel Puzzle Verse framework aims to enhance LLMs' lateral thinking in puzzle-solving games. Complementing this, we propose a creativity metric to ensure comprehensive evaluations. Experiments show that the selected LLMs, after being trained with Puzzle Verse, have an average improvement of 93.1% compared to their performance before Puzzle Verse training among all metrics. We also validate the robustness of Puzzle Verse that trained LLMs perform better in other reasoning tasks.
evidence_items.title: Do Large Language Models have Lateral Thinking in Puzzle-Solving Games?

evidence_items.summary: Intelligent tutoring systems predict student achievement with increasing accuracy, yet they do not model the feedback-conditioned learning states that sustain engagement and guide intervention. A central obstacle is scale: large educational datasets lack validated motivation annotations, while using large language models (LLMs) to infer such labels risks creating a self-referential supervision loop. We propose FIA-LLM, a dual-stream framework that jointly produces a learning-state surrogate grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), a next-item achievement prediction, an SDT dimension label, and a structured diagnostic explanation. FIA-LLM integrates three components. Confidence-Aware Robust Distillation (CARD) combines 2,000 human teacher annotations with LLM pseudo-labels validated against human judgments (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textrm{ICC}=0.83$$\end{document}), using confidence-weighted training to suppress noisy supervision. Feedback Intervention Attention (FIA), a multi-head feedback-as-Query cross-attention mechanism, fuses feedback proxies with behavioral histories. Joint Structured Decoding (JSD) produces four outputs from shared representations through a motivation-related surrogate head, an achievement head, an SDT dimension head, and a diagnostic generation module. On frozen human expert test sets, FIA-LLM reduces macro-average RMSE by 8.6% against the strongest baseline and improves macro-average AUC by 1.2 percentage points (paired across seeds, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$p<0.01$$\end{document}). Gains persist under ASSISTments platform-derived hint/scaffold proxies, and human teacher blind review provides external evidence of diagnostic quality.
evidence_items.title: FIA-LLM: feedback conditioned learning state estimation with large language models

evidence_items.summary: We present RadMultiBench, a multimodal benchmark of 6,148 medical images paired with expert radiological impressions across five categories—Breast Cancer, Lung Benign, Lung Malignant, Pneumonia, and Tuberculosis—targeting two core clinical tasks: automated report generation and disease classification. To enable reliable, repeatable experimentation, we provide a reproducible pipeline for data ingestion, de-identification, split management, and standardized reporting of text and classification metrics, facilitating dataset versioning and continuous benchmark testing. We compare three architectures: (1) a classical CNN-RNN with Bahdanau attention (ResNet-LSTM), (2) a general-domain vision-language (V-L) prefix-projection model (CLIP-GPT), and (3) a domain-specific V-L prefix-projection model (BioViL-T). Results reveal a sharp performance divide: the ResNet-LSTM attains near-perfect classification (99.5% accuracy) and is the only model to generate coherent reports (BLEU-4 = 0.021), whereas both prefix-projection models catastrophically fail generation (BLEU-4 ≤ 0.0001); moreover, the domain-specific BioViL-T also fails classification (11.5% accuracy). From a data-engineering angle, the pipeline is productionizable with lineage, feature registries, and continuous integration to guard against silent regressions when updating models or data; from a data-science angle, the benchmark provides baselines and analyses that foreground feature alignment and architectural suitability as first-order concerns, inviting ablations on multimodal objectives, retrieval-augmented encoders, and uncertainty-aware decoding. Overall, RadMultiBench highlights that state-of-the-art status in general V-L domains does not translate automatically to high-stakes clinical tasks, and it furnishes the tooling and evidence base needed to develop robust, clinically viable multimodal systems.
evidence_items.title: RadMultiBench: A Reproducible Dual-Task Benchmark Exposing the Limits of Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models Across Thoracic and Breast Imaging

organizations: Student at School of Law, SASTRA Deemed to be University, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, India
evidence_items.summary: The emergence of cybercrime committed by autonomous artificial intelligence is no longer hypothetical. During cyber-range evaluations run by the UK AI Security Institute in July 2026, AI agents took nineteen unsanctioned actions on the live internet, seventeen by Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and two by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, including an attempted supply-chain attack, social engineering and prompt injection. In the same summer, a swarm of OpenAI agents under evaluation breached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure, in what has been described as the first publicly documented fully autonomous AI cyberattack. No human directed either set of actions. This exposes a structural fracture in existing liability regimes. India’s Information Technology Act, 2000 and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 and the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 all condition liability on mens rea, while the EU AI Act imposes procedural safety obligations but is silent on liability, a gap left open since the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn in 2025. The gap is widest where a developer has complied fully with its safety obligations, yet its system acts autonomously and unlawfully. Through a comparative doctrinal analysis tested in the light of the documented 2026 incidents, this paper examines who can be held liable and whether vicarious liability, strict liability and regulatory non-compliance models can be adapted to answer that question. Both civil and criminal law are considered in this regard, including in a few EU and Asian countries. It finds that criminal liability generally fails against a developer, that vicarious liability works only through statutory deeming, and that civil strict liability, especially India’s M.C. Mehta absolute liability rule and section 43 of the IT Act, offers solutions, though not complete ones. It recommends specific amendments to the IT Act and parallel reforms elsewhere.
evidence_items.title: Liability for Cybercrimes Committed by Autonomous Artificial Intelligence

organizations: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
evidence_items.summary: We present Ed-Alpha, an open benchmark platform for predicting and evaluating investment-relevant corporate events using public data. Existing event-driven investment research often relies on expensive, proprietary data, making methods difficult to reproduce or compare. Ed-Alpha addresses this challenge by providing a transparent and fully reproducible pipeline. Specifically, it uses regulatory filings from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as ground-truth event labels and combines them with high-volume news signals from the GDELT project. Using Ed-Alpha, our initial analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art LLMs achieve only limited effectiveness in predicting corporate events; we therefore expect the platform to facilitate more efficient and transparent experimentation toward future improvements in effectiveness. The benchmark platform and a demonstration video, as well as all related code and methods, are available in our repository. https://github.com/E9Technologies/ed-alpha
evidence_items.title: Ed-Alpha: An Open Benchmark for Predicting Investment-Relevant Corporate Events from Open Data

evidence_items.summary: This study develops a benchmark-relative application of geometric Brownian motion (GBM) for evaluating the capital-value performance of real estate under uncertainty. It introduces a valuation-regime taxonomy that distinguishes the growth conditions for benchmark-adjusted mean, median, and modal property values and links them to benchmark underperformance and downside risk over alternative holding horizons. Using a compiled annual median residential property-price series for Accra and Tema (2016–2026), the Ghanaian application illustrates how nominal property appreciation can coexist with deteriorating benchmark-relative performance when appreciation is insufficient relative to the selected investment benchmark. The analysis further demonstrates that expected and median benchmark-adjusted values may exhibit opposing growth patterns, while the probability of benchmark underperformance depends on the interaction among appreciation, benchmark return, volatility, and investment horizon. Rental-yield sensitivity further shows that relatively small positive net yields can alter the classification. The proposed approach provides a probabilistic assessment of benchmark-relative capital-value performance, complementing conventional nominal growth projections.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Adjusted Stochastic Valuation of Real Estate Assets: Evidence from Ghana

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Benchmarks measure what healthcare AI agents can do, not what they may be authorized to do. We built a live-agent benchmark holding task, model, prompt and tools fixed, varying only whether an independent authorization layer gated execution. 576 synthetic care-coordination episodes ran under four arms: deterministic rules, an unconstrained agent, a gateway-governed agent, and a gateway plus autonomy controller. Episodes carry hidden truth and a lossy observable projection, so the gateway can both wrongly authorize and wrongly block. A prespecified rule set blinded to arm adjudicated safety. Unsafe actions occurred in 0.7% of fully governed versus 0.4% of unconstrained episodes (+ 0.4 points, 95% CI -0.5 to + 1.2, P = 0.6875). Routine task success, escalation accuracy, and calibration were each significantly worse under full governance, which also required more time and human effort. These synthetic findings use rule-based adjudication, lack a human comparator, and do not establish clinical effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: A live agent benchmark of independent action authorization for healthcare AI agents

evidence_items.summary: SUMO (Simulation of Urban MObility) is a widely used open-source traffic simulator for urban mobility research, operations, and planning. While recent work has integrated SUMO with large language models (LLMs) to automate scenario generation and result interpretation, a fundamental question remains unanswered: can LLMs answer decision-relevant questions grounded in SUMO simulation files? This setting is uniquely challenging because most practitioner questions require integrating evidence across multiple files, and even a single log file can exceed the context window of current LLMs. To answer this question, we introduce SUMO-SimQA, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLM reasoning over SUMO simulation files. SUMO-SimQA comprises 480 questions that span five SUMO file types and three traffic networks, organized into three levels of reasoning complexity (retrieval, reasoning, and cross-file reasoning). We find that naive approaches fail substantially on cross-file reasoning tasks, revealing a critical gap in existing LLM-SUMO pipelines. To address this challenge, we propose Plan-Execute-Revise (PER), adapting planning and iterative revision to the large, cross-file setting of SUMO-based traffic QA. PER improves accuracy on the hardest cross-file reasoning tasks over ReAct-based approaches (56.0%?82.0%), demonstrating that structured reasoning strategies are essential for reliable performance on these tasks. Our benchmark and code are available on GitHub.
evidence_items.title: SUMO-SimQA: A Benchmark for LLM Cross-File Reasoning over Traffic Simulation Files

evidence_items.summary: Quantum-assisted UAV path planning has recently been studied using QAOA-style obstacle-avoidance formulations, but a low-energy binary sample is not necessarily a valid UAV trajectory. This paper presents a feasibility-aware evaluation protocol on one discrete 8 × 8, L = 20 UAV grid-planning instance with obstacle avoidance, a line-of-sight visibility cost, and a higher-order temporal buffer-risk term. The horizon L denotes discrete planning layers, not physical seconds. The model uses binary variables x {t,v} indicating whether the UAV occupies cell v at time layer t and forms a HUBO objective with one-hot, start, motion, obstacle, visibility, terminal-goal, and sustained near-obstacle proximity terms. The instance has 1,280 original binary variables and 118,344 polynomial terms, including 4,392 cubic monomials. We compare A , RRT-best, a QUAV-style QAOA candidate-path selector, native trajectory-level simulated annealing (SA), the classical neal BQM sampler after HUBO-to-QUBO reduction, and an exact CP-SAT baseline that minimizes the native HUBO soft objective over hard-feasible paths. The CP-SAT solver returns OPTIMAL and certifies that the best observed SA path is globally optimal for the enforced feasible-path objective, with implementation HUBO energy −20752.43, soft cost 247.57, path length 14, six turns, and 85% visibility. On the tested instance, the results show why feasibility-aware decoding, exact baselines, and quadratization effects matter; they do not establish quantum speedup or performance across an instance suite.
evidence_items.title: A Feasibility-Aware HUBO/QUBO Benchmark for UAV Obstacle-Avoidance with Visibility Cost

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Early diagnosis of periodontal disease is critical to prevent tissue destruction and tooth loss. This study evaluates six modern deep learning architectures for four-class radiographic periodontal bone loss grading on panoramic radiographs. Methods: This retrospective study analyzed 1053 images. Two periodontologists independently classified each image according to the most severely affected tooth into four bone loss categories: Healthy, Mild (<25%), Moderate (25–50%), and Severe (>50%). Six convolutional, transformer, and hybrid backbones (ConvNeXt-Tiny, MaxViT-Tiny, EfficientViT-B1, FocalNet-Tiny, CAFormer-S18, and DaViT-Tiny) were trained on a 70/10/20 stratified split using an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, the AdamW optimizer, Cosine Annealing, and early stopping. Performance was assessed using standard classification metrics, Matthews Correlation Coefficient, Cohen’s and Quadratic Weighted Kappa, Expected Calibration Error, Area Under the Curve (AUC), McNemar’s test, and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Results: FocalNet-Tiny achieved the highest numerical scores among the tested models, reaching 83.41% accuracy, 84.70% balanced accuracy, 83.50% macro-F1, and 0.9610 OvR AUC. The p-values obtained from the comparisons of the models were all above 0.05, indicating that the classification performances of the evaluated models are quite similar. Bootstrap analysis confirmed stable prediction metrics for the top-scoring model. Conclusions: This study provides a controlled benchmark of modern deep learning backbones for four-class radiographic periodontal bone loss grading. FocalNet-Tiny achieved the highest numerical metrics and stable bootstrap estimates, yet performed comparably to other contemporary architectures such as ConvNeXt-Tiny.
evidence_items.title: A Comparative Benchmark of Modern Deep Learning Backbones for Multi-Class Periodontal Bone Loss Staging

organizations: Sejong University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly fine-tuned and deployed for nutrition and food-related advisory roles, yet their foundational food knowledge is rarely audited before deployment. We introduce FoodVitals, a public benchmark of 1,158 verified items spanning three high-stakes aspects of food knowledge: nutritional literacy, nutrient–health relations, and food safety. Each aspect is grounded in an authoritative source (USDA, EFSA, USDA FSIS), and the benchmark uses multiple answer formats (multiple-choice (MCQ), Yes/No (Y/N), short answer, and ranking) to characterize model performance across these aspects and assess within-aspect format sensitivity. Evaluating six instruction-following LLMs reveals two consistent patterns: (i) models that correctly identify the highest-nutrient food in a multiple-choice setting show markedly weaker ranking and uneven threshold-checking on the same nutrients, revealing a gap between coarse-grained nutritional knowledge and precise magnitude reasoning; and (ii) food-safety performance varies substantially across answer formats even when all formats draw from the same regulatory topic set, meaning a high score in one format does not reflect uniform competence across that topic area. Together, these patterns show that single-format evaluation gives an incomplete picture of where an LLM is unreliable and motivate multi-format auditing before high-stakes food deployment.
evidence_items.title: FoodVitals: A Diagnostic Benchmark for LLMs on Nutritional Literacy, Nutrient–Health Relations, and Food Safety

organizations: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University, Changchun, Jilin, China

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) distillation offers an efficient paradigm for deploying compact language models, yet it raises a critical safety concern: Does evidence-conditioned supervision inadvertently encode transient retrieved facts into the student model's parametric memory? If transient retrieved facts pollute model parameters, the core premise of externalizing knowledge in RAG is compromised. To audit this risk, we introduce PCD-RAG, a negative-control diagnostic benchmark and metric suite. By utilizing 5,000 synthetic facts with 0% pre-training exposure baseline, this atomic-level probe cleanly disentangles closed-book memorization from context-conditioned reading. Under these strictly controlled zero-exposure settings, our comprehensive evaluation across Qwen2.5 students reveals a counterintuitive finding: RAG distillation does not induce surface-level exact-match retention. Answer-only distillation leaves retrieval-free answer recovery near zero (< = 0.8%). Furthermore, extending our probe to realistic noisy multi-document distillation reveals a stark contrast in training stability: while traditional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) triggers catastrophic optimization collapse when architectural constraints are relaxed (e.g., LoRA R=16), distillation targets (Hard KD) act as an implicit regularizer that successfully stabilizes the model. By bounding parametric contamination and identifying complementary architectural safeguards, our framework lays the empirical groundwork for future community exploration of complex multi-hop reasoning, safeguarding the deployment of reliable RAG pipelines.
evidence_items.title: PCD-RAG: A Diagnostic Framework for Auditing Parametric Contamination in RAG Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Memory-enabled AI agents can retrieve successful precedents without establishing whether their actions remain admissible. We introduce ATM-MEMORYTRAP, an action-conditioned assurance benchmark and selective Operational Transferability Gate (OTG) for post-retrieval reuse in air traffic management (ATM). Matched duels hold source state, target state, text, action family, magnitude, command count, and nominal cost constant; only one signed action is labelled transferable by the benchmark’s kinematic-response engine (KRE). The benchmark comprises 240 anchors, 960 duels, and 1,920 candidates with grouped partitions and an internally hash-locked test. A structured OTG reaches 1.000 duel accuracy under KRE, yet an intent-excluded leave-one-family-out fit and a separately locked externality suite each yield 0.500 for that gate architecture. A separately implemented dynamic point-mass engine (DPME) reproduces only 380/640 target labels (0.594; mirror-group 95% CI [0.556, 0.631]) despite strongly correlated nominal margins (ρs = 0.906). A four-valued model-set certificate yields 160 safe, 206 unsafe, 248 mixed, and 26 source-invalid candidates: 57.2% receive a decisive safe/unsafe classification, but only half of 320 KRE-positive memories remain admissible across both engine families. The assurance object is therefore action reuse under a declared information, interaction, horizon, and dynamics contract, not semantic relevance alone. These controlled simulation results qualify a post-retrieval admission boundary, not end-to-end language-agent competence or operational safety.
evidence_items.title: ATM-MEMORYTRAP: A Benchmark for Auditing Action Transferability Beyond Semantic Similarity in Agentic Air Traffic Management

evidence_items.summary: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) predictions are sensitive to cohort definition, molecular representation, model selection, and uncertainty assumptions. We developed MechTox as an audited benchmark/workflow for ordinal DILI concern prediction and reserve MechTox-NN for the dual-branch neural model. From a pool of 1,336 DILIrank source records, we resolved 1,216 compound identities, where 1,081 records had usable standardized structures, 674 had verified transcriptomic profiles, and 672 were dual-modal records; the primary three-class cohort comprised 512 compounds (147 vNo, 234 vLess, and 131 vMost), and 160 accepted ambiguous records were retained separately. The primary performance was evaluated through five repeats of five outer scaffold folds and five grouped inner folds. The pooled outer quadratic-weighted kappa (QWK) was 0.287 for Morgan fingerprint logistic regression, 0.232 for the ordinal RDKit descriptor model, 0.058 for late-average structure–pathway fusion, and 0.252 for MechTox-NN. A separate compound-bootstrap sensitivity based on repeat-averaged predictions resulted in a median QWK of 0.296 [0.207, 0.377] for MechTox-NN and was not treated as the confidence interval for the pooled estimate. The canonical single-sample gene-set enrichment analysis served as the primary pathway representation, and a custom signed rank-integral score was evaluated only as a sensitivity comparator. Source-shift cohorts and empirical prediction-set containment were used to characterize the behaviors under source composition changes and were interpreted descriptively. In the held-out permutation-calibrated mechanism analysis, cationic amine dealkylation alone met the family-wise support criterion; this finding was interpreted as an exploratory association. Thus, MechTox provides a documented uncertainty-aware framework for protocol-specific ordinal DILI benchmarking and mechanism-oriented hypothesis generation.
evidence_items.title: MechTox: an audited benchmark for ordinal drug-induced liver injury prediction with uncertainty and mechanism-oriented interpretation

evidence_items.summary: Purpose Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) sensing is a candidate technology for future Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-assisted, device-free human sensing. This paper benchmarks convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures for CSI-based activity and gesture recognition under a controlled, repeated protocol, as a first step towards selecting models for resource-constrained platforms. Design/methodology/approach Two public CSI datasets collected with fixed indoor Wi-Fi infrastructure were used: UT-HAR (activity recognition, 7 classes) and Widar (gesture recognition, 22 classes, body-coordinate velocity profile). Two VGG-inspired CSI-adapted networks (CSI-VGGNet-S and CSI-VGGNet-D), GoogLeNet and DenseNet were compared with four retrained SenseFi baselines (MLP, ResNet-18, LSTM and CNN-GRU). All models were trained with three random seeds under one common budget (at most 20 epochs, early stopping on a held-out validation partition), and the test partitions were used once per run. Sliding-window overlap in UT-HAR was quantified, and recording-level (UT-HAR) and cross-user (Widar) splits were used to probe generalization. No UAV hardware or UAV-collected CSI was used. Findings CSI-VGGNet-D achieved the highest mean test accuracy on UT-HAR (96.80 ± 0.87%) and on Widar (74.43 ± 1.31%). Depth alone did not predict accuracy: GoogLeNet and DenseNet varied strongly across seeds on UT-HAR (SD 16.1 and 12.8 percentage points) despite high training accuracy, and model rankings differed between the two tasks. In the released UT-HAR split, 92% of test windows share at least half of their raw frames with a training window; on a recording-level split without shared frames, the accuracy of CSI-VGGNet-D fell by 6.6 percentage points. Released-split accuracies therefore overstate generalization to unseen recordings, and accuracy, model size and latency must be weighed jointly.
evidence_items.title: Toward UAV-assisted Wi-Fi sensing via deep neural networks: a benchmark study on activity and gesture recognition

organizations: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN
evidence_items.summary: Background: Discharge summaries are essential for safe transitions of care, but writing the hospital course narrative is time intensive. Large language models can generate plausible clinical narratives, yet prior approaches often rely on static inputs and remain vulnerable to omissions and factual inconsistencies. Methods: We developed an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated agentic artificial intelligence (AI) system that uses Gemini 2.5 Pro and Model Context Protocol tools to retrieve clinical notes, diagnostic reports, diagnoses, medications, and appointments on demand. In this retrospective, blinded, paired study, 50 inpatient cardiology encounters were randomly selected from admissions July 13 to 27, 2024, at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota. Five physicians rated AI-generated and clinician-authored hospital course narratives for each encounter (250 ratings) on 0-to-10 scales for overall quality, clarity, completeness, accuracy, and readability and indicated a preference. The primary outcome was the paired difference in overall quality (linear mixed-effects model with crossed random intercepts for encounter and reviewer). Secondary domains were analyzed similarly with Bonferroni adjustment, and preference with a crossed random-effects logistic model. Results: Clinician-authored narratives were preferred in 132 ratings (52.8%) and AI-generated narratives in 118 (47.2%) (odds ratio for clinician-authored preference, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.71 to 1.78). Overall quality did not differ significantly (mean, 7.27 AI-generated versus 7.42 clinician-authored; difference, -0.15; 95% CI, -0.86 to 0.56; p=0.627). AI-generated narratives were rated higher for clarity (0.36; 95% CI, 0.07 to 0.65) and readability (0.72; 95% CI, 0.20 to 1.24) but lower for completeness (-0.84; 95% CI, -1.36 to -0.32) and accuracy (-0.35; 95% CI, -0.66 to -0.05). After Bonferroni correction, only lower completeness remained significant (adjusted p=0.012).
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI-Generated vs. Clinician-Authored Hospital Course Narratives for Cardiology Hospitalizations: A Blinded Physician Evaluation

organizations: Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA

evidence_items.summary: Personalization is being rebuilt around generative models. Large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic systems now shape how recommenders retrieve, rank, explain, converse, and even simulate users—yet they also surface hard problems of hallucination, control, evaluation, privacy, and fairness. GRAIL 2026 brings together academic researchers and industry practitioners to advance generative, retrieval-augmented, and agentic approaches to recommendation—including LLM-based retrieval and ranking, retrieval-augmented and knowledge-grounded personalization, conversational and agentic recommenders, multimodal content generation, user simulation, and synthetic data—while giving equal attention to these open challenges and their long-term user impact.
evidence_items.title: GRAIL 2026: Workshop on Generative, Retrieval-augmented, and Agentic Intelligence for Personalization

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge Tracing (KT) models student learning from interaction histories. Recent work has begun applying large language models (LLMs) to KT through prompting, option weighting, and test-time reasoning, but the resulting AUC remains substantially below ID-based KT. We propose Language Model-based Knowledge Tracing (LKT), a PLM-agnostic supervised KT framework that reformulates each interaction as a natural-language sequence of concept text, question text, and a response token, allowing any encoder-based pre-trained language model (PLM), or any decoder LLM after LLM2Vec adaptation, to be fine-tuned end-to-end under a unified protocol. Across three datasets, LKT achieves the highest supervised AUC among Language Model-based KT methods on every dataset, outperforming LOKT and Thinking-KT (best 0.7105 and 0.7185 on DBE-KT22) and frontier LLM prompting baselines (AUC near 0.5 to 0.6). Among the LKT backbones, ModernBERT provides the most cross-dataset stable performance and is our recommended deployment default. Beyond benchmark performance, we analyze LKT's behavior with performance comparisons and explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including attention maps, LIME, and t-SNE visualization of the [MASK]-position embeddings, to characterize which textual cues drive predictions and how the learned representation encodes correctness. Our work contributes a PLM-agnostic and interpretable KT framework that future PLM advances can directly plug into.
evidence_items.title: Language Model-based Knowledge Tracing: A Comprehensive Study on Architectures, Domain Adaptation, and Cold Start Problem

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge Tracing (KT), a core component of intelligent tutoring systems, aims to model the dynamic evolution of students' knowledge states based on their historical interaction data. However, mainstream methods rely heavily on large-scale students' response logs, hindering generalization to unseen students, and often overlook the semantic structure of knowledge points in knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we propose Semantic Knowledge Graph-Based Knowledge Tracing (SKG-KT), a novel KT framework that leverages the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) to enhance the modelling of unseen students, without relying on numerous students with historical records. SKG-KT consists of two stages: ATC-ruled Semantic Graph Extraction and a Concept-aware Reasoning mechanism. In the first stage, we design a semantic student knowledge graph extraction method grounded in ATC rules, which captures the semantic structure across three hierarchical layers—domain, cluster, and standard—aligned with established educational theory. To extend beyond mathematics, we further introduce a multi-disciplinary semantic graph extraction method that induces an ATC-inspired hierarchical schema for other disciplines via LLM-based label induction. In the second stage, the Concept-aware Reasoning mechanism first applies knowledge concept reasoning to infer key knowledge concepts for unseen students with limited previous student data, and then fine-tunes an open-source LLM for correctness prediction based on the reasoned knowledge concepts, adapting the LLM to the KT task. Extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available educational benchmark datasets, namely Xes3g5m-small, Xes3g5m-large, and MOOCRadar, demonstrate that SKG-KT achieves state-of-the-art performance in knowledge tracing. Furthermore, SKG-KT has been validated to achieve robust predictive performance compared to others, while relying on a limited number of students with historical records. Our code and prompts are publicly available at the link . https://github.com/linqingliDestinyController/SKG_KT/tree/main.
evidence_items.title: SKG-KT: Semantic Knowledge Graph Construction and Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing by Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: User tracking aims to identify network activities belonging to the same user across websites and network environments, supporting applications such as personalized recommendation and targeted advertising. As dynamic address allocation and modern privacy protections constrain traditional tracking methods, traffic-based tracking techniques have emerged to link dynamic addresses through traffic patterns. However, existing methods usually rely on large-scale user labels for supervised training, while such labels are difficult to obtain in TLS encrypted traffic, severely limiting model generalization. In this paper, we propose SLATE, a self-supervised address linkage framework integrated with LLMs under limited labeled data. Specifically, SLATE introduces a homologous subgraph discrimination task based on address behavior partitioning, which encourages the encoder to capture stable behavior patterns across temporal evolution from large-scale unlabeled data. Moreover, SLATE develops a graph semantic projection module, which enables the LLM to better interpret behavior graph representations through graph-text matching and node semantic classification, and further leverages its reasoning capability to support address linkage decisions. We evaluate SLATE on two real-world user datasets. Experimental results show that SLATE substantially outperforms the strongest self-supervised methods, achieving an average improvement of over 15% in Hits@1, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art supervised methods. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of combining self-supervised learning with LLMs for address linkage in tracking ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Address Linkage in Tracking Ecosystems via Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) grounds large language model (LLM) outputs in structured facts by retrieving a query-relevant subgraph before generation. However, existing KG-RAG systems often assume that the retrieved graph contains sufficient evidence to answer the query. When this assumption fails, the LLM may produce an answer that is factually plausible but not faithfully grounded in the KG. To address this problem, we introduce Query-Graph Compatibility (QGC), a formal, model-independent pre-condition for faithful KG-grounded generation. Given a natural-language query parsed into a typed conjunctive query and a KG with schema, QGC checks whether the query has a valid typed match in the graph, formalized as a typed homomorphism. If QGC=0, the KG lacks the structural evidence required by the query, so no generation model, regardless of architecture or scale, can produce a faithful answer from the KG alone-a consequence that follows directly from our definitions but yields a checkable pre-generation condition. QGC inherits the classical complexity of conjunctive-query evaluation: NP-complete in general, yet tractable for the bounded-width query structures that cover all KGQA queries in our evaluation. We validate QGC across six datasets and four domains. Under controlled edge deletion on MetaQA, QGC predicts LLM failure with AUC 0.78-0.93 for 1-2 hop queries across five LLMs, with accuracy gaps of +55 to +86 percentage points. Under natural incompleteness in clinical KGs (MIMIC-III, CORAL), all five evaluated models show positive QGC accuracy gaps (+5 to +31 percentage points), while PrimeKGQA exposes a boundary condition: structurally simpler QGC=0 contexts can yield higher correctness despite lacking faithful grounding. QGC checking runs in under 0.1 ms per query, making it practical as a real-time pre-filter or retrieval stopping criterion.
evidence_items.title: Query-Graph Compatibility: A Formal Pre-Condition for Faithful Knowledge-Grounded Language Model Generation

evidence_items.summary: Accurately routing patient-generated messages is a major challenge in primary care, where clinicians must manage large volumes of unstructured text. In this work, we propose a novel method for message routing in family medicine that integrates large language models (LLMs) with a domain-specific clinical ontology. Developed in close collaboration with pharmacists and physicians, the ontology encodes textual indicators relevant to message routing decisions. We incorporate this ontology by leveraging two LLMs, aiming to improve routing accuracy while generating natural language explanations that clarify the rationale behind each decision, thus enhancing primary care experts' trust in the system. We evaluate our method using a large-scale dataset from a healthcare provider, comprising a substantial volume of patient messages. This setting introduces an additional challenge, as the messages are written in Hebrew, a morphologically rich language. Despite this complexity, our results show high classification accuracy alongside high-quality, interpretable explanations. We further evaluated the proposed method in a real-world online setting, demonstrating its practical value for supporting message triage in clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Routing Patient Messages in Primary Care Using Explainable Ontology-Guided Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Clinical diagnosis of tic disorders (TDs) is often delayed by fluctuating symptoms and the subjective nature of assessments. While automated methods have been proposed to bridge this gap, traditional machine learning models frequently lack robustness in unconstrained environments and fail to capture the complex, multisite tics characteristic of severe TDs.


OBJECTIVE
This study aimed to develop and evaluate a fine-tuned large vision-language model framework for the automated, interpretable detection of pediatric motor tics, addressing the clinical need for objective and efficient symptom assessment in unconstrained environments.


METHODS
In this multicenter study, 168 pediatric participants (n=83, 49.4% with TDs and n=85, 50.6% healthy controls) underwent 12-hour continuous video-electroencephalography monitoring. We fine-tuned the Qwen3-VL-8B model using 3- to 5-minute video segments via low-rank adaptation. The framework used chain-of-thought prompting to generate both binary classifications and textual justifications. A strict patient-wise split ensured zero identity overlap between training and test sets. Diagnostic precision was evaluated using 95% CIs calculated with the Clopper-Pearson exact method.


RESULTS
In total, 168 pediatric participants (age: mean 8.3, SD 2.3 years) were enrolled, providing 559 expert-validated video segments for analysis. On the independent test set (n=55), the framework achieved 89.1% (49/55; 95% CI 77.8%-95.9%) accuracy and an area under the curve of 0.950 (95% CI 0.892-1.000), significantly outperforming the landmark-based deep neural network (accuracy 74.1%; P=.004); recall reached 100% (25/25 positive episodes; 95% CI 86.3%-100.0%). Model-generated justifications showed substantial agreement with expert annotations (κ=0.784, 95% CI 0.625-0.943; P<.001).


CONCLUSIONS
These findings suggest that a vision-language model framework can capture clinically relevant tic features beyond conventional geometric descriptors. By combining high sensitivity (recall) with text-based diagnostic justifications aligned with clinical severity dimensions (eg, frequency and intensity), the approach may support automated video review and preliminary symptom quantification in controlled monitoring settings.
evidence_items.title: Large Vision-Language Models for Pediatric Motor Tic Detection: Case-Control Diagnostic Study.

evidence_items.summary: The massive redundancy of visual tokens in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) creates a critical computational bottleneck during large language model (LLM) prefill. Recent training-free pruning methods provide plug-and-play acceleration, yet their pruning decisions often rely on limited visual states or delayed in-LLM signals, which may underexploit both the layer-wise evolution of visual representations and the query-specific relevance of local regions. We propose DATP (Depth-Aware Token Pruning), a training-free early-pruning framework that selects compact visual tokens before they enter the LLM. DATP combines two complementary signals: Depth-aware Layer Aggregation (DALA), which aggregates multi-layer visual saliency trajectories to construct a high-recall structural prior, and Cross-modal Attention Gating (CMAG), which introduces a lightweight prompt-conditioned relevance signal to suppress visually salient but task-irrelevant tokens. Experiments on LLaVA-v1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Qwen2.5-VL show that DATP achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off under aggressive token budgets. On LLaVA-v1.5, DATP preserves 95.7% of the full-token performance while retaining only 11% of the visual tokens. Across the reported multimodal reasoning and hallucination-sensitive benchmark settings, DATP generally outperforms the evaluated training-free pruning baselines.
evidence_items.title: DATP: Training-Free Depth-Aware Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Generative recommendations (GRs) reframe recommendation as autoregressive generation over Semantic IDs (SIDs), enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to model user intent and sequential preference patterns in a unified manner. Most existing systems discretize continuous item representations into SIDs via codebook-based residual quantization, and then generate subsequent SID tokens through next-token prediction. However, conventional residual quantization relies on deterministic, hard nearest-neighbor assignments. This rigid mapping fails to account for semantic ambiguity, suffering from error propagation across quantization levels and often leading to under-utilized codebooks. To address these limitations, we propose the Bayesian Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoder (BRQ-VAE), a probabilistic reformulation of residual quantization that introduces stochastic quantization and stochastic dequantization under an ELBO-driven objective. We further develop alignment strategies to integrate language semantics and collaborative signals for end-to-end LLM-based recommendation. Experiments on public benchmarks, large-scale industrial datasets, and online A/B tests on a commercial music platform show that BRQ-VAE consistently improves codebook quality, downstream recommendation performance, and key engagement metrics over strong baselines.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Language Models for Music Recommendation with Bayesian Residual Quantization

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence in medical imaging is shifting from task-specific algorithms toward adaptable foundation models (FMs) and vision-language models (VLMs). However, applying these models to MRI remains challenging because clinical interpretation requires integrating multi-parametric, volumetric imaging across multiple sequences with clinical context. This systematic review evaluates 35 studies on unimodal FMs and multimodal VLMs in MRI, summarizing emerging architectures, downstream applications, and challenges to clinical translation. Current research is concentrated in neuroimaging, with diagnostic classification representing the most mature application. Segmentation and outcome prediction also show promise, whereas automated report generation remains limited by poor clinical fidelity despite strong linguistic fluency. Broader adoption is hindered by heterogeneous MRI acquisition, limited large-scale paired image-text datasets, and inadequate safety-focused evaluation metrics. Advancing clinical translation will require standardized multicenter datasets, stronger integration with electronic health records and pathology, robust evaluation frameworks, and improved model explainability.
evidence_items.title: Unimodal imaging foundation models and vision-language models in MRI: A systematic review of emerging methods and clinical applications.

evidence_items.summary: Text-attributed graph (TAG) learning aims to leverage both textual attributes and graph structures for node classification. Recent studies have utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-labels and rationales for few-label TAG learning. However, existing approaches typically rely solely on the textual attribute of target nodes, making the generated knowledge susceptible to noise and unreliability. To address this limitation, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Reliable Imitation with Semantic Multiplicity), a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework for few-label TAG learning. PRISM constructs multiple structural-context perspectives for each target node and estimates the reliability of LLM-generated knowledge based on cross-perspective consistency. The resulting reliability weights are then incorporated into the distillation process, enabling GNNs to place greater emphasis on more reliable supervision signals. Extensive experiments on five TAG benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms existing methods in few-label node classification.
evidence_items.title: PRISM: Reliable LLM Knowledge Distillation from Graph-Context Perspectives for Text-Attributed Graph Learning

evidence_items.summary: One major challenge of sensor-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) is data heterogeneity, where domain shifts between training and testing data could significantly degrade recognition performance. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong cross-domain generalization capabilities by modeling language with next-token prediction, offering a promising paradigm for mitigating domain shifts in HAR. In this paper, we propose NextHAR, a novel self-supervised sensor pretraining framework for generalizable HAR. NextHAR first tokenizes sensor data in the frequency space, converting them into motion-semantic tokens. Then, to learn human motion dynamics, NextHAR jointly models inter-channel correlations and temporal dependencies by predicting the next sensor token groups. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive cross-domain HAR benchmark to enable systematic evaluation. Extensive experiments on this benchmark show that NextHAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 13.83% in accuracy and 15.00% in F1-score. Moreover, NextHAR achieves an average inference latency of 0.033 seconds on wearable devices, highlighting its efficiency for real-world applications. Our code and organized benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/saiketa/NextHAR.
evidence_items.title: Next Token Prediction for Generalizable Human Activity Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Graph-based indexes such as HNSW are widely used for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search due to their strong empirical performance. Prior work (Morozov and Babenko, NeurIPS 2018) suggests that these methods remain effective even for non-metric maximum inner product search (MIPS). We show that this assumption fails for the attention-derived embeddings from modern large language models available in the recent VIBE benchmark. We trace the failure to HNSW's neighbor-selection heuristic, which prunes almost every candidate at build time and yields graphs too sparse to effectively support greedy descent. As a remedy we revisit an index-agnostic transformation that maps the database onto the unit hypersphere while preserving the inner-product ranking, without any knowledge of the query distribution. The transformation restores the assumed geometry of the datasets and raises HNSW recall above 95%. Moreover, a query-agnostic adaption of the query-aware index RoarGraph (Chen et al., VLDB 2024) stays below 40% recall. This means that RoarGraph's strong performance needs access to the query sample rather than purely relying on its bipartite graph construction.
evidence_items.title: Recovering Graph ANN Search on Attention-Derived Workloads via a Query-Agnostic Spherical Transformation

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on many NLP tasks, but their ability to reason about complex supply chain relationships remains unclear. We introduce the Supply Chain Intuition Exam (SCIE), a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can identify and infer direct and indirect supplier relationships. We compare standard LLMs, models with grounding-based retrieval, and deep research (DR) systems. Despite access to public financial reports and real-world data, recall remains low: standard and grounded models achieve approximately 3--16%, while the best DR systems reach only 22%. These results suggest that retrieval alone is insufficient for professional-grade supply chain reasoning. SCIE highlights the need for methods that better integrate domain knowledge, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning in business and finance applications.
evidence_items.title: Can Frontier LLMs Capture $40 Billion in Supply Chain Value?

evidence_items.summary: Vehicle diagnosis begins with structured signals—an Electronic Control Unit (ECU) identifier, a Diagnostic Trouble Code (DTC), and trigger conditions—but technicians must translate them into an accurate fault description and appropriate repair measures. Automotive repair reasoning is both long-tailed and safety-critical: rare ECU/DTC combinations provide few training examples, while associating a fault with the wrong control unit or recommending unnecessary repairs can mislead maintenance decisions. Benchmarking this capability is challenging because diagnostic resources are fragmented, general-purpose large language models (LLMs) often fail to follow repair constraints, and exact-match metrics may reject valid answers expressed differently. We introduce AutoRepairBench, a BMW-centered benchmark and evaluation framework for long-tailed, safety-critical automotive repair reasoning.
