It supports single-turn diagnosis, multi-pair prompting, and frequency-aware analysis of common and rare cases. Its validated hierarchical evaluator accepts valid paraphrases while checking ECU/DTC associations, component relationships, repair severity, and unnecessary repair recommendations. We also develop RepairLLM-7B, a compact, retrieval-free model trained through two-stage distillation: the first stage reduces the dominance of frequent cases, while knowledge-graph-anchored online distillation emphasizes uncertain and rare cases. On a double-blind set of 585 cases labeled by three automotive experts, the evaluator achieved 94.19% accuracy and an F1 score of 94.67%. On the 500-instance main evaluation set, RepairLLM-7B achieved 95.0% single-turn joint accuracy (475/500) and 94.2% per-pair joint accuracy under multi-pair prompting (471/500); it also improved tail accuracy on the separate 100-instance generalization set and reduced safety-critical errors relative to supervised fine-tuning. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly benchmarking overall accuracy, rare-case performance, and repair safety in automotive repair reasoning.
evidence_items.title: AutoRepairBench: Benchmarking Long-Tailed, Safety-Critical Automotive Repair Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Virtual interactive manipulatives help elementary students transition from concrete to abstract mathematical thinking through hands-on digital activities. However, creating them requires both pedagogical and programming expertise, while existing platforms only offer fixed templates that cannot adapt to individual teaching needs. We present ManipulativeAgent, a multi-agent system that allows teachers to create customized manipulatives from natural language descriptions of their instructional goals, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints for review and revision at each stage. Rather than relying on a single large language model (LLM) for end-to-end generation, ManipulativeAgent distributes the task across specialized agents that collaborate through a shared component library of pre-tested virtual tools. This design separates pedagogical reasoning from code implementation, enabling each agent to focus on its strength while the component library ensures interaction reliability. Evaluation on 40 real teaching scenarios shows improvements over commercial platforms and general-purpose LLMs, with the largest gain in interaction richness. A user study with 89 frontline teachers from 15 provinces shows that 92.1% would continue using the system for lesson preparation. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/7eclhXhRy0A.
evidence_items.title: ManipulativeAgent: A Multi-Agent System for Generating Interactive Mathematical Manipulatives

evidence_items.summary: The automated extraction of structured phenotypic profiles from clinical narratives is a critical step in genetic diagnosis, but it is hindered by the unstructured nature of medical reports, the contextual complexity of clinical language, and strict privacy requirements that forbid sending clinical data to external services. We present PHASE, a modular pipeline for the extraction of phenotypic profiles from clinical referral reports, designed to work under on-premise deployment constraints. Instead of using a single Large Language Model (LLM) monolithically, PHASE decomposes the task across specialized modules that interleave generative reasoning with explicit ontological alignment: a high-recall semantic extractor, a hybrid ontological aligner against the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), a generative concept normalizer, and an ontology-grounded validator. The resulting phenotypic profile consists of records that link each phenotype to its HPO concept, identify its subject (proband or family member) and assertion status (confirmed, negated, or suspected), and provide a natural-language rationale supporting the prediction. We further propose an ontology-aware evaluation metric that complements strict identifier matching with bounded partial credit based on HPO topology. We evaluate PHASE on a public dataset of clinical case reports, against five state-of-the-art systems, and show consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1 score under both exact-match and ontology-aware metrics, while operating exclusively on quantized LLMs deployable on a single workstation GPU. An ablation study quantifies the antagonistic and complementary contributions of generative normalization (recall amplifier) and ontology-grounded validation (precision filter), with consistent qualitative behavior across two open-weight LLMs.
evidence_items.title: PHASE: A Modular LLM Pipeline for On-Premise Phenotype Profile Extraction from Clinical Referral Reports

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MAS) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex tasks through collaboration among multiple agents. Nevertheless, this graph-structured communication inherently introduces a vulnerable attack surface, allowing adversarial instructions to propagate from compromised nodes across the entire system. Existing defenses often rely on runtime intervention or topology modification, which are often inapplicable to practical LLM-MAS deployments constrained by fixed communication structures, predefined roles, and execution protocols. A practical alternative is to selectively upgrade some agents to stronger model backbones before deployment. However, upgrading all agents to strong-tier models is costly, and the placement decision should be source-aware because adversarial content enters from specific attacker agents. To address this problem, we propose SpecGuard, a heterogeneous agent placement framework for fixed-topology LLM-MAS. SpecGuard upgrades a small set of weak agents before execution while preserving the original graph, agent set, and runtime protocol. Within SpecGuard, we design H-NetShield, a source-aware algorithm that estimates the exposure risk considering attacker locations, graph structure, deliberation horizon, and calibrated model susceptibility. It also incorporates a structural score to reduce redundant placements caused by overlapping protection. Empirical evaluations on CommonsenseQA across representative topologies demonstrate that upgrading just a single selected agent recovers 54.8%-90.3% of the defense benefit of an all-strong deployment. Moreover, H-NetShield further outperforms common graph-based baselines, and its exposure risk aligns well with empirical attack success rates.
evidence_items.title: SpecGuard: Source-Aware Heterogeneous Agent Placement for Defending LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems against Adversarial Communication

evidence_items.summary: Recent studies have explored the use of pretrained large language model (LLM) representations for long-term time series forecasting.While direct LLM-based forecasting methods adapt time series into LLM-compatible inputs, recent multimodal approaches further use LLM representations as auxiliary semantic representations and introduce interaction mechanisms between time series and language branches. However, existing methods mainly focus on aligning or combining these representations, leaving underexplored how LLM representations should be selectively utilized for different forecasting inputs. In particular, not all LLM layers are equally informative for time series forecasting, and different temporal regions may require different predictive cues from LLM representations. To address these challenges, we propose SeleRT (Selective Retrieval of LLM Representations for Long-term Time Series Forecasting), a multimodal forecasting framework designed to selectively utilize LLM representations for time series prediction. SeleRT consists of two key components: Statistics-Aware Dynamic Layer Fusion (SADLF), which dynamically generates layer weights from input time series statistics, and Patch-Wise Learnable Query Retrieval (PLQR), which enables patch-grounded queries to retrieve information from the fused LLM representation. We evaluate SeleRT on eight standard long-term forecasting benchmarks under full-shot and few-shot protocols. Experimental results show that SeleRT achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains in the few-shot setting. Ablation and visualization analyses further support the effectiveness of input-adaptive layer fusion and patch-wise selective retrieval.
evidence_items.title: SeleRT: Selective Retrieval of LLM Representations for Long-term Time Series Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on retrieved documents to ground large language model outputs, yet evaluating whether those documents are truly useful for generation remains an open challenge. Recent work has shown that retrieval quality measured by conventional relevance-based metrics does not necessarily align with end-to-end RAG performance: a document judged relevant to a query may not help the model answer correctly, while an irrelevant document may actively distract generation[6, 18, 24]. Existing utility-aware evaluation methods address this limitation by estimating the utility of retrieved documents through isolated document-level probes. However, these approaches estimate document utility independently of the reasoning process. We argue that a document is useful not because it can answer a question in isolation, but because it contributes to the reasoning process that produces the final answer. To capture this behavior, we introduce Trace Utility Gain (TUG), a family of retrieval evaluation metrics that estimate document utility directly from chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces generated over the full retrieval context. Specifically, TUG measures utility through three complementary signals: citation behavior, semantic alignment between retrieved documents and reasoning traces, and model self-assessment of document reliance. By estimating utility from the model's observed reasoning process, TUG captures how retrieved evidence contributes to answer generation rather than how useful it appears in isolation. We evaluate TUG on five question-answering benchmarks using three instruction-tuned large language models. Results show that TUG consistently achieves stronger correlation with end-to-end answer correctness than both traditional retrieval metrics and prior utility-aware approaches.
evidence_items.title: Reasoning-Aware Utility Estimation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Multivariate time series forecasting supports state estimation and trend analysis of complex dynamic systems by modeling temporal dependencies among multiple variables. However, real-world time series are often sparse and incomplete due to irregular or constrained data collection, which degrades forecasting performance. Existing methods typically adopt either imputation-then-forecasting or direct forecasting from incomplete observations. The former separates imputation from forecasting, causing interpolation errors to propagate into prediction, while the latter may overlook latent evolution patterns in missing segments. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) suggest their potential to capture high-level sequential semantics and infer contextual patterns beyond observed numerical values, making them promising for reasoning over incomplete temporal dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose LIPTS (Large language model-based interpolation and prediction for Time Series), an end-to-end framework for time series imputation and forecasting based on LLMs. LIPTS jointly optimizes missing value interpolation and downstream forecasting within a unified framework, thereby alleviating the propagation of interpolation errors in two-stage pipelines. Moreover, it introduces an LLM-enhanced cross-modal semantic branch to infer global temporal semantics behind incomplete observations and provide complementary information for latent evolution in missing segments. The numerical branch captures historical and seasonal dependencies from observed values, while latent alignment bridges semantic representations and the numerical forecasting space, encouraging interpolated values to follow the temporal distribution required for downstream forecasting. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that LIPTS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in prediction accuracy and robustness across different missing rates and prediction horizons.
evidence_items.title: LIPTS: LLM-enhanced Time Series Interpolation and Prediction with Incomplete Data

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are moving rapidly from demos to production, but the methodology for getting them there reliably remains fragmented: architecture, observability, evaluation, and online measurement are usually taught and built in isolation. This half-day tutorial presents a practical playbook for building, evaluating, and deploying LLM agents in high-stakes production settings like healthcare and finance. We cover modular context engineering, user simulation, tool and knowledge design, and - as the centerpiece - rigorous evaluation and harness optimization: calibrated LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, inter-rater reliability, and automated judge-prompt optimization, culminating in offline-online correlation that lets teams predict production impact before shipping. Principles are grounded in two regulated, high-stakes domains: customer support in finance and agentic AI in healthcare. Attendees leave with reusable recipes, evaluation code patterns, and a clear mental model connecting offline development to online outcomes. No production experience is required.
evidence_items.title: Building Production LLM Agents: An Evaluation-Driven Playbook

evidence_items.summary: Numerical question answering (QA) over Knowledge Graphs (KGs) requires retrieving numerical values from structured sources. Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) and KG-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) methods exploit multi-hop connectivity for entity-centric questions but remain brittle for numerical queries, whose values typically appear as sparse attribute leaves. When required triples are missing, target values can become unreachable by explicit traversal; structural methods may retrieve values from the wrong numerical attribute, while numerical solvers assuming directly attached values cannot access non-local evidence. We propose SEMAPHORE, a neuro-symbolic framework that reformulates numerical QA over KGs as a semantic detour problem. SEMAPHORE combines symbolic path planning with embedding-based geometric navigation and decoupled scoring that separates relational navigation from numerical attribute grounding. This design identifies plausible detours while preserving the metric semantics required for accurate numerical answers. On numerical QA benchmarks derived from FB15K-237 and YAGO15K, SEMAPHORE outperforms strong LLM and KG-augmented baselines, demonstrating the value of semantic detours for robust numerical knowledge access over KGs. Sparsity and cross-dataset transfer experiments show that this advantage persists under severe graph incompleteness and when target-specific Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) training is replaced with transferred schema embeddings. Code is available at https://github.com/orcies8147/SEMAPHORE.
evidence_items.title: SEMAPHORE: Semantic Detour over Incomplete Knowledge Graphs for Multi-hop Numerical QA

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality public data, making private data essential for further improvement. However, private data is typically distributed across resource-constrained devices and cannot be shared due to strict privacy requirements, rendering conventional federated fine-tuning of LLMs impractical under limited computation and communication budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache (FedICL-KVc), a novel framework that enables effective utilization of private data without parameter updates. Instead of transmitting raw demonstrations, clients upload only the corresponding key--value (KV) caches generated during auto-regressive inference, which are compact, smaller than full-model parameter payloads, and subject to an empirical reconstruction-risk evaluation under a restricted attack model. To further enhance efficiency and effectiveness, we introduce a confidence-based demonstration selection strategy to identify informative client samples, and a server-side KV cache compression method guided by a proxy dataset to reduce inference cost and suppress irrelevant information. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate that FedICL-KVc achieves competitive performance without client-side parameter updates or full-model parameter transmission while avoiding direct raw-data transmission.
evidence_items.title: FedICL-KVc: Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache

evidence_items.summary: Existing financial time series generation (FTSG) approaches predominantly model unconditional distributions, lacking the semantic controllability required to simulate deliberate market dynamics, such as macroeconomic shifts and geopolitical shocks. To bridge this gap, this paper studies text-conditioned FTSG that synthesizes realistic multivariate price sequences guided by natural language market descriptions. We propose Fin-CoDiT, a novel diffusion transformer framework engineered around a profound architectural inductive bias: the structural isomorphism between the hierarchical semantic depth of large language models (LLMs) and the spectral frequencies of time-series signals. To exploit this, Fin-CoDiT introduces a Semantics-Frequency Alignment mechanism via Grouped Routing Attention, which dynamically routes explicit LLM layers to their targeted frequency bands during the denoising process. To encode cross-variable dependencies of time series without violating the temporal arrow, we propose Time-Frequency Causal Variational Autoencoder, which strictly operates as a channel-wise bottleneck equipped with orthogonal causal convolutions to fundamentally eliminate future information leakage. Furthermore, it incorporates a branched decoder with in-network differentiable morphological projections, guaranteeing absolute physical market constraints (e.g., Pricehigh ≥ Pricelow). For the training and evaluation of this novel paradigm, we construct an automated multi-agent workflow that creates high-quality text-time series pairs from real-world market states spanning January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2025. Extensive experiments on treasury futures and ETFs demonstrate that Fin-CoDiT establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing baselines in both generation fidelity and controllability.
evidence_items.title: Exploring Semantics-Frequency Alignment in Diffusion Transformers for Financial Time Series Generation

evidence_items.summary: Recommender systems increasingly influence what users discover and consume online, yet the decision logic behind their outputs often remains opaque. Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods provide an effective way to show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation. In recommendation settings, however, CFXs often require many edits, producing long, low-level lists that are hard for users to interpret. Moreover, most evaluations emphasize edit counts while largely overlooking whether the resulting CFXs are coherent and actionable for users. We argue that this gap between generating valid CFXs and communicating model behavior stems from the lack of user-centered abstraction and limited qualitative evaluation. To bridge this gap, we investigate large language models as mediators that summarize raw CFX interaction edit lists into concise natural language explanations describing higher-level preference patterns. We optimize these mediators for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality through preference optimization, and evaluate the resulting explanations with human-calibrated metrics derived from separate human-labeled datasets. On the MovieLens-1M dataset, across multiple counterfactual generators and language models, the resulting summaries achieve high overall linguistic quality, while the strongest semantic results are obtained with high-success CFX methods such as ACCENT and SPINRec. Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings.
evidence_items.title: From Counterfactual Edits to Human Narratives: LLM-Driven Interpretations for Recommender System Explanations

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate news articles that closely resemble human-written journalism, raising concerns about misinformation and the reliability of online information. Existing AI-generated text detectors primarily rely on lexical, stylistic, or contextual representations, which often struggle to generalize to unseen generators and do not explicitly model article-level structure in news. We propose GRAIN, a framework for AI-generated news detection that jointly models semantic representations and article-level structural patterns. Through empirical analysis, we identify recurring article-level structural patterns in AI-generated news that remain consistent across multiple LLM families and a real-world AI-generated news dataset. Experiments on RAID, DetectRL, an in-house dataset comprising 157K AI-generated news articles from 11 LLMs, and the real-world NewsGPT dataset show that GRAIN improves ROC-AUC over the strongest baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average across evaluation settings. These results suggest that article-level structural patterns provide effective complementary signals for improving the robustness and generalization of AI-generated news detection. The code is available at: https://github.com/DSAIL-SKKU/GRAIN-CIKM-2026.
evidence_items.title: GRAIN: Detecting AI-Generated News via Article-Level Structure

evidence_items.summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant paradigm in recommender systems by modeling collaborative signals over user--item interaction graphs. Recent LLM-enhanced recommenders seek to complement such structural signals with semantic knowledge from Large Language Models (LLMs). However, most existing methods implicitly follow a direct semantic fusion paradigm, where LLM-derived representations are treated as reliable semantic features and directly fused with collaborative representations. We argue that this paradigm is incomplete: LLM semantics are informative, but not directly trustworthy for recommendation. Through controlled diagnostic analyses, we identify two failure modes of raw LLM semantics: Unreliable Semantic Signals, where representations are sensitive to task-irrelevant textual noise, and Semantic--Behavioral Misalignment, where semantic proximity does not necessarily imply behavioral relevance. To address these issues, we propose PSCRec, a model-agnostic framework for preference-conditioned semantic calibration in LLM-enhanced graph recommendation. PSCRec progressively transforms noisy LLM-derived priors into behavior-consistent semantic evidence by structuring semantic profiles, grounding them in dynamic user preferences, filtering unreliable semantic associations, purifying residual semantic redundancy, and aligning calibrated semantic representations with collaborative signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that PSCRec consistently improves multiple graph-based backbones and outperforms representative LLM-enhanced recommendation methods. Further ablation, robustness, semantic--behavioral calibration, and efficiency analyses demonstrate the effectiveness and practical feasibility of the proposed calibration framework.
evidence_items.title: PSCRec: Preference-Conditioned Semantic Calibration for LLM-Enhanced Graph Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to search biomedical knowledge bases. In this setting, queries describe the desired biomedical entity in natural language, and the system retrieves matching candidates. Existing methods typically represent candidate entities through text, leaving out available structural information such as molecular structure or protein sequence. Text descriptions can omit fine-grained structural information, making it difficult for text-only representations to distinguish candidates with similar descriptions but different structures. A natural idea is to introduce structural modalities. However, structural and textual representations of the same entity can encode partially overlapping information, creating cross-modal redundancy. Naive fusion can then reinforce shared information and reduce the contribution of additional structural signals. We present OrthoMol, a multi-modal framework for biomedical entity retrieval whose entity-side fusion explicitly accounts for this redundancy. Its core step, Residual Orthogonal Projection (ROP), decomposes the structural embedding into two parts: a text-aligned component and an orthogonal residual. ROP then removes the text-aligned component and uses the orthogonal residual to augment the text embedding as a complementary structural signal. We evaluate OrthoMol on STaRK-Prime and ProtDescribe, two biomedical retrieval benchmarks in which natural-language queries are matched against candidate entities described in text. On both benchmarks, OrthoMol outperforms foundation-model retrieval baselines and improves over the text-only version of the same backbone. Notably, on ProtDescribe, it reduces the mean rank of the target protein by 29% relative to the text-only backbone.
evidence_items.title: Residual Orthogonal Projection for Multi-Modal Molecular Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are foundational infrastructure for search, question answering, and entity-centric applications, on the open web and within domain-specific platforms. Their lifecycle, from construction over heterogeneous sources to evaluation at scale and use in downstream tasks, raises a coupled set of data management problems that shape the reliability and utility of every system built on top of them. This tutorial offers a high-level view of KG data quality at scale, organized along KG lifecycle stages. We first frame KG construction and the open challenges that arise when facts are extracted from noisy, evolving sources. We then turn to evaluation, covering efficient quality estimation, as well as the role of Large Language Models (LLMs) as validators and auxiliary signals. We close with downstream applications, including entity-oriented search and scalable defect detection, which translate evaluation outcomes into operational decisions.
evidence_items.title: Knowledge Graphs Data Quality at Scale: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly solve multi-step reasoning tasks, where a single sampled chain of reasoning is frequently unreliable. Reaching a correct answer therefore requires aggregating many sampled reasoning paths into one trustworthy decision. The dominant family, self-consistency and its sampling-and-voting variants, suits such reasoning tasks, but its raw-count vote treats sampled paths as separate units of evidence, even when their reasoning is highly redundant. Within this regime, adaptive-budget methods curb the cost by deciding when to stop, yet their stopping signals are commonly based on the same redundancy-blind counts. We therefore propose Redundancy-Aware Consistency (RAC), which strengthens self-consistency by aggregating reasoning paths according to their effective support rather than their raw count. We establish the boundedness of this effective support and show that RAC recovers self-consistency when within-answer paths are mutually dissimilar. Experiments on four benchmarks with the primary backbone and a three-benchmark subset with a second backbone show that RAC achieves higher observed accuracy than the evaluated self-consistency and adaptive-budget baselines. On the primary backbone, it also uses substantially fewer samples.
evidence_items.title: Redundancy-Aware Self-Consistency for Efficient LLM Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Explanations in Recommender Systems (RS) play a crucial role in enhancing transparency, trust, and user satisfaction. Benchmarking such explanations, however, is not trivial, as existing evaluation frameworks typically do not assess all explanation stages (i.e., generation, abstraction, formatting, and communication) or evaluate them in isolation. In this paper, we present TE4 RS, an end-to-end explanation evaluation framework for RS that assesses explanation methods across all four stages: generation, abstraction, format, and communication. It contains 20 explanation methods covering seven categories and 31 evaluation metrics. We also integrate large language models to format the explainers' abstract outputs and to serve as proxy evaluators for human evaluation. TE4 RS allows to set up an evaluation pipeline that mimics a specific application scenario and compares multiple explanation methods, thereby fostering a holistic, structured evaluation of RS explanations. The code can be found at: https://gitlab.ifi.uzh.ch/DDIS-Public/te4-rs.
evidence_items.title: TE4 RS: Toward End-to-End Explanation Evaluation for Recommender Systems

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to produce the relevance labels that underpin the evaluation of information retrieval (IR) and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Yet delegating relevance assessment to an LLM raises a meta-evaluation question that is hard to answer with existing resources: when, and how much, can we trust an automatic judge? We present LLMJudge, a resource for meta-evaluating LLM-generated relevance judgments. LLMJudge collects 42 complete judgment sets over the TREC 2023 Deep Learning track, spanning fine-tuned, proprietary, and open-source models and a wide range of prompting strategies. Each judgment set is paired with official human qrels, enabling two complementary axes of analysis: label agreement with human assessors (e.g., Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α) and system-ranking fidelity (e.g., Kendall's τ, Spearman's ρ). Beyond the data, we release a standardized format, baselines, and an evaluation harness so that new judges can be plugged in and compared reproducibly. Our analysis shows that high label agreement is neither necessary nor sufficient for faithful system ranking, that open-source judges are markedly more stable than proprietary ones, and that fine-tuning improves correlation at the cost of reliability. LLMJudge is publicly available and provides a reusable testbed for auditing the judges who increasingly judge our systems. Full resources, data, and detailed results are available at https://llm4eval.github.io/LLMJudge-benchmark/.
evidence_items.title: LLMJudge: Meta-Evaluating Automatic Relevance Judgments

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced text-attributed graph (TAG) learning in recent years, leading to strong performance in Graph-LLM systems. However, these gains may partially arise from target-correlated parametric priors memorized during LLM pre-training rather than genuine graph reasoning. This issue is particularly critical in TAGs, where graph topology can propagate memory-triggered signals beyond individual nodes. Once encoded as node representations, memorized priors may spread through neighborhood aggregation, introducing topology-level bias amplification absent in conventional NLP tasks. Despite its importance, the interaction between LLM memorization and graph message passing remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a leakage analysis framework guided by Structural Causal Models (SCMs) for Graph-LLMs. Specifically, we investigate how prompt interventions influence downstream graph prediction and examine whether entity-level anonymization suppresses memory-triggering cues. We further construct globally consistent entity-anonymized graph benchmarks that preserve graph structure while masking identity-sensitive entities. Experiments on citation and person relational networks across multiple embedding models and graph backbones reveal three findings: (1) Target-related meta-information can act as shortcut signals when highly correlated with downstream labels; (2) Graph message passing may further propagate memory-induced bias across neighboring nodes; and (3) Graph-LLM performance drops notably after entity anonymization. These findings suggest that current Graph-LLM benchmarks may overestimate generalization ability when memorized priors are not properly controlled. The code and anonymized datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mrjc12/GL-DataLeakage.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Graph-LLMs: Are Performance Gains Confounded by Data Leakage?

evidence_items.summary: Emotion recognition (ER) aims to identify affective states from facial expressions, speech, text, and physiological signals. The context-dependent and multimodal nature of emotion presents challenges for systems that rely on statistical associations alone. Knowledge graphs (KGs) organize affective concepts and their relations, providing explicit knowledge for contextual modeling, multimodal integration, and reasoning. This survey reviews KG-based emotion recognition and related affective tasks, covering knowledge extraction and graph construction, unimodal and multimodal systems, representation learning, reasoning, and integration with large language models (LLMs). The synthesis draws on 49 core studies and uses additional literature for theoretical and methodological context. It distinguishes semantic KGs from computational graphs and characterizes graph construction along five dimensions: knowledge scope, semantic foundation, construction mechanism, human involvement, and multimodal representation. Selected within-study comparisons report gains from enabling knowledge-related components, while differences in tasks, protocols, and comparison designs limit conclusions across systems. The survey also examines evaluation datasets, knowledge quality, and the computational and grounding challenges of LLM and KG integration. It identifies research priorities in knowledge validation, cross-domain generalization, privacy, temporal modeling, and multimodal alignment, with evaluation procedures for assessing their contribution to reliable affective systems.
evidence_items.title: A Survey of Knowledge Graph-based Emotion Recognition: Technologies, Models, and Applications

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) rely on structured representations of entities and relations to enable effective information access and integration. Building and populating KGs from semi-structured sources such as tables remains a challenging task, particularly due to the need to adhere to strict ontology constraints on valid entity types and relations. Large Language Models (LLMs) provide strong capabilities for understanding and generalising from text, but ensuring that their outputs conform to a target KG schema without explicitly providing the full ontology remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose WikiTabLLM, a few-shot, example-driven framework for ontology-compliant knowledge graph population. Instead of explicitly specifying ontology constraints, WikiTabLLM leverages partially linked Wikipedia tables to implicitly induce valid typing and relation patterns. Each table is partitioned into (i) rows containing entities already linked to the Wikidata knowledge graph, which serve as in-context supervision signals, and (ii) rows with unlinked entities, for which we aim to generate RDF triples for KG population. WikiTabLLM learns to infer valid properties and relations by conditioning on the structured patterns exhibited in existing triples, effectively enforcing ontology compliance through examples. We evaluate WikiTabLLM on a newly constructed dataset of Wikipedia tables and compare against Semantic Table Interpretation, relation extraction baselines, and zero-shot LLM prompting. Results show that our approach produces more accurate and schema-consistent triples (up to a 3× improvement in macro F1), demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging in-context examples to guide ontology-constrained knowledge graph population.
evidence_items.title: Few-Shot Guided Knowledge Graph Population with Implicit Ontology Compliance from Partially Linked Tables

evidence_items.summary: Historical digital archives present new challenges for retrieval systems because of OCR errors introduced by degraded page quality, old typefaces, and complex page layouts. Large language models (LLMs) offer an effective means of correcting transcription errors. However, applying LLM-based correction at scale can become prohibitively expensive. We investigate a selective, cost-aware strategy for LLM-assisted OCR post-correction, using a regression-guided router to predict when LLM correction is likely to improve transcription quality, thereby reducing unnecessary LLM processing and associated costs while preserving historically valid text. We evaluate this strategy on a dataset comprising historical Swiss newspapers published between 1733 and 1945. Our results show that selective correction can retain most of the quality gains of full correction while substantially reducing the LLM token cost. Using Tesseract OCR, sending all text segments for LLM correction improves CER from 6.3% to 2.9% (best approach). In contrast, our regression-guided router achieves CER of 3.1% (0.2% worse) while avoiding routing 40% of segments for LLM correction. Finally, we show that our regression-guided LLM router closely trails the decisions of an oracle that knows in advance which segments benefit from correction.
evidence_items.title: Knowing When to Correct: Cost-Aware LLM Routing for OCR Post-Correction in Historical Documents

evidence_items.summary: Pointwise reranking with large language models (LLMs) evaluates query-document pairs independently and allows parallel processing, but it often struggles with absolute relevance estimation. In this work, we investigate whether non-relevance prompting provides a signal that differs from ordinary relevance prompting in LLM-based pointwise reranking. Specifically, we compute both relevance and non-relevance scores for each query-passage pair and examine two simple ways to combine them: (1) a simple product and (2) a probability-weighted RMSE to the ideal label targets. We evaluate these scores on 10 datasets from TREC and BEIR using nDCG@10 with GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. With GPT-4o-mini, bidirectional scoring significantly improves over relevance-only scoring and achieves performance comparable to RankGPT, although gains over a two-prompt relevance-only control are not statistically significant. Further analysis on highly relevant DL19 pairs shows that flipped non-relevance scores often raise the scores of documents underestimated by the relevance prompt. In contrast, the effectiveness of using non-relevance scores for Llama varies across datasets, suggesting that the utility of non-relevance prompting is model-dependent.
evidence_items.title: On Non-Relevance Signals in Pointwise LLM-based Reranking

evidence_items.summary: Reconstruction-based multivariate time-series anomaly detection (MTSAD) typically assigns anomaly scores using the mean squared reconstruction error (MSE). We show that this score has a spectral blind spot : because MSE responds strongly to large errors, anomaly signals in low-energy bands of the training spectrum are ignored by the score. The per-dataset oracle headroom, measured on 9 of 12 well-known benchmark datasets, objectively confirms this diagnosis. From this, we propose SBAND (Spectral Band-wise Score Debiasing for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), a post-hoc correction determined in closed form from the spectrum statistics of the training input alone, without labels, validation, or separate tuning. SBAND is attached only at the scoring stage without retraining: an activation gate automatically disables the correction on diffuse datasets, and a closed-form gain determines the correction strength from the training spectrum negentropy. On the 12 benchmark datasets, SBAND with an average AUROC of 0.802 (only 0.007 below the per-dataset oracle of 0.809), outperforms the state-of-the-art model CATCH (0.759) by +0.043 as well as all 13 external baselines. SBAND is backbone-agnostic. We apply it on CATCH, replacing the FFT with a real-valued FFT (rFFT) for efficiency, yielding a 2.6× training speedup over CATCH (6.48h vs 16.97h) and improving both accuracy and efficiency over the state of the art. The code is available at https://github.com/bigbases/SBAND.
evidence_items.title: SBAND: Spectral Band-wise Score Debiasing for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Decoder-only language models score text through next-token likelihoods over tokenizer-induced token sequences. This scoring interface becomes unstable when tokenizer segmentation shapes candidate selection or passage relevance scores rather than contextual fit alone. Agglutinative languages expose this problem sharply because morphosyntactic information is densely packed into surface forms. Korean offers a representative agglutinative stress case through particles, endings, compounds, and spacing variation. We propose Interleave Attention, a decoder augmentation that injects morphology-aware auxiliary representations into the scoring path. Prefix-aligned interleaving integrates these representations into a fused causal sequence rather than a separate cross-attention memory. Under matched initialization, continued-pretraining corpus, objective, and scoring interface, Interleave continued pretraining (CPT) produces stable trajectory-level gains over a parameter-matched decoder-only baseline, improving the overall benchmark average by 3.34 points and the context-conditioned average by 7.12 points. Controlled relevance scoring shows improved rank-sensitive scoring under a fixed hard-negative pool, and Korean surface-form stress tests indicate additional Korean-side robustness under surface variation. These results support a bottleneck-mitigation interpretation that separates the general Interleave effect from the morphology-based auxiliary-tokenizer effect.
evidence_items.title: Mitigating the Morpheme Tokenization Bottleneck in Agglutinative Languages: A Korean Case Study with Interleave Attention

evidence_items.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) persistently suffer from object hallucinations, generating plausible yet factually incorrect outputs that fabricate objects non-existent in the visual input. Existing mitigation methods typically fall into three paradigms: fine-tuning with targeted data, which incurs prohibitive computational costs; applying contrastive decoding, which introduces high inference latency and may penalize beneficial language priors; or intervening in attention weights via heuristic hard-truncation or head-homogeneous shifts, operations that may discard information from selected attention paths. Building upon the third paradigm, we present Spatial-Aware Dynamic Intervention (SADI). SADI discards conventional rigid truncations in favor of a spatial-aware soft mask to adaptively correct visual-semantic misalignments. Specifically, it establishes a robust median consensus among multiple attention heads to anchor reliable visual representations. Guided by the spatial variance across these heads, SADI dynamically allocates intervention weights and employs a soft mask to gently suppress anomalous attention distributions. As a lightweight, training-free inference solution, our method reframes attention modulation as a smooth, continuous recalibration process. Ultimately, SADI effectively rectifies semantic drift while maintaining comparable generation fluency and description richness in our evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SADI significantly reduces both sentence- and instance-level hallucinations while maintaining description richness. Across the evaluated CHAIR, POPE, and MME benchmarks, SADI shows consistent gains in the tested settings. Code is released at https://github.com/yz-8/SADI.
evidence_items.title: SADI: Spatial-Aware Dynamic Intervention for Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multivariate time-series anomaly detection commonly relies on reconstruction errors produced by autoencoders as anomaly scores. However, in real-world industrial systems, normal states are often heterogeneous: normal windows that are difficult to model may yield large reconstruction errors, whereas some anomalous windows can still be well reconstructed. As a result, raw reconstruction errors are not always directly comparable across different test windows. To address this issue, we propose RNEC, a post-training reference-guided neighborhood evidence calibration framework. Without modifying the parameters of a trained autoencoder, RNEC constructs a latent representation–reconstruction error reference field from training windows. During inference, it combines the relative reconstruction difficulty measured against latent neighbors with the degree to which a test window is covered by the training reference distribution, thereby producing calibrated anomaly evidence. Experiments on five public multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks show that RNEC achieves the best macro-average F1, AUROC, and AUPR, with the best performance in 11 out of 15 dataset–metric combinations, while remaining lightweight and plug-and-play. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/RNEC-code/rnec.
evidence_items.title: RNEC: Reference-Guided Neighborhood Evidence Calibration for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Unsupervised graph anomaly detection (UGAD) is crucial to identify anomalous behavior in graph-structured data. Most existing methods rely on contrastive learning, typically adopting node-subgraph and node-node contrastive paradigms. However, anomalous nodes can interfere with local neighborhood modeling, compromising node-subgraph contrast. Moreover, the training of these two paradigms is often coupled, which limits their ability to fully capture node-level anomaly cues. To address these limitations, we propose DeSEN, a novel two-stage UGAD learning framework that decouples the two contrastive learning paradigms. In Stage 1, we introduce a structural-semantic neighborhood enhancement strategy based on biased views to suppress anomalous interference during neighborhood modeling. In Stage 2, we leverage the confident node sets constructed by affinity ranking in Stage 1 to guide node-node contrast, thereby providing effective global node-level anomaly signals. Extensive experiments on eight real-world benchmark datasets, including a large-scale Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) dataset, against ten state-of-the-art baselines show that DeSEN significantly improves both AUROC and AUPRC, while the training and inference pipeline completes within a few minutes. These results validate the effectiveness and efficiency of DeSEN.
evidence_items.title: Towards Decoupled Contrastive Learning with Neighborhood Enhancement for Graph Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Technical-medical documentation poses a challenging setting for grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): valid answers often depend on exact thresholds, workflow constraints and combinations of documented conditions. However, existing RAG benchmarks rarely provide the fine-grained evidence, completeness, citation, abstention and safety annotations needed to evaluate such behaviour. We introduce QFR-RAG, a multi-level evaluation resource for grounded RAG over Quantitative Flow Ratio (QFR) documentation for cardiology software used in angiography-based assessment of coronary disease. QFR-RAG comprises a 400-question benchmark: 50 technical extraction questions with reference answers and gold evidence, 50 multi-evidence questions annotated with 103 required evidence slots and 278 atomic answer nuggets and 300 paired adversarial questions targeting nonsensical requests, false premises and unsafe relaxation of documented constraints. Its layered evaluation protocol separates retrieval sufficiency, exact correctness, nugget-level completeness, citation grounding, abstention and safety-preserving refusal or correction, revealing empirically distinct failure modes across retrieval and generation. As a baseline validation, we benchmark retrieval pipelines and general-purpose and medically specialised language models of different sizes, showing that strong performance on exact technical extraction does not imply complete multi-evidence answering. QFR-RAG provides a deeply annotated framework for evaluating grounded, complete and safety-aware RAG in controlled technical-medical software documentation and illustrates an annotation design that can be adapted to similar parameter-dense domains.
evidence_items.title: QFR-RAG: A Multi-Level Evaluation Resource for Grounded RAG over Technical-Medical Documentation

evidence_items.summary: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.
evidence_items.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.

evidence_items.summary: Image manipulation has been a common practice since the early days of photography, and has evolved into a sophisticated threat with the rise of powerful image editing tools and generative AI. It can be used to spread misinformation, manipulate public opinion, and cause harm to individuals and communities. In this article, we study the problem of determining whether an image is misleading, i.e. edited in a misleading way. We introduce a risk framework to assess the intrinsic interpretive shift (ITS) of an ordered image pair, which evaluates whether the final edited image changes the interpretation supported by a source reference image. We show our risk framework can be operationalized with the Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) provenance framework. We estimate ITS with a single-call vision-language implementation of our risk framework, which first checks for meaningful visual differences, then tests whether the differences induce interpretive shift, and finally determines whether the shift is fully explained by permissible transformations rather than content-level changes. The system outputs a binary label (potentially misleading or not) together with interpretive clues and a short justification. To test the approach and show that ITS is a measurable proxy for misleading edits, we built a benchmark of 418 ordered pairs, drawn from real-world fact-check cases and meaning-preserving transformations. The best-performing model configuration (gpt-5.4) achieves 88.2% precision, 94.2% recall, and 96.5% balanced accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/liyu0x/ITS_detection/.
evidence_items.title: Interpretation-Aware Image Manipulation Detection

evidence_items.summary: Traffic flow forecasting requires modeling rapidly changing local fluctuations and slowly evolving regional trends. Existing Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE)-based traffic forecasting models usually evolve states at a single spatial granularity, which may entangle node-level volatility with macroscopic evolution and lead to over-smoothed peak predictions under volatile traffic conditions. To capture such mixed-scale dynamics, we propose Hierarchical Slow-Fast Spatial-Temporal Graph ODE (HSF-STGODE), a region-guided slow-fast continuous framework for traffic flow forecasting. HSF-STGODE decomposes traffic evolution into two coupled continuous processes: a Fast Graph ODE modeling node-level short-term fluctuations on the sensor graph, and a Slow Graph ODE capturing region-level trends on a learnable latent region graph. The two processes are connected through bottom-up aggregation and top-down guidance, enabling regional trends to provide stable context for fine-grained node evolution. To further model lagged propagation and irregular local variations, we incorporate a delay-aware pattern module, a flow-consistency regularizer, and a dual-gated fusion mechanism for scale-specific multi-period initialization. Experiments on four widely used PeMS benchmarks show HSF-STGODE achieves the best or tied-best RMSE across all datasets, with strong MAPE performance and competitive MAE results against representative and strong baselines. These results suggest region-guided slow-fast continuous modeling is particularly effective in reducing large forecasting deviations for traffic flow forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/KYasmaine/HSF-STGODE.
evidence_items.title: Region-Guided Slow-Fast Graph ODEs for Traffic Flow Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Ordering-based causal discovery decomposes DAG learning into topological order estimation and edge pruning. Existing work has focused on order estimation, while pruning often relies on component-wise additive tests that can miss parent effects expressed through co-parent context. We propose Context-Aware Pruning of Edges (CAPE), a plug-in pruning module that formulates post-ordering edge pruning as local model selection. For each candidate edge, CAPE computes the out-of-sample gain in conditional log-predictive density of the child when the candidate parent is included in the current parent context. It retains the edge only when this contextual gain exceeds an MDL-inspired adaptive structural penalty. This criterion evaluates conditional predictive evidence rather than isolated additive effects, enabling CAPE to retain interaction-driven dependencies while pruning weak finite-sample edges. Across six ordering backbones, CAPE improves SHD, SID, and F1 on synthetic nonlinear graphs and assumption-violation benchmarks, including simulated latent confounding, measurement error, post-nonlinear mechanisms, and non-i.i.d. sampling. On empirical benchmarks, CAPE lowers average SHD and SID under the same estimated orders. Its hierarchical group-pruning strategy reduces pruning time by up to 7.5 times on larger graphs. Source code is available at https://github.com/ku-milab/CAPE.
evidence_items.title: Context-Aware Pruning for Ordering-Based Causal Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Temporal distribution shift (TDS) degrades the generalization of recommender systems: models trained on past interactions face systematically different user behavior in future time windows. While incremental training on recent data is widely used in industry production, it can over-adapt to transient patterns and exacerbate instability. Existing approaches such as invariant learning and self-supervised learning offer partial solutions but often suffer from unstable temporal generalization, representation collapse, or inefficient data utilization. To address these limitations, we propose ELBOTDS, a probabilistic framework for temporally robust recommendation. First, we identify key shifting factors on real-world production data and design a simple yet effective data augmentation strategy that simulate realistic time-varying factors to extend the training support. Second, we derive a self-supervised variational objective ELBOTDS to harness the benefits of this extended distribution while preventing representation collapse. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate ELBOTDS consistently improves next-period ranking performance over strong baselines, yielding a 2.33% uplift in GMV per user online and has been successfully deployed in production. Code is available at https://github.com/FuCongResearchSquad/ELBO4TDS.
evidence_items.title: ELBOTDS: Temporal Distribution Shift Generalization for Industry-Scale Recommender Systems

evidence_items.summary: We introduce HiSAC (Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression), a framework that compresses ultra-long user behavior sequences into compact, personalized interest representations for industrial recommendation. Modeling histories with thousands of interactions is essential for capturing dynamic user preferences, yet existing compression methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: they impose a fixed number of global interest centers that ignore per-user granularity, and they rely on hard assignment that introduces quantization error and discards long-tail behaviors. HiSAC addresses both via three tightly integrated components: (1)multimodal tokenization with Residual Quantized VAE that maps items to a hierarchical discrete codebook, (2)a hierarchical voting mechanism that sparsely activates user-specific interest-agents as adaptive preference centers, and (3)a Soft-Routing Attention that aggregates all historical signals in a debiased semantic space, weighting contributions by similarity to minimize quantization error and preserve sparse long-tail preferences. We validate HiSAC on a large-scale industrial dataset (200M users, 30B interactions) and the public Taobao-MM benchmark, where it consistently outperforms both generic compression baselines and state-of-the-art sequence models. Deployed on Taobao's ''Guess What You Like'' homepage serving hundreds of millions of daily active users, HiSAC delivers a 1.65% CTR uplift, 2.24% CTCVR improvement, and 2.56% increase in orders while reducing end-to-end inference latency by over 40% relative to the deployed compression baseline.
evidence_items.title: HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommendation Systems

evidence_items.summary: Generative models have demonstrated significant potential in semi-supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD) by synthesizing pseudo-anomalies to mitigate extreme label scarcity. However, existing Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based frameworks face two key limitations: mode collapse during generation and poor topological adaptability. Specifically, traditional methods usually enforce rigid structural alignment, which wrongly treats normal heterophilic connections as anomalies, leading to performance degradation on heterophilic graphs. In this paper, we argue that these failures stem from indiscriminate learning, where models lack an adaptive mechanism to evaluate the quality and reliability of generated pseudo-anomalies and structural priors. To bridge this gap, we propose Meta-ResGAD, a novel bi-level optimization framework that introduces a ''learning-to-reweight'' paradigm into generative GAD. By reformulating GAD as a nested optimization problem, we divide the learning process into two levels: in the upper level, we utilize unrolled differentiation to optimize an upper-level Scorer using clean validation feedback; in the lower level, a structure-aware generation process explicitly decouples semantic and structural signals. Guided by meta-gradients, the Scorer acts as a dynamic sample filter that penalizes uninformative noise to prevent mode collapse, and adaptively down-weights unreliable structural priors to disentangle structural anomalies from normal heterophily. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Meta-ResGAD achieves state-of-the-art performance with robust topology-adaptive generalization, while maintaining the high inference efficiency and low memory consumption crucial for large-scale industrial deployment. Our code is now available at: https://github.com/TDSCX/AJAX.
evidence_items.title: Meta-ResGAD: Bi-Level Optimization for Topology-Adaptive Graph Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Lifetime value (LTV) prediction is a key component of decision-making in online advertising, e-commerce, and recommender systems. In practice, however, LTV modeling is scenario-dependent because data distributions differ across applications. Practitioners often rely on scenario-specific pipelines with repeated feature engineering, objective adjustment, and tuning. These workflows require manual effort and are hard to transfer. We propose AgentLTV, an automated multi-agent search-then-evolution framework for lifetime value prediction. AgentLTV treats each candidate solution as an executable pipeline program. LLM-driven agents generate code, run and repair pipelines, and analyze execution feedback. Two decision agents coordinate a two-stage search. The Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) stage explores a broad space of modeling choices under a fixed budget, guided by the Polynomial Upper Confidence bounds for Trees criterion and a Pareto-aware multi-metric value function. The Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) stage refines the best MCTS program via island-based evolution with crossover, mutation, and migration. Experiments on a large-scale proprietary dataset and a public benchmark show that AgentLTV consistently discovers strong models across ranking and error metrics. Online bucket-level analysis further indicates improved ranking consistency and value calibration, especially for high-value and negative-LTV segments. We summarize practitioner-oriented takeaways: use MCTS for rapid adaptation to new data patterns, use EA for stable refinement, and validate deployment readiness with bucket-level ranking and calibration diagnostics. The proposed AgentLTV has been successfully deployed online. Details of our optimal model and prompts are available at https://github.com/wuchaowei123/AgentLTV.
evidence_items.title: An Automated Multi-Agent Search-then-Evolution Framework for Lifetime Value Prediction

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to temporomandibular disorders (TMD), particularly in imaging, diagnosis, classification, and prediction. However, the global research landscape, knowledge structure, and evolving research priorities remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to systematically map the development and emerging trends of AI research in TMD.


METHODS
A total of 311 publications from 2015 to 2026 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. Bibliometric and visualization analyses were conducted using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and R (bibliometrix) to examine publication trends, scientific collaboration, citation networks, research hotspots, and thematic evolution.


RESULTS
Publication output increased markedly after 2019, reaching its highest level in 2025. China contributed the most publications (n = 111), followed by the United States (n = 70), South Korea (n = 45), and Turkey (n = 33), with differences in international collaboration patterns. The knowledge structure reflected interdisciplinary connections among dentistry, medical imaging, computer science, and engineering. Major research hotspots included machine learning, deep learning, magnetic resonance imaging, automated diagnosis, disease classification, and prediction. Temporal analyses revealed a shift from algorithm development toward imaging-based assessment, TMD classification, and clinically oriented predictive applications.


CONCLUSION
AI-related TMD research has expanded rapidly, with increasing emphasis on diagnostic and predictive applications. Future research should prioritize standardized protocols, multicenter datasets, external validation, and evaluation of clinical applicability to facilitate reliable integration into TMD management.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in temporomandibular disorders: A bibliometric analysis of research trends, hotspots, and emerging frontiers.

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal conversational recommender systems (CRS) integrate dialogue, knowledge graphs, and visual signals. Recent work reports substantial gains over the knowledge-graph baseline KGSF on the INSPIRED dataset (R@10: 0.132→0.257). However, this pipeline couples ViT-based image embeddings with zero-fill handling for 23.7% of items missing poster data and augments training with LLM-generated synthetic dialogues, failing to isolate the visual modality. We present a controlled reproducibility study, maintaining the MSCRS backbone and training fixed while intervening on data and image-embedding inputs. To isolate item-specific visual correspondence from representation-level artifacts, we replace ViT embeddings with three distractor conditions: random Gaussian vectors, zero vectors, and shuffled real ViT embeddings. We also apply an artificial 23.7% missingness mask to ReDial and probe synthetic-dialogue training using a valid-best checkpoint protocol. Across INSPIRED and ReDial, the distractor conditions do not consistently separate from the original ViT condition; the multi-seed mean R@10 spread is only 0.007. Conversely, synthetic dialogue shows a directional paired difference (Δ R@10 = +0.031 \pm 0.020, Cohen's d_z=1.59). Furthermore, selection bias introduces a max-test versus valid-best gap of up to +0.035 R@10. These results do not imply that images are unhelpful, but rather that modality-specific visual effects are currently confounded by missing-node graph effects and augmentation artifacts. We propose a reproducibility-oriented audit procedure for multimodal CRS evaluation, covering distractor controls, missingness validation, and strict checkpoint selection.
evidence_items.title: Auditing Multimodal Claims: A Controlled Reproducibility Study of Graph-based Conversational Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: An efficient urban drainage solution, sustainable pervious concrete mitigates stormwater runoff but exhibits highly non-linear hydraulic behavior based on its constituents. This study presents an explainable data-driven framework to accurately predict pervious concrete permeability. A 70:30 holdout partitioning strategy was applied to a meta-dataset of 150 experimental records to train and validate four distinct machine learning algorithms: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB). The input space comprised critical mix design parameters (aggregate-to-binder, fly ash-to-binder, and water-to-binder ratios, alongside mean aggregate size), while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) interpreted the optimal model. Among the evaluated machine learning algorithms, the XGB model demonstrated superior predictive capability for pervious concrete permeability compared to ANN, SVR, and KNN models. Post-hoc SHAP analysis successfully decoded the model’s “black box,” proving that the aggregate-to-binder ratio and aggregate size are primary drivers governing interconnected void space. In conclusion, the developed framework replaces tedious, trial-and-error laboratory iterations with highly accurate, physically consistent virtual simulations.
evidence_items.title: Explainable machine learning modeling for predicting the hydraulic permeability of fly ash pervious concrete

evidence_items.summary:
This paper aims to develop and validate a legally grounded accounting measurement framework for modern-slavery governance and examines whether the resulting governance measures are associated with firms' financial distress risk. Existing research predominantly relies on ESG ratings, disclosure proxies, or qualitative assessments that do not clearly distinguish externally specified governance obligations from firms' disclosed governance architecture. We address this measurement gap by translating mandatory modern-slavery governance requirements into reproducible firm-level accounting measures and evaluating their informational relevance for accounting-based risk assessment.
 
 
 
 This research adopts a two-corpus measurement framework. The first corpus comprises mandatory modern-slavery legislation and internationally recognised institutional frameworks issued between 1930 and 2024, including the Tariff Act (1930), California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, UK Modern Slavery Act, French Duty of Vigilance Law, Australian Modern Slavery Act, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, Norwegian Transparency Act, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and complementary institutional frameworks including the ILO, OECD, PRI, and the United Nations Guiding Principles. Rather than serving as institutional background, these sources are used to define the governance construct by identifying legally codified organisational obligations and harmonising them into a unified governance ontology representing implementation-oriented governance mechanisms.The second corpus comprises more than 5,000 annual reports of S&P 500 firms covering the period 2010–2022. Artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and supervised machine-learning techniques operationalise the predefined governance ontology to identify disclosed evidence of implementation-oriented governance mechanisms within corporate reports, thereby generating firm-year Modern Slavery Index (MSI) measures. A complementary Digital Transformation Index (DTI) captures disclosed digital capability. The empirical design combines firm and year fixed-effects estimation with 2SLS endogeneity-sensitivity analysis and additional tests addressing disclosure intensity and boilerplate reporting, institutional validity, digital-capability interactions, competing explanations and potential mechanisms.
 
 
 
 The findings show that firms disclosing stronger implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance mechanisms exhibit lower financial distress risk, although the strength of this association varies across the underlying institutional architectures. Among the four governance measures, the California-based MSI2 provides the strongest evidence, indicating that disclosed governance mechanisms centred on supplier verification, monitoring, accountability, and supply-chain oversight are associated with lower financial distress risk. Digital transformation, by contrast, does not independently reduce financial distress risk and is associated with lower Altman Z-scores in several specifications, a pattern consistent with – but not establishing – the organisational costs and implementation challenges that may accompany technological transformation. Importantly, digital capability also conditions the association between disclosed modern-slavery governance and financial distress risk, with the positive MSI4 × DTI interaction indicating that the financial relevance of governance disclosure varies with firms' digital capabilities under particular institutional arrangements. Overall, the findings indicate that legally grounded measures of disclosed modern-slavery governance contain economically relevant information for financial-distress assessment, while their associations vary across governance architectures and according to firms' digital capabilities.
 
 
 
 This paper makes four contributions to the accounting literature. First, it develops four transparent, legally grounded, and fully reproducible Modern Slavery Indices (MSI1–MSI4), each derived from distinct regulatory and institutional governance frameworks, providing researchers, practitioners, managers, auditors, and policymakers with standardised accounting measures of implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance. Second, it introduces a novel two-corpus measurement framework that explicitly separates construct definition from empirical observation by deriving the governance construct from mandatory legislation and internationally recognised frameworks before operationalising it through AI-enabled textual analysis of corporate reports. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and supervised machine-learning techniques can operationalise externally defined governance obligations into scalable firm-level accounting information while preserving construct validity. Finally, it provides evidence that these legally grounded accounting measures contain decision-useful information for accounting-based risk assessment, advancing research on non-financial accounting measurement, governance architecture, disclosure credibility, internal control systems, and corporate resilience under emerging mandatory reporting regimes.
evidence_items.title: Modern slavery governance, digital transformation and financial distress risk: evidence from legally grounded text-based accounting measures

evidence_items.summary: Attributed Question Answering systems increasingly ground answers in tabular structured corpora—Wikipedia infoboxes and relational tables, the dominant structured evidence in open-domain RAG—yet citation faithfulness methods remain designed for text passages. This mismatch allows LLMs to cite the correct table but the wrong row, silently aggregate values without justification, or attribute claims to schema fields that do not semantically entail them. We formalize multiple structural hallucination modes specific to structured-data attribution and introduce CiteAlign-Table, a hybrid neuro-symbolic verifier that checks schema-path validity, cell-level semantic alignment, and arithmetic consistency between claims and their cited records. A schema-aware entailment module detects entity and content misalignments, while a lightweight program synthesizer verifies numerical aggregation, temporal consistency, and unit correctness. Experiments on a hybrid benchmark of Wikipedia infoboxes and WikiTables show that CiteAlign-Table achieves 0.84 F1 in detecting unfaithful structured citations, while text-only baselines degrade to 0.61 F1. By extending citation faithfulness from passages to structured records, our work makes attributed QA trustworthy over the heterogeneous data that production RAG systems actually retrieve.
evidence_items.title: CiteAlign-Table: Verifying Citation Faithfulness when LLMs Attribute to Structured Data

evidence_items.summary: The central challenge of one-class tabular anomaly detection lies not only in the absence of anomaly labels, but also in that abnormality can only be defined relative to normality. Such deviations do not have a fixed form in heterogeneous tabular spaces, and thus detection methods have to rely on implicit assumptions about anomaly patterns. For example, reconstruction-based paradigms expect anomalies hard to reconstruct through normal mappings, while distance-based paradigms expect anomalies to exhibit irregularity in local neighborhoods. However, real anomalies do not always follow these assumptions. They may be well reconstructed due to the generalization ability of deep models, or appear locally plausible. Therefore, this paper no longer seeks new reconstruction tricks or local constraints, but instead investigates whether discriminative cues can be discovered from the overall organization of normal patterns themselves. To this end, we analyze the inter-sample connection structure (T-Graph), and find that, under this data-dependent organization, anomalies induce stronger high-frequency responses. This suggests that spectral information captures structural changes induced by anomalous perturbations to normal connection patterns, thereby providing a new structural cue for distinguishing normal and anomalous data. Motivated by this, we propose FASEN (Frequency-Aware Spectral Encoding Network). It first employs wavelet filters to decouple graph signals into multi-scale spectral representations. Subsequently, we design a Frequency Selection module to adaptively learn the frequency preference of normal data, thereby guiding the model to reconstruct utilizing the topological features dominated by normal patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that FASEN outperforms SOTA methods. Further analysis indicates that this mechanism behaves as a physically interpretable matched filter. The complete code is available at https://github.com/criticcc/FASEN.
evidence_items.title: Frequency-Aware Anomaly Detection in Tabular Data

evidence_items.summary: Data integration remains labor-intensive, making projects lengthy, costly, and difficult to automate end to end. Although substantial progress has been made on core subtasks such as schema matching, ontology alignment, and entity matching, these subtasks often stop short of producing executable transformations. In ontology-based data integration, mappings can identify corresponding classes and properties, but value normalization, literal conversion, and multi-fact generation are still commonly implemented through bespoke scripts. We introduce Fact Generating Functions (FGFs), executable triple-conversion functions that transform RDF triples expressed under source semantics into semantically corresponding triples under target semantics. FGFs bridge the gap between ontology alignment and RDF materialization by making transformation logic explicit, inspectable, and executable. We present an automated pipeline that instantiates the approach by converting relational data into RDF, identifying source-to-target correspondences, generating intermediate logical rules, and materializing target triples through executable FGFs. We evaluate the method on benchmark scenarios for relational data-to-ontology integration and show competitive results across diverse mapping settings. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using FGFs as a practical abstraction to automate semantic data mapping and reduce the need for manually engineered transformation scripts.
evidence_items.title: From Ontology Alignments to Executable Code: Automating Data Integration with Fact Generating Functions

evidence_items.summary: Diversity-driven data selection offers a scalable way to reduce code instruction-tuning costs, yet it relies on a fragile assumption: geometric spread in representation space should correspond to training-useful semantic coverage.
