In code data selection, our diagnosis reveals a geometric bias behind this assumption: dense embedding geometry can be strongly influenced by rare surface forms, verbose constraints, and implementation artifacts, causing diversity objectives to over-explore locally sparse or globally peripheral samples whose training utility is not guaranteed. To correct this bias, we propose Semantically Anchored Geometric Coverage (SAGC), a framework for reshaping representation geometry using LLM-generated macro-intent labels as semantic anchors for dense micro-context representations. Rather than replacing standard diversity objectives, SAGC reshapes the geometry exposed to them, using macro-intent anchors to constrain dense-space exploration toward high-level algorithmic structure without requiring downstream validation signals, gradient feedback, or evaluation results. Using only 20k samples selected from a 446k pool, SAGC reaches 0.4006 on LiveCodeBench, approaching full-data training at 0.4027. Further diagnostics and out-of-benchmark evaluations show that semantic anchoring provides a structured correction to this geometric bias.
evidence_items.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Geometric Bias in Diversity-Driven Code Instruction Data Selection

evidence_items.summary: Three-dimensional virtual histology using synchrotron radiation micro-computed tomography enables non-destructive visualization of biological tissue microarchitecture with isotropic resolution. To support quantitative studies of human pancreatic morphology, we provide high-resolution 3D X-ray imaging datasets of 55 pancreatic tissue cores from 32 individuals. The collection comprises histologically non-diseased pancreatic tissue from organ donors and non-neoplastic regions of surgical resection specimens from patients with pancreatic cancer, including subgroups with insulin-dependent diabetes or following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue cores with a diameter of 1 mm were imaged at 650 nm isotropic voxel size, yielding a mean effective spatial resolution of 1.66 µm. The cohort includes reconstructed volumes, corresponding immunohistochemistry, clinical metadata, expert-validated annotations, and dataset-specific example 2.5D U-Net models for automated segmentation of islets of Langerhans. A representative co-registered section yielded a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.81 and intersection-over-union of 0.67. This openly accessible, FAIR-compliant resource supports quantitative analysis of endocrine, exocrine, ductal, and stromal architecture and provides a reproducible reference framework for three-dimensional virtual histology of human pancreatic tissue and computational benchmarking.
evidence_items.title: Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we propose a prototype-learning framework that addresses a common limitation of proximity-based methods: the need to specify proximity weights in advance. Rather than relying on a fixed proximity matrix computed from raw observations, the proposed method jointly learns the prototype representation and the proximity structure. We implement this idea by extending the convex-clustering framework, replacing the pre-specified proximity input with a self-representation matrix learned from the prototype-level representation. The resulting adaptive proximity matrix captures intrinsic relationships among prototypes, yielding prototypes that better reflect the underlying data geometry rather than merely serving as cluster centers. We solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem using an optimization algorithm based on multiaffine ADMM. Experiments on synthetic non-Euclidean datasets and real benchmark datasets show that the proposed method learns prototypes that better cover the underlying data geometry than standard convex clustering, while removing the need to manually specify proximity weights.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Local Centers toward Prototypes: Joint Learning of Self-Representation and Adaptive Clustering

evidence_items.summary: Previous gas-sensing datasets were designed and collected in sealed environments primarily for laboratory research or domain-specific applications. The lack of air-exposed settings limits the study and modeling of the gas properties under natural volatilization. This work bridges this gap by building an unsealed gas-sensing dataset for real-world gas classification, dubbed Daily52, collected from 52 everyday items measured using a self-developed electronic nose (e-nose). We thoroughly benchmark various odor classification models as baselines, among which InceptionTime is found to achieve an impressive 88.24% accuracy in recognizing items. Comprehensive analysis further demonstrates that our dataset is high-resolution and effective for studying the olfactory modality. Potential olfactory research is also discussed beyond our dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first dataset that enables benchmarking methods for classifying real-world gas-sensing data of natural volatiles.
evidence_items.title: Daily52: An Air-exposed Smell Dataset for Real-world Odor Classification

evidence_items.summary: Anomaly detection in data streams is vital in areas such as network security, finance, and IoT, but it is hindered by the scarcity and cost of labels. We propose the Streaming Semi-Supervised Adaptive Isolation Forest (S3AIF), which extends the Adaptive Isolation Forest to partially labelled data, evolving streams by using discrimination power as a unifying principle to: (i) weight isolation trees when scoring; (ii) replace the least discriminative tree at each window; and (iii) select query instances for active learning by path-length disagreement. Across 22 benchmark datasets with a labelling budget below 1%, S3 AIF outperforms HiLAD in both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC while running more than three times faster and ranks first against 10 unsupervised baselines in ROC-AUC. An ablation confirms that discrimination-power-based tree replacement is the main driver of S3 AIF's performance.
evidence_items.title: Streaming Semi-Supervised Adaptive Isolation Forest

evidence_items.summary: Layout-conditioned image generation aims to synthesize images that match specified object categories and bounding boxes. However, generated images often fail to follow the intended layout conditions, resulting in hallucinations such as missing or spurious objects and spatial misalignment. When such inconsistent image-layout pairs are used as augmented training data, they can degrade the performance of object detectors. To address this issue, we propose LG-PLO, a layout-grounded Plackett–Luce optimization framework for instance-aware image generation. LG-PLO jointly considers image- and layout-level preferences using three candidates: a preferred image with correct layout, a rejected image with correct layout, and a preferred image with incorrect layout. LG-PLO then optimizes a Plackett-Luce objective that ranks images satisfying both preferences higher than those satisfying only one. Experiments on the COCO benchmark show that LG-PLO achieves a better balance between visual fidelity and layout adherence compared to baselines, while also improving detector performance when generated images are used for data augmentation.
evidence_items.title: LG-PLO: Layout-Grounded Plackett–Luce Optimization for Instance-Aware Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Obesity in patients with chronic ischemic heart disease (IHD) reflects a metabolically active state involving low-grade inflammation, insulin resistance, and accelerated atherosclerosis, yet conventional risk scores capture these processes poorly. This study examined the relationships between epicardial adipose tissue, coronary artery calcification, and systemic inflammatory and metabolic markers in patients with IHD and obesity, and evaluated an integrative risk model. A total of 135 inpatients with confirmed chronic IHD (mean age 54.2 ± 12.8 years; 34.8% women; mean body mass index [BMI] 28.3 ± 5.8 kg/m²) were grouped by BMI. Assessment included SCORE2 risk estimation, multislice computed tomography of coronary calcium and epicardial fat volume, and measurement of interleukin-6, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, fasting glucose, insulin, and HOMA-IR. The prevalence of arterial hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia rose with increasing adiposity, and clinically significant calcification (calcium score ≥ 100) became more frequent at higher BMI, whereas SCORE2 values remained in the moderate range. Inflammatory markers increased with BMI, and HOMA-IR was about twice as high in obese as in normal-weight patients (3.3 vs. 1.6). An integrative model combining clinical, inflammatory, epicardial fat, and calcification data showed high discriminative ability (AUC = 0.948). Integrating imaging and inflammatory-metabolic markers may improve risk stratification beyond SCORE2 in obese patients with IHD.
evidence_items.title: APPLICATION OF INTEGRATIVE MODELS IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE AND OBESITY

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains R source code and supporting documentation associated with the study entitled "Documented enteral energy and post-landmark mortality: A retrospective cohort study." The study uses MIMIC-IV version 3.1 to investigate associations between electronic health record (EHR)-documented enteral energy and subsequent 28-day mortality among mechanically ventilated adult intensive care unit patients. The code package includes scripts for cohort construction, enteral nutrition record processing, energy and protein exposure reconstruction, clinical severity assessment using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, landmark mortality classification, multivariable logistic regression, sensitivity analyses, and the unadjusted analyses prepared for Table 2 of the manuscript. The primary analysis uses a 48-hour enteral nutrition landmark, with a 72-hour landmark sensitivity analysis. Data availability and restrictions The repository contains source code and documentation only. No patient-level MIMIC-IV records, restricted derived datasets, clinical timestamps, credentials, or confidential research outputs are included. MIMIC-IV version 3.1 is available to independently credentialed researchers through PhysioNet, subject to the required training and data use agreement. Reproducibility limitations The analytical models were verified within the original authorized research environment. However, some historical upstream preprocessing scripts and local quality-control dependencies are not included. Consequently, this release should not be interpreted as an independently validated, fully automated raw-data-to-results pipeline. EHR-documented nutritional exposure does not represent independently verified nutrient administration. The observational analyses do not establish causal effects or recommended enteral energy targets. License Original source code and documentation are provided under the MIT License, subject to applicable ownership rights.
evidence_items.title: R analysis code for EHR-documented enteral energy and 28-day post-landmark mortality in MIMIC-IV v3.1

evidence_items.summary: <p>Code and archived results for the manuscript <i>Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography</i>. Ten scripts reproduce every number in the paper: the closed-form shot floor for the family verdict, the power at a 10^5 budget, the sixty-four designs repriced, the seven normalisations, the strength convention, the five-qubit sample, and the check against a real three-qubit calibration. Every script writes a JSON file into <code>results/</code>; the archived copies of those files are included, so the tables can be checked without running anything.</p> <p>The archive also contains <code>nm 10 verify.py</code>, which is the check itself and not a description of one. It compares a fresh run against the archived run (6851 floats, agreeing to 0 relative difference), recomputes the analytic quantities from primitives rather than reading them back (the non-centrality constants, the floor, the acceptance window, the readout penalty, the incoherent allowance), looks for each headline number in the manuscript source as the manuscript prints it, and fails if the compile log contains a TeX error.</p> <p>The fingerprint, the design algebra and the exact rank machinery are shared with a companion note on gate counts, whose supplementary material is deposited separately (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23993247). This deposit is self-contained: the shared modules travel with the scripts, so nothing has to be fetched from the other deposit to run them.</p> <p>One script, <code>nm 09 device.py</code>, reads a third-party dataset that is not redistributed here (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20767110); the download command is in the archive's README.
evidence_items.title: Code and results for: Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains all the numerical models and simulation results used in the paper "Anthropogenic aromatics suppress atmospheric new particle formation," totaling 7 compressed archives. CESM SourceMods.tar contains the source code of the CESM/IMPACT model, which simulates secondary organic aerosols and other atmospheric components and can be added to the standard CESM1.2.2 version for use. Radiation DRF.tar and Radiation IRF.tar are offline radiation models used to calculate aerosol radiative forcing; DRF is used to calculate direct radiative forcing, and IRF is used to calculate indirect radiative forcing. Aerosol PD.tar contains the experimental results calculated by the CESM/IMPACT model based on the 2020 emission scenario (the PD experiment). Aerosol PI.tar contains the experimental results calculated by the CESM/IMPACT model based on the 1850 emission scenario (the PI experiment). DRF.tar contains the calculation results of aerosol direct radiative forcing. IRF.tar contains the calculation results of aerosol indirect radiative forcing. All simulation result archives each contain 12 files, ending with numbers 01–12, representing the results for the 12 months respectively.
evidence_items.title: Anthropogenic aromatics suppress atmospheric new particle formation

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the possibilities of music creation, yet technically convincing audio does not necessarily demonstrate culturally informed musical representation. This position paper introduces Musical DNA, a structured and culturally contextualized research framework for documenting, generating, evaluating, and creatively combining distinctive musical traditions. Developed within the BAMBUGARE AI Music Studio research program, the framework integrates rhythm, instrumentation, vocal and linguistic expression, melodic organization, cultural history, performance practices, and intentional creative transformation. Senegalese mbalax and musical encounters between Senegambian traditions, African American jazz and gospel, and Louisiana zydeco serve as illustrative applications. A six-stage research cycle is proposed, encompassing musical documentation, Musical DNA specification, AI production design, controlled generation, listening evaluation, and iterative refinement. The paper contributes a conceptual and methodological foundation for culturally grounded generative AI music research. It does not report completed controlled listening-study results. Empirical validation of the framework remains a future research objective.
evidence_items.title: Musical DNA and Culturally Grounded Generative AI: A Research Framework for African Musical Heritage and Cross-Cultural Innovation

evidence_items.summary: Habenaria plantaginea is an underexplored terrestrial orchid of ethnomedicinal importance with emerging pharmacological relevance. The species is morphologically characterized by its distinctive bright white flowers and a trilobed labellum bearing conspicuously enlarged, semi-ovate lateral lobes relative to the linear-oblong median lobe. Traditionally, different plant parts, particularly the tubers, have been utilized by indigenous communities in various medicinal preparations for managing a range of health conditions. Present study provides a comprehensive synthesis of the available information on the species, encompassing its botanical characteristics, geographical distribution, ethnomedicinal applications, phytochemical constituents and experimentally investigated pharmacological properties. Published studies have documented diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antinociceptive, antipyretic, antibacterial, antidiabetic and potential anti-Alzheimer effects. These findings indicate considerable scope for further pharmacological investigation. However, the available evidence remains preliminary and requires systematic validation. In particular, bioassay-guided isolation and characterization of active constituents, elucidation of molecular mechanisms, dose-dependent efficacy assessment, toxicological evaluation and pharmacokinetic investigations are necessary to establish its pharmacological relevance. Furthermore, sustainable harvesting, propagation and habitat conservation are essential for safeguarding natural populations of this terrestrial orchid.
evidence_items.title: Habenaria plantaginea Lindl. (Orchidaceae): An underutilized medicinal herb with emerging pharmacological significance

evidence_items.summary: This analysis examines whether scientific abstract characteristics distinguish supporting from refuting evidence, addressing the interpretation of document presentation in scientific verification. Using the 2020 SciFact benchmark, it analyses 773 annotated claim document pairs covering 693 claims and 437 abstracts through descriptive comparisons, document weighting and partition sensitivity checks. Refuting pairs contain abstracts averaging 32.46 words longer than supporting pairs. The refuting share is 14.1 percentage points higher among structured abstracts, while mean relative evidence position differs by only 0.007. Equal document weighting preserves these pooled directions, but length and structure differences narrow substantially in the development partition. Furthermore, 179 abstracts support some claims and refute others despite unchanged document characteristics. These findings distinguish document presentation from the semantic relationship between evidence and a specific claim. The contribution is a descriptive account of how pooled presentation patterns coexist with partition sensitivity and claim dependent stance. Evidence services and benchmark developers should preserve claim specific provenance and disclose document overlap and weighting choices when reporting aggregate comparisons.
evidence_items.title: SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE CHARACTERISTICS AND THEIR ASSOCIATION WITH SUPPORTIVE VERSUS REFUTING ATTRIBUTION IN AUTOMATED CLAIM VERIFICATION

evidence_items.summary: 349,975 Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) pull requests (PRs) from 49,241 public GitHub repositories, opened between January 2025 and May 2026, each labeled by who authored it: a human (199,368), an automation bot (110,814), a silent AI agent (27,684), or a disclosed AI agent (11,290); 819 PRs are unverifiable. IaC tools covered: Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible, Puppet, Chef. Disclosed agents are identified from PR authors and metadata. Silent agents are detected by a commit-level census of 14 signature rules (co-author trailers, generation footers, agent identities); every label is backed by evidence (202,066 rule matches) that can be re-verified on GitHub. Two annotators checked 400 labels (Cohen's kappa 0.96); silent-agent labels have a precision of 99.3%. The archive contains 16 linked Parquet tables (pull requests, authorship labels, evidence, 2.1 million commits, 1.5 million IaC file paths, review and post-merge events, cloud services, repositories), the validation annotations of both reviewers, scripts that recompute the paper's numbers and figures, and a README with setup instructions and a running example. The collection pipeline is available at https://github.com/Charles00119/agentic-iac-mining.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract As there i​s growing interest in utilizing large language models (LLMs) in healthcare education, there are still concerns about their accuracy. The primary study question is to evaluate the accuracy of five LLMs in answering infectious disease (ID) related questions. We compared five LLMs—ChatGPT-4.1, ChatGPT-4o-mini, Claude, Copilot, and Gemini—on 227 exam items from an infectious diseases (ID) course in a Doctor of Pharmacy program. Items were categorized by topic, Bloom’s taxonomy, and format. LLM accuracy across different categories was summarized using descriptive statistics. The Chi-Square test was used to compare results among the different LLMs. Agreement across responses from different LLMs was investigated via Cohen’s Kappa Coefficient. The overall accuracy across all models ranged from 89.4% to 91.2% with ChatGPT 4o-mini scoring highest and Claude and Copilot scoring lowest. LLMs had highest accuracy answering pharmacology questions (93.6%), followed by therapeutics (93.0%), PK/PD (91.1%), microbiology (87.5%), and medicinal chemistry (84%). Medicinal chemistry and microbiology performed significantly worse compared to therapeutics (p < 0.05). Questions categorized as Evaluate/Create performed significantly worse compared to Remember/Understand category (85.6% vs. 92.0%, p < 0.05). The accuracy of questions with a picture was significantly worse than those with no picture (69% vs 91%, respectively). Inter-model agreement was moderate (κ = 0.497–0.613). Contemporary LLMs show high accuracy on ID coursework, with weaknesses in chemistry/microbiology content, higher-order reasoning, and image interpretation; careful integration and guidance are warranted.
evidence_items.title: Performance of five large language models (LLM) on infectious diseases related questions

evidence_items.summary: This study compares the emotion scores assigned by ten locally deployed large language models to English Reddit comments from the GoEmotions dataset. The models were run through Ollama in the same hardware environment, and recorded scores for 27 emotion categories and the neutral category were examined. Each model covered 987–2,493 distinct texts, corresponding to 3,857–9,681 annotation rows in the dataset. Scores were weighted by the number of rows containing each text, following the existing data loading procedure. The analysis covered category means, model profiles, emotion-group totals, score distributions, and correlations between category means across models. For llama2:7b, the mean scores for love, grief, and excitement were 0.528, 0.520, and 0.518, respectively. The highest mean neutral score was observed for olmo2:7b at 0.702. The median across the 28 category means was 0.343 for llama2:7b and 0.042 for gpt-oss:20b. The findings show that the models assigned different score levels to emotion categories within the examined records. The results describe scoring tendencies within the available records, taking differences in text coverage across models into account.
evidence_items.title: Emotion Scoring Profiles of Local Large Language Models on the GoEmotions Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Subjective biases and unreliable evaluation procedures make evaluating higher education faculty challenging. A Fuzzy-AI-Metaheuristic Framework for Teaching Assessment (FAM-Teach) is presented in this research to assess instructional performance adaptively, data-driven, and objectively. It uses AI to analyze massive amounts of feedback data, fuzzy logic to manage qualitative evaluation uncertainty, and the Firefly Algorithm (FA) to improve indicator interaction and weighting. Instruction, student involvement, fair evaluation, and measurable learning outcomes are essential for teaching success. FA optimisation’s quicker convergence and precise parameter weight calculation allow the model to adapt to changing instructional conditions. Experimental validation with 1,200 students from five departments showed that FAM-Teach outperforms traditional methods in performance, consistency, and interpretability. The data were preprocessed, and incomplete data were removed, resulting in 650 instances for training and testing. Success requires participants, timely feedback, and tailored training, according to the study. The findings demonstrate that FAM-Teach is a smart and scalable technique to assess higher education teaching using evidence.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of higher education teaching effectiveness based on fuzzy algorithms and artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: To examine the use of artificial intelligence in the tourism industry and evaluate its impact on operational efficiency and service quality in the context of smart tourism. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study combines an analysis of 32 tourism enterprises operating in the European market with a survey of 124 consumers conducted in 2024–2025. Artificial intelligence adoption was assessed through the level of operational process automation, and content analysis of enterprise reports and platform analytics was used to measure performance before and after implementation. Research Limitation: The study is limited to European tourism enterprises and a relatively small consumer sample. Future research should include broader geographical coverage and longitudinal analysis. Findings: Artificial intelligence significantly improved operational performance. Average service time decreased from 18.6 to 11.2 minutes, automation increased from 27.4% to 61.8%, and customer interaction intensity rose from 1.8 to 2.6 contacts per user. Consumers reported high satisfaction with service quality and personalisation, although trust in intelligent systems remained moderate, indicating that behavioural barriers still constrain the full benefits of AI adoption. Practical Implication: The findings support the adoption of hybrid service models that combine artificial intelligence with human interaction. Social Implication: Effective AI implementation can improve service accessibility, customer satisfaction, and the sustainable development of smart tourism. Originality/Value: The novelty lies in an integrated model linking the share of AI-automated processes with operational variables (service time, customer contacts) and consumer variables (service quality, personalisation, trust).
evidence_items.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Tourism Business

evidence_items.summary: A sequence model can identify a base substitution predicted to alter a splice junction, and a cancer model can assign a tumour to a pathway-defined group. Researchers often interpret these outputs as explanations, although each calls for a different experimental test. This narrative review examines how explainable artificial intelligence is used in regulatory genomics, RNA processing, cancer genomics, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, protein science, molecular property prediction and microbial genomics. It compares the biological entity being explained, the reference used to calculate an effect and the evidence available beyond the original model. Base substitutions and matched molecular pairs permit explicit contrasts. Pathway scores, tissue neighbourhoods and internal protein features require additional tests to separate the proposed mechanism from correlated measurements. Recent evaluations of foundation models also show why comparisons with simple predictors and genuinely held-out biological units matter before interpretation. Across applications, the clearest route to experimental follow-up is to specify an expected molecular event, its direction and a result that would challenge the prediction. This approach separates faithful descriptions of model behaviour from claims supported by an independent assay and clarifies what an explanation contributes to the selection of the next experiment.
evidence_items.title: Applications of Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Bioinformatics and Their Experimental Validation

evidence_items.summary: Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction are key Information Extraction tasks that enable the transformation of unstructured text into structured, machine-interpretable knowledge. In the biomedical domain, the extraction process must be guided by semantic constraints and domain knowledge to prevent the introduction of incorrect, inconsistent, or irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a framework for constrained multi-stage information extraction pipelines guided by biomedical ontologies. The approach relies on the specification of a schema describing the entities, relations, constraints, and semantic dependencies relevant to the target domain. The schema is used to automatically generate a list of context-aware prompts that guide a general-purpose LLM during the extraction process (avoiding specific fine-tuning). The framework further supports mapping to ontology terms, extraction guidelines, and ontology-derived examples to improve extraction consistency and semantic validation. The proposed approach has been integrated into ShemaLink, an intelligent web platform supporting schema specification, prompt generation and execution, ontology-aware mapping, and visualization of extracted entities and relations. Extensive experiments on biomedical information extraction benchmarks show that our approach outperforms existing schema-guided prompt engineering methods by more effectively modeling dependencies between entity and relation extraction tasks, while achieving performance comparable to fine-tuned domain-specific models.
evidence_items.title: Schema-Driven Structured Information Extraction from Biomedical Literature via Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Text-attributed graph (TAG) clustering seeks to identify node groups by jointly exploiting the semantic information encoded in textual attributes and the structural information captured by graph connectivity. Despite significant progress, their performance often becomes less satisfactory under long-tailed distributions. To address this challenge, we introduce Minority-Aware Semantic Alignment via Knowledge Enhancement (MASK), an unsupervised framework designed for long-tailed TAG clustering. The core idea of MASK is to integrate the textual understanding capability of large language models (LLMs) with canonical correlation maximization to construct minority-aware semantic groups. More specifically, MASK first leverages LLMs to augment textual attributes and generate multiple textual views, which are then aligned via canonical correlation. Subsequently, we randomly assign samples into balanced groups with mixed semantics for consistency learning and then emphasize those with higher semantic discrepancy as minority candidates. To enhance clustering with external knowledge, we leverage LLMs to fine-tune the model with ranking guidance, which is then formulated as a regularization term. Extensive experiments on four datasets under two varying imbalance ratios demonstrate the effectiveness of MASK. The implementation of MASK is publicly available at https://github.com/fuyw-aisw/MASK.
evidence_items.title: MASK: Minority-aware Semantic Alignment via Knowledge Enhancement for Long-tailed Graph Clustering

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale web corpora (e.g., C4) are severely imbalanced in terms of political perspective: on the death penalty issue, e.g., left-leaning documents outnumber right-leaning ones by more than 8-fold. Such imbalances can transfer to downstream large language models, reinforcing political bias. We propose Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion (simply, FAIR-PIVOT), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based two-level-agent framework that builds balanced perspective-inverted synthetic data for politically sensitive topics. After annotating web texts with multi-persona LLMs, FAIR-PIVOT retrieves documents from contrasting orientations and inverts their viewpoint, preserving authentic discourse structure rather than rephrasing the same-view text. Across nine topics, FAIR-PIVOT generates 13,954 instances and reduces the total variation distance, a measure of how far the orientation distribution deviates from uniform balance, by up to 83%, while improving linguistic fluency as measured by Perplexity (25.5 → 21.8 ↓). Fine-tuning small language models on the balanced corpus further shifts their downstream behavior toward the intended orientation (Gemma (L--R)% +48 → +34, Qwen +55 → +50), confirming that data-level balancing can yield fairer model responses. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/bigbases/FAIR-PIVOT.
evidence_items.title: FAIR-PIVOT: Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion for Mitigating Political Bias in Web Corpora

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have recently been shown to be vulnerable to fairness and bias manipulation, with prior attacks predominantly targeting the data layer via corpus poisoning. In this work, we expose a fundamentally different and largely unexplored attack surface: the retriever itself. Motivated by the widespread deployment of off-the-shelf neural retrievers as plug-and-play components in modular RAG pipelines, we formalize the Adversarial Fairness Attack against RAG (AFA-RAG), where an adversary manipulates only retriever parameters, leaving both the corpus and generator untouched, to systematically skew evidence exposure toward a target demographic while preserving semantic relevance and stealth. To instantiate this threat, we propose AFA-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that treats the retriever as a strategic ranking agent interacting with a RAG environment. AFA-RL learns adversarial ranking policies that subtly reshape retrieved evidence to bias downstream response generation, guided by a fairness-aware reward with strict relevance and distributional constraints. Experiments across multiple datasets and large language model backbones show that AFA-RL can cause disproportionate fairness degradation with negligible impact on standard retrieval metrics. Our results uncover a previously overlooked supply-chain vulnerability in modular RAG systems and underscore the urgent need for robustness guarantees at the retriever level.
evidence_items.title: Retriever as an Attack Surface: Exploring Fairness Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Sequential Recommendation Systems (SRS) aim to predict the next item based on their historical interaction sequence. To address the data sparsity issue that commonly existed in SRS, Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) has emerged, which aims to improve recommendation performance in a sparse domain (usually called target domain) by transferring knowledge from an information-rich domain (usually called source domain). However, existing CDSR methods mainly rely on ID-based representations and provide limited semantics across domains. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have begun to incorporate LLM-generated item or user embeddings with rich semantic information into CDSR models, substantially enriching the representation space and improving modeling expressiveness. However, these LLM-enhanced methods typically treat all source domains equally and overlook the varying semantic relevance of different domains, which will lead to low-relevance domains introducing noise and consequently degrade recommendation performance. To tackle these issues, we propose LLMAW4CDSR, a Large Language Model-guided Adaptive source-domain Weighting framework. The core idea is to first leverage the semantic reasoning abilities of LLMs to produce semantically enriched user and item representations, and then use them as semantic guidance for more effective cross-domain knowledge transfer. Building on this guidance, we design an source-domain weighting mechanism that estimates the contribution of each source domain to the target domain. By integrating LLM-driven semantic alignment with adaptive domain weighting, LLMAW4CDSR highlights relevant domains while suppressing noisy ones, enabling fine-grained cross-domain knowledge transfer. Comprehensive experiments on four cross-domain datasets demonstrate that LLMAW4CDSR consistently outperforms both state-of-the-art CDSR methods and LLM-based baselines.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Guided Adaptive Source-Domain Weighting for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Quality investigations in heat treatment require inspection results to be linked with processing histories, while conventional manufacturing execution systems distribute these records across separate modules. This study develops a read-only language-model interface with product and basket-time linkage and evaluates query execution separately from evidence correctness. A same-model comparison using GPT–OSS 20B covers 48 tasks and 288 attempted executions, with 273 complete responses. Frozen condition-screen counts were similar; asymmetrically reviewed scope corrections are not used as comparative evidence. Independent backend checks identified alarm-count inconsistencies before evidence reached the model. A retrospective, non-blinded review of 41 numerical fallbacks, assisted by artificial intelligence (AI), found six pre-fallback answers supported relative to the saved evidence, 34 containing unsupported or incorrect claims, and one indeterminate. These assessments do not independently validate the enterprise records. Three quality cases illustrate linkage to stage-specific furnace evidence, but incomplete basket coverage leaves the relationship between temperature deviations and hardness nonconformity undetermined. The study separates returned states, answer support, and independently verified facts when evaluating language-model access to manufacturing records.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model-Based Manufacturing Execution System for Heat Treatment and Its Evaluation Method

evidence_items.summary: Background Qualitative research is critical in transplantation science for understanding stakeholder perspectives and informing implementation, ethics, and operations. However, qualitative analysis is time-intensive and requires multiple trained team members. Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have emerged as potential tools for qualitative analysis, but their performance relative to trained human coders remains unclear. The study compared LLM-generated and human thematic analyses across three transplant studies. Methods The Naeem et al. six-step thematic analysis process was applied to three existing Datasets: (1) semi-structured interviews with United States (US) Organ Procurement Organization executives about normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) practices and ethical concerns; (2) open-ended survey responses from parents of pediatric heart transplant recipients addressing daily concerns, quality of life, and transition to adult care; and (3) semi-structured interviews with infectious disease providers exploring attitudes toward living donation from donors with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) to recipients with HIV. These datasets had previously been analyzed by humans trained in traditional qualitative analysis. A Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)-compliant instance of OpenAI’s Generative Pre-trained Transformer 5.4.(GPT-5.4) generated thematic outputs for comparison. Results Across all three studies, LLM-Generated themes largely overlapped with those identified by humans. However, interpretive depth and contextualization of findings still required human expertise. Conclusions GPT-5.4 generated themes that showed conceptual overlap with previously completed human-led analyses across three transplantation datasets, supporting a hybrid model in which AI may assist with early analytic tasks while human researchers provide interpretation and rigor.
evidence_items.title: Feasibility of large language Model–Generated thematic analysis in healthcare qualitative research: A comparative study

evidence_items.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Still, its deterministic formulation provides only point estimates of the adapter parameters and therefore cannot represent epistemic uncertainty. Existing Bayesian LoRA methods address this limitation by learning distributions over adapter weights; however, commonly used variational posteriors fully factorize across adapter parameters, limiting them from capturing posterior correlations and potentially underestimating uncertainty. We introduce HiVE, a Bayesian LoRA method with a structured posterior. At each LoRA layer, HiVE uses a layer-specific stochastic latent parameter to introduce structured and correlated adaptation in the adapter weights. These stochastic parameters modulate the down-projection LoRA factors, increasing the posterior expressiveness and allowing it to capture correlated uncertainty among its parameters. Marginalizing the latent variable induces a diagonal-plus-low-rank covariance structure over the effective adapter weights, capturing posterior dependencies while retaining parameter efficiency. HiVE learns the resulting variational posterior end-to-end using stochastic-gradient descent and integrates into existing LoRA pipelines with only modest trainable-parameter overhead. HiVE achieves comparable or superior predictive accuracy while providing more reliable uncertainty estimates across natural-language benchmarks under both in-distribution and distribution-shift conditions.
evidence_items.title: Low-Rank Bayesian Structured Adaptation of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The title of a playlist often reflects an intended mood or theme, allowing creators to easily locate their content and enabling other users to discover music that matches specific situations and needs. This work presents a novel approach to playlist generation using language models to leverage the thematic coherence between a playlist title and its tracks. Our method consists of creating semantic clusters from text embeddings, followed by fine-tuning a transformer model on these thematic clusters. Playlists are then generated considering the cosine similarity scores between known and unknown titles and applying a ranking mechanism, for which we compare a voting system and an LLM-based ranker. Performance evaluation, combining quantitative and qualitative metrics, demonstrates that using the playlist title as a seed provides useful recommendations, even in a zero-shot scenario.
evidence_items.title: Playlist Generation from Titles: Transformers vs. Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Background Patient education materials (PEMs) are essential for improving health literacy and clinical outcomes. Although large language models (LLMs) hold promise for optimizing content, their performance in generating new PEMs remains unclear. Objective This study aimed to summarize the current evidence on LLMs in generating new PEMs, evaluate readability, quality, and usability in various health care settings, and guide future research and practice. Methods This review followed PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus from January 1, 2000, to January 1, 2026. Eligible studies were English-language original research studies that evaluated new PEMs generated by LLMs in health care using information assessment tools. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. We conducted a quantitative analysis of the characteristics of the included literature. Furthermore, we classified the PEMs based on core educational tasks and clinical scenarios, and compared their readability, quality, and usability. Results Thirty studies were included, including 11 LLMs and more than 30 diseases; most compared multiple LLMs and used a single prompt. PEMs were classified into 5 categories: perioperative patient education (n=8), chronic disease management education (n=6), specialty disease diagnostic and therapeutic education (n=9), pharmacotherapy safety and adherence education (n=3), and public health and prevention education (n=4). In terms of readability, only 3 records achieved a sixth-grade reading level. Specialty disease diagnostic and therapeutic education performed relatively well, while chronic disease management education had poor readability. The DeepSeek series demonstrated the most consistent performance.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Generating Patient Education Materials: Scoping Review

organizations: LNBio, CNPEM, R. Giuseppe Máximo Scolfaro, Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil, 13083-100
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate drug-like molecules and may be used locally in drug discovery projects where confidentiality and intellectual-property constraints preclude the use of external APIs. Weight quantization enables deployment of large open-source LLMs on limited hardware, but its impact on molecular generation and on the ability of models to follow reference chemical spaces remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral-Small-4-119B, and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B at the BF16 (original precision), Q8, Q6, and Q4 quantization levels in two molecular generation tasks. The models were prompted either to generate small molecules without constraints or to generate drug-like molecules conditioned on 69 reference kinase inhibitors provided in-context. Quantization increased inference throughput in a model-dependent manner, with the largest gains, up to 24-fold increase in performance, occurring for Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B. In the task of unconstrained generation, model quantization did not affect molecular validity, uniqueness, drug-likeness, diversity and synthesizability. In the task of reference-guided generation, however, the models displayed markedly different levels of adherence to the provided chemical space. Gemma-4-31B was the only model that consistently generated small molecules similar to the reference compounds at all precision levels. Mistral-Small-4-119B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B failed to generate small molecules according to the reference chemical space. GPT-OSS-120B showed adherence to the reference molecules at BF16, Q8, and Q6, but lost the capacity to generate molecules in the desired chemical space at the Q4 quantization level. These results show that quantization can substantially improve the performance of local LLMs for molecular generation without compromising output quality, although model selection and validation is essential for guided exploration of the chemical space.
evidence_items.title: Lost in Chemical Space: Local Open-Source Large Language Models Display Model-Dependent Adherence to Reference Data in Molecular Generation

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: Nurse-led telephone triage, frequently guided by the United Kingdom Oncology Nursing Society (UKONS) tool, is a cornerstone of supportive oncology care, yet the appropriateness of triage decisions varies across settings. Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in medical communication but remain unvalidated for autonomous clinical decision-making, particularly in gynecologic oncology, where remote and telephone-based care pose distinct challenges. Methods and Materials: Twenty fictitious case vignettes representing common treatment-related toxicities in gynecologic oncology were developed. Three board-certified gynecologic consultants independently assigned UKONS Red–Amber–Green (RAG) triage categories, reaching unanimous consensus that served as the reference standard. Vignettes were submitted verbatim, as single-turn queries with no follow-up prompting, to three publicly available LLMs (OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Google Gemini). LLM responses were mapped to RAG categories and compared descriptively against the reference standard, stratified by treatment type and platform. Results: All three LLMs achieved 100% concordance with the reference standard for all Red cases across both treatment groups, with no high-acuity case downgraded to self-care. Discrepancies clustered at lower-acuity boundaries. In the chemotherapy-alone group, errors were limited to omission of an explicit 24-h follow-up window for 1 Amber-rated complaints. In the combined group, all LLMs over-triaged intermediate-risk complaints toward immediate or same-day evaluation; low-risk complaints showed more variable over-triage. Conclusions: LLMs identified unambiguous emergent gynecologic oncology symptoms, preserving the UKONS safety floor, but showed relatively reduced precision and a conservative over-triage bias at lower-acuity margins, especially in the combined-therapy collective.
evidence_items.title: The Potential of Large Language Models in Gynecologic Oncology Telephone Triage

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into information retrieval pipelines to reason over retrieved textual evidence and produce final decisions in tasks such as fact verification. However, causal fact verification presents a more specialised challenge than conventional claim verification: models must aggregate multiple pieces of evidence and assess whether the evidence supports a claimed causal relation, rather than merely verifying factual consistency. This setting is captured by CHECKWHY, which, to the best of our knowledge, is currently the only publicly available benchmark specifically designed for causal ''why'' fact verification. Motivated by this specialised problem, we propose Evidence-Aware Prompting (EAP), an evidence-centric framework that separates evidence selection from decision generation to enhance LLM reasoning. EAP models query-conditioned evidence selection as an explicit intermediate step and aggregates decisions over selected evidence subsets, mitigating query-only shortcuts and reducing the influence of irrelevant context. Experiments on CHECKWHY across multiple closed-source LLMs show that EAP consistently outperforms strong prompting baselines and achieves more balanced and robust evidence-grounded decisions for causal fact verification.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Aware Prompting for Causal Fact Verification with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: High-quality tickets are essential for software development, serving as a means of knowledge transfer between product owners and developers. Poorly written tickets create additional work and increase development costs. Creating tickets is time-consuming, and product owners often lack insight into the codebase, resulting in descriptions that may not reflect existing implementations. Large language models (LLMs) excel at processing natural language and possess strong programming knowledge, making them promising tools for automating ticket generation. However, research on LLM-based ticket generation remains limited. Recent work has shown that combining LLMs with code graphs improves querying of large codebases, which may benefit ticket generation. We propose TicketAgent, a repository-aware workflow for automated software ticket generation that combines LLM-based ticket writing with code-graph-based code localization and project-specific domain knowledge. We evaluate TicketAgent alongside two baselines: an LLM-only workflow and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow. Across automated and human evaluations, providing LLMs with additional information sources consistently improves ticket quality. In particular, structured access to the source code via code-based querying yields the largest improvements, outperforming both the LLM-only and RAG baselines.
evidence_items.title: Automated Software Ticket Generation Using Large Language Models and Code Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated evaluators of medical text (“LLM-as-judge”). We tested whether LLM-evaluator performance validated on one medical task against a human reference standard remains stable on a structurally different task. Materials and methods We evaluated 10 LLMs (3 locally served open-source and 7 API models: Claude, GPT, DeepSeek) as autonomous judges on 3 tasks with human reference labels: LiveQA-Med answer quality (n = 300), PubMedQA research appraisal (n = 300), and Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage on MIMIC-IV-Ext (n = 256). Each case was scored 3 times per model at temperature zero (25 680 judgments). Analyses used cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ, and false-discovery-rate correction. Results Evaluator performance was unstable across tasks: no model ranked in the top 3 on all 3 tasks, and every model shifted by 3 or more rank positions between at least one pair of tasks. In the highest-stakes task, ESI level 1 (Resuscitation) cases were under-triaged in 89.1% of evaluations, in all 10 models (range 70.2%-96.9%). Best triage agreement only reached the human inter-rater range (Claude Opus quadratic-weighted κ = 0.60 [0.54, 0.66]). Locally served 7-27B models (no per-query charge) occupied the Pareto frontier on the text tasks but only its low-concordance end on triage. Discussion LLM-evaluator performance is unstable between medical tasks that differ in cognitive structure; performance validated on one task should not be assumed to transfer to another. Conclusion Task-specific validation against human reference labels is required before deployment, and emergency triage demands human oversight at the highest-acuity tier.
evidence_items.title: Large language models are unstable as autonomous medical evaluators across clinical tasks

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly shape human decision-making as conversational assistants and act on human behalf as autonomous agents, making the cultural values they encode consequential across both settings. Yet ensuring that these systems reflect the values of diverse cultural groups remains an open challenge, as existing alignment approaches offer limited ability to precisely control cultural value orientations on demand. In this work, we investigate cultural value representations in LLM activation space through the lens of Hofstede's six-dimensional framework. We first demonstrate that contrastive activation steering reliably controls individual cultural value dimensions, significantly and consistently outperforming prompt-based steering across two models and two independent evaluation protocols. We then show that cultural value dimensions are not geometrically independent: positively correlated value vectors mutually amplify each other's effects at the cost of response coherence, while negatively correlated vectors attenuate each other through directional cancellation. These interference patterns impose a fundamental constraint on naive multi-dimensional steering. Motivated by this geometric analysis, we propose a selective projection decoupling method that removes inter-dimension interference prior to joint injection and fits steering coefficients to country-level Hofstede profiles. Evaluated on Brazil, China, and the United States, our method achieves consistent improvements in alignment accuracy, direction hits, and cultural similarity across both Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Ministral-8B-Instruct models, demonstrating that steered models are not only more culturally accurate but achieve high cultural similarity to their intended target profiles.
evidence_items.title: Steering Large Language Models toward Cross-Cultural Value Alignment via Activation Engineering

evidence_items.summary: Purpose of review Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in dialysis have matured beyond the initial phase of algorithm development. Recent work has shifted toward clinical implementation, evaluation, and governance. During the past year, the first randomized trial of AI-guided dosing in maintenance hemodialysis has been published, a meta-analysis of technology-guided dry-weight adjustment has appeared, and the first professional society framework for the responsible use of AI in kidney care has been released. Recent findings The Anemia Control Model is now supported by hospitalization outcomes and cost-effectiveness analyses. A randomized trial demonstrated that AI-guided erythropoiesis-stimulating agent dosing achieved outcomes comparable to physician-directed dosing. Technology-guided dry-weight adjustment is supported by a meta-analysis of 21 randomized trials. Machine learning for vascular access is evolving toward preoperative clinical decision support, while peritoneal dialysis is beginning to receive greater attention from the machine learning community. Large language models are entering nephrology along two complementary paths: open generative systems for education and clinical support, and deterministic, protocol-driven frameworks designed for safety-critical bedside applications. At the same time, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has released comprehensive lifecycle guidance for AI-enabled medical devices. Summary The major challenge for AI in dialysis is no longer developing accurate prediction models. Instead, success will depend on effective workflow integration, validation across diverse patient populations, ongoing postdeployment monitoring, and demonstrating meaningful improvements in patient outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in dialysis

organizations: University of Pittsburgh, Department of Radiology, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
evidence_items.summary: PurposeWe aim to present a consolidated overview of current achievements in generative artificial intelligence (AI) in breast imaging, identify prevalent technical and clinical challenges alongside the strategies employed to overcome them, and highlight critical directions for future investigation.ApproachA comprehensive literature search has been conducted in PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase for peer-reviewed journal publications since 2020, with the final search performed in October 2025. The review focuses on common methodologies, performance metrics, and strategies used to address existing hurdles in breast imaging.ResultsThe 120 included papers were categorized by application, ranging from technical and/or clinical tasks—image synthesis (including 24 data augmentation, 10 enhancement, 20 image-to-image translation, and 2 secure data sharing papers), 12 segmentation, 5 reconstruction, and 16 classification papers—as well as 17 papers in radiology workflow improvement, 13 papers in the development of medical education materials, and 7 papers on solving beyond our defined tasks (six papers were assigned more than one application). Papers in each category showed their own potential to solve the task of interests. However, we identified six common challenges and concerns, such as lack of standardized evaluation for synthetic outputs, across papers that the future research should be focused on.ConclusionsRecent works across the field of generative AI in breast imaging have demonstrated transformative potential in clinical workflows. However, there still exists technical and ethical gaps to be addressed for safe, reliable, and equitable deployment of the generative AI models to routine medical practice.
evidence_items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in breast imaging

organizations: BURDUR MEHMET AKİF ERSOY ÜNİVERSİTESİ, EĞİTİM FAKÜLTESİ
evidence_items.summary: The aim of this research is to examine the experiences and practices of faculty members working in the field of science education in higher education regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in educational and academic contexts. The study was conducted within the framework of a basic qualitative research design. The participants of the study consisted of seven faculty members. A structured interview form was used for data collection in line with the interview guide approach. The data were analyzed through inductive content analysis, following the stages of preparing the data for analysis, reading the data, coding and creating themes, interpreting the data, and reaching the findings. The findings of the research emerged under five themes: “Conceptualization of GAI,” “Coexistence of Opportunity and Anxiety,” “Supportive Use in Educational and Academic Processes,” “Awareness of Competencies and Limitations,” and “Transformation of Academic Role and an Uncertain Future.” The findings show that faculty members mainly use GAI as a supportive tool in content creation, preparation of course materials, literature review, and academic writing processes. However, concerns about ethical issues, accuracy, student laziness, cognitive dependency, and the transformation of academic roles were also found to be prominent. As a result, the science education academics participating in the study revealed that GAI offers significant opportunities in higher education; however, pedagogical, ethical, and institutional regulations are needed for effective and safe use.
evidence_items.title: Science education academics’ generative artificial intelligence experiences

evidence_items.summary: Background: Cardiovascular diagnostic capacity is limited in many low-resource settings. We evaluated the HeartLINK Triage for Risk-Informed Allocation and Guided Evaluation (H-TRIAGE) index, a prespecified strategy combining clinical information and AI-enabled digital auscultation to prioritize cardiovascular evaluation. Methods: In this prospective study in Ghana (February–July 2026), consecutively enrolled adults underwent a standardized assessment by trained frontline nurses and community health workers. H-TRIAGE used predefined additive symptom, vital-sign, and AI-stethoscope weights to assign Low (0–3), Intermediate (4–7), or High (≥8) Risk. Four cardiologists, blinded to H-TRIAGE, independently reviewed all participants; a fifth adjudicated disagreements. The reference standard (adjudicated indication) was a recommendation for further diagnostic testing, cardiologist-led evaluation, or both. The primary cohort comprised 5 facilities across 3 districts of the Ashanti Region; external validation used a held-out facility in a separate district of the Eastern Region. In a modeled allocation analysis, Intermediate- and High-Risk participants were considered prioritized; we calculated sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). Results: Among 3,800 participants (primary, n=3,123; external validation, n=677; median age, 52 years [IQR, 39–64]; 77.7% women), 1,707 (44.9%) had an adjudicated indication. By H-TRIAGE category, the proportion with an indication was 2.5% (Low), 87.9% (Intermediate), and 100% (High) (P for trend<0.001). Prioritizing Intermediate- and High-Risk participants yielded 1,656 true positives, 142 false positives, 1,951 true negatives, and 51 false negatives: sensitivity, 97.0% (95% CI, 96.1%–97.8%); specificity, 93.2% (92.1%–94.3%); PPV, 92.1% (90.8%–93.3%); and NPV, 97.5% (96.7%–98.1%). This approach would prioritize 47.3% of participants for evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Identifying Patients for Cardiovascular Evaluation Using Artificial Intelligence and Team-Based Care in Ghana: The H-TRIAGE Study

organizations: Department of Mathematics and Natural Science in Primary Education, Teachers’ School, Mongolian National University of Education, Ulaanbaatar 14191, Mongolia
evidence_items.summary: This study examined attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) among pre-service primary school teachers in Mongolia and evaluated the psychometric properties of a Mongolian adaptation of the Students’ Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence (SATAI) scale. A cross-sectional survey yielded an analytic sample of 672 students at a public teacher education university, randomly divided by academic-year strata into exploratory (n = 334) and confirmatory (n = 338) subsamples. Factor-retention criteria disagreed, and the exploratory solution did not match the component grouping of the source adaptation. A model reproducing that structure fitted poorly and yielded an inadmissible solution. Of seven measurement models estimated from polychoric correlations by diagonally weighted least squares, a bifactor model fitted best (CFI = 0.975; TLI = 0.970), although RMSEA remained 0.086; a four-factor model fitted comparably, but its factor correlations (0.86–0.93) failed the Fornell–Larcker criterion for every pair. Omega hierarchical (0.949) and explained common variance (0.876) indicated a dominant source of common variance, while subscale-specific reliability was limited; internal consistency of the total score was high (α = 0.972). Attitudes were moderately positive (M = 3.59, SD = 0.85), with enjoyment and educational relevance endorsed more strongly than everyday application and self-rated competence. Metric and scalar invariance across academic years was supported by change-in-fit criteria, and fourth-year students scored higher than all earlier cohorts. The findings favor cautious use of the total score rather than subscale scores, and they provide a descriptive basis for designing and then evaluating structured, ethically informed AI preparation in teacher education rather than evidence that such provision is effective.
evidence_items.title: Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence Among Pre-Service Primary Teachers in Mongolia: A Psychometric Evaluation of the Mongolian SATAI Scale

evidence_items.summary: There is still uncertainty surrounding whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enhances or decreases human cognition, as the proof is scattered all around. This thematic analysis synthesises 46 core peer-reviewed articles (2011–2026), selected from 165 Scopus records after an assessment, to conclude how AI applications affect the development of human cognition in learning. The six-phase process proposed by Braun and Clarke (2006) yielded six themes: (1) AI-assisted performance does not equal productive learning; (2) cognitive offloading is mixed in quality and dependent and autonomous vary in approach; (3) critical and higher-order thinking depend on usage of AI rather than simply on AI existence; (4) metacognition, self-regulation, and calibration play the main role; (5) either strengths of creativity and cognitive agency depend on process of engagement; and (6) pedagogical design has implications for all listed above. The proof of a long-lasting, self-sufficient gain is scarce and varies, whereas the data largely comprise cross-sectional opinions of university undergraduates. The final evaluation shows that the cognitive influence of artificial intelligence is variable. It's dependent on the governing behaviour and the teaching method. The research gives rise to a human-centred agenda, which aims to maintain productive effort, use artificial intelligence indirectly, and assess the process besides the result.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Cognitive Development: A Thematic Analysis

organizations: Tasmanian School of Medicine, University of Tasmania
Menzies Institute for Medical Research, University of Tasmania
evidence_items.summary: The evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, intelligence-based medicine. Driven by the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), this emerging era offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care within high-stakes environments like emergency departments. However, this paradigm shift simultaneously introduces a critical risk of modernised, digital dogma, manifesting as algorithmic paternalism. If AI systems are deployed without rigorous oversight, they threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics, trading the unquestioned authority of historical figures for the presumed infallibility of machines. To safeguard care in emergency departments, AI must not operate unchecked. Adapting existing Learning Health System frameworks offers a pragmatic solution to govern AI integration. By embedding these computational technologies within continuous, self-correcting clinical ecosystems, departments can enforce robust data hygiene and rigorously audit data provenance. An essential component of this approach is separating objective safety surveillance and adverse event reporting from the algorithm’s internal learning mechanisms to detect epistemic drift and automation bias. Ultimately, the successful and safe integration of intelligence-based medicine depends on an unwavering commitment to transparent governance. When computational power is harnessed as a regulated, transparent tool within an LHS, AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma, ensuring future care is anchored in dynamic, validated evidence rather than perpetuating the medical errors propagated by eminence from the past.
evidence_items.title: From eminence to evidence to intelligence-based medicine: optimising artificial intelligence to disrupt dogma in emergency departments

evidence_items.summary: Education stands as one of the primary institutions most profoundly impacted by the advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technologies, a trajectory that is poised to persist. The manifestations of AI’s influence are discernable across the core constituents of education: the student, the educator, and the pedagogical space. While AI technologies directly impinge upon these components, they simultaneously exert an indirect influence on the relational dynamics and interactions between them. This study seeks to examine the nexus between education and artificial intelligence through a sociological and critical lens. It is well-established that the integration of artificial intelligence into educational systems elicits a spectrum of both affirmative and divergent perspectives. The objective of this research is to re-evaluate the utilization of AI in education through the sociological frameworks of surplus value, digital labor, surveillance, and algorithmic control. In doing so, it attempts to elucidate how education and its fundamental elements are re-conceptualized within the digital age under the influence of AI. Designed as a review article, this study utilizes a literature review methodology, which is situated within qualitative research paradigms. The findings suggest that while artificial intelligence ought to function as an object within the educational system, it harbors the inherent risk of transforming into a subject under various pretexts.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking the relationship between artificial intelligence and education: A sociological assessment

evidence_items.summary: Pemilihan framework backend dalam pengembangan aplikasi berbasis web sering didasarkan pada popularitas atau pengalaman pribadi tanpa evaluasi yang objektif, sehingga berpotensi menghasilkan keputusan yang kurang optimal. Penelitian ini menerapkan metode Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) untuk menentukan framework backend terbaik di antara Express.js, Laravel, Gin, dan Django, yang dievaluasi berdasarkan lima kriteria: performa, konsumsi memori, ekosistem library, kemudahan pembelajaran, dan keamanan bawaan. Data performa dan memori diperoleh dari benchmark objektif, sedangkan kriteria lainnya dinilai melalui kajian literatur. Hasil menunjukkan Gin menempati peringkat tertinggi dengan nilai preferensi 0,8225, terutama karena keunggulan performa dan efisiensi memorinya, yang berimplikasi pada penggunaan sumber daya server yang lebih hemat, skalabilitas lebih baik, dan biaya operasional lebih rendah. Penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa SAW memberikan dasar pemilihan framework backend yang objektif, terukur, dan transparan.
evidence_items.title: Pemilihan Framework Backend Berbasis Data Benchmark Menggunakan Metode SAW

evidence_items.summary: Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval (UCDR) requires models to generalize to unseen domains and unseen categories at inference time. Recent prompt-learning methods for vision--language models have achieved strong performance on object-centric benchmarks, yet their behavior under cluttered multi-object scenes remains under-explored. In such scenes, co-occurring objects can act as contextual distractors and induce prompt contamination: visually salient distractors may dominate the candidate tokens used for instance-adaptive prompt generation, causing retrieval representations to drift away from the designated primary target. To diagnose this gap, we construct DomainCOCO, a Realistic UCDR benchmark with 180,000 images across six domains, where each sample contains a designated primary category and contextual distractors. DomainCOCO is intended as a controlled diagnostic benchmark for studying target-aware retrieval under multi-object clutter and stylized domain shifts. We further provide Text-Guided Rectification Network (TGR-Net), a practical rectification baseline that uses text embeddings as semantic guidance to re-weight patch-level visual evidence before prompt generation. Its Candidate Prompt Purification (CPP) module reduces distractor-dominated prompt synthesis, while a teacher--student strategy with a learnable null token enables label-free inference. Multi-scale feature fusion and gallery-side refinement are used as optional inference components for accuracy-oriented deployment. Experiments on DomainNet and DomainCOCO show that TGR-Net provides consistent gains over strong CLIP-based baselines, with larger gains in the more cluttered DomainCOCO setting. Code is available at https://github.com/YUEcjy13/TGR-Net.
evidence_items.title: Prompt Contamination in Realistic Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval: Diagnosis and Text-Guided Rectification

evidence_items.summary: A method for predicting landmine contamination risk in Ukraine is proposed that combines machine learning and geospatial data. A multilayer dataset of more than 0.55 million 0,25 km² grid cells was compiled from geospatial, socio-economic and military features. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and Invariant Risk Minimization were combined in a stacked generalization ensemble, which outperformed the best single model (XGBoost) in AUC-ROC, Precision, Recall and F1-score.
evidence_items.title: PREDICTING THE RISK OF LANDMINE CONTAMINATION USING A STACKED ENSEMBLE OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents a hierarchical multi-agent architecture in which independent large language model (LLM) planners perform strategic role assignment for attacking and defend- ing robot teams, decoupled from low-level control execution. At each planning cycle, each team’s LLM planner observes its own team in full but the opposing team only within its robots’ combined field of view, then assigns each robot a tactical role – e.g., hold a perimeter, neutralize an intruder on contact, or converge with teammates for capture – to- gether with a natural-language justification. Each robot in- dependently executes its assigned role through a receding- horizon model predictive control (MPC) controller, followed by a discrete-time control barrier function (CBF) filter for safety and role-dependent engagement constraints. Differen- tiated capture and neutralization incentives require the de- fending planner to balance threat resolution against resource allocation under partial observability. We evaluate the frame- work across variable-sized adversary teams using both state- based tactical reasoning and image-based contact classifi- cation. Results show that collective team behavior can be adapted through high-level LLM role assignment while re- taining the same underlying low-level control architecture.
evidence_items.title: Engagement-Aware Agentic Pursuit-Evasion

evidence_items.summary: The emergence of large language models and agentic search systems is transforming query expansion, elevating it from a standalone preprocessing step to a central reasoning component in modern retrieval pipelines. The shift from classical term-selection methods to LLM-based generation has opened new possibilities for expansion, while deep search agents, retrieval-augmented generation, and conversational retrieval have introduced fundamentally new settings in which query expansion must operate. This tutorial offers a comprehensive treatment of query expansion methods, tracing their progression from classical statistical techniques through neural and transformer-based approaches to LLM-based generation, while covering evaluation methodology, cross-paradigm deployment, failure analysis, and emerging research opportunities. The tutorial is accompanied by hands-on experimentation for implementing and comparing expansion methods across retrieval settings.
evidence_items.title: Query Expansion Revisited: From Classical Retrieval to Agentic Search

evidence_items.summary: With the adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) in critical infrastructures, investigating security incidents across connected devices has become challenging. Graph-based intrusion detection approaches show promising detection performance. However, an anomaly alert does not explain how the surrounding activity developed, and manually following this evidence is difficult in large provenance graphs that contain many benign events and highly connected entities. Threat hunting is a proactive methodology that searches for hidden or undetected threats and reconstructs the activity surrounding an alert. Existing language-model-based approaches mainly rely on computationally expensive Large Language Models (LLMs) and model-generated graph queries, while directly presenting a complete provenance graph exceeds the reasoning and context capacity of Small Language Models (SLMs). In this paper, we propose ProvNav-SLM, an agentic threat-hunting framework that combines a Graph Neural Network (GNN) with an SLM for provenance investigation. The framework operates through three systematic phases: Detect, where the GNN identifies anomalous entities; Investigate, where an SLM agent repeatedly selects among recorded graph-navigation actions; and Verify, where a rule-based executor retrieves the selected relationships and preserves their links to the collected logs. To support SLM reasoning, the framework transforms large graph neighborhoods into small action groups organized by direction, relation, and entity type. The main novelty of ProvNav-SLM is its ability to perform closed-loop provenance threat hunting with a local SLM while separating graph-wide anomaly detection, semantic action selection, and evidence verification across dedicated components. In an exploratory evaluation on four ProvICS campaigns, the local SLM recovered more target processes on average than the evaluated graph-based rules.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Small Language Models for Closed-Loop Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection
