evidence_items.summary: Agentic research pipelines produce structured knowledge artifacts with human oversight, but agreement between an agent and a reviewer who has seen its proposal does not establish independent inter-rater reliability. We argue that these pipelines should publish their decision records, including revisions and withdrawals, and explicitly label agreement measured under proposal-visible review. We implemented a pipeline in which an AI agent drafts records and proposes classifications, while a single human reviewer, who also authored the coding rules, checks each record against cited sources. Proposals, decisions, and withdrawals are preserved in the published record. In a corpus of 84 institutional investors classified for AI adoption, 74 retained rows had recorded proposals; the reviewer accepted 69 proposed stages (93.2%). Including six additional proposals withdrawn during review reduced acceptance to 69 of 80 (86.3%). Six of eleven disagreements therefore concerned inclusion rather than classification, a distinction concealed by reporting agreement only on retained rows. These figures describe proposal-visible agreement; they do not establish classification accuracy or measure anchoring bias. A planned blind re-code will assess agreement without exposure to proposed labels. We advocate publishing transparently labeled agreement alongside the full disagreement record and, when available, independent reliability estimates.
evidence_items.title: Publish the Disagreement: Instrumented Human Verification in an Agentic Research Pipeline

organizations: Boston Children's Hospital, Harvard Medical School
evidence_items.summary: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst–identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88–0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90–0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87–0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records

organizations: CNR-IRCRES, National Research Council of Italy, Turin Research Area, Strada delle Cacce 73, 10135 Turin, Italy
School of Complex Adaptive Systems, Arizona State University, Engineering Center—Building A 1031 S. Palm Walk, Tempe, AZ 85281-2701, USA
evidence_items.summary: This study examines the emerging technological trajectories in artificial intelligence (AI) paradigm: generative AI, agentic AI, and quantum AI. It aims to compare evolutionary growth shaping the overall AI technological system. A comparative scientometric and technometric analysis was applied on publication data and keyword-frequency corpora, by using linear regression, and Shannon’s entropy to measure growth, thematic breadth, and structural diversity. The empirical results reveal that agentic AI demonstrates the most rapid acceleration (B=3.201, p<0.05), despite its later emergence in 2023. Quantum AI displays the most consistent, statistically significant growth rate (B=0.70, p<0.001), driven by advances in hardware foundations and security. Generative AI has a strong positive trend (B=1.44, p<0.001). The findings indicate a technological evolution in AI system from passive content generation toward “stack thickening,” involving autonomous orchestration, grounding, and multi-agent coordination. These results suggest that technology management should move toward Agent Operations (AgentOps) strategic frameworks for orchestrating, governing, and securing autonomous multi-agent AI workflows, where multiple AI agents interact to execute complex operational tasks with high action reliability, while innovation policy should prioritize the development and adoption of post-quantum cryptography standards and strengthen institutional AI literacy, for supporting effective regulatory frameworks that safeguard society and promote the responsible use of emerging AI technologies.
evidence_items.title: From Generative to Agentic and Quantum AI Technological Trajectories: Evolution in AI Paradigm

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved recommender systems by enabling richer semantic modeling of user preferences. However, existing LLM-based recommenders typically require expensive per-user inference over long interaction sequences, causing computational costs to scale rapidly with both model size and the number of users. To address this challenge, we propose ClusterRec, a framework that decouples LLM-based recommendation into two stages: (1) group-level preference modeling and (2) user-level personalization. Specifically, users are first clustered based on behavioral representations, and LLMs are employed to construct a group-level semantic representation for each cluster. Individual user representations are then constructed by integrating shared group representations with personalized collaborative filtering embeddings. This design amortizes LLM inference at the group level, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving personalization. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that ClusterRec achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, including conventional CF-SRec (e.g., SASRec) and recent LLM-based recommenders, while significantly reducing LLM inference cost. These results highlight that group-level semantic modeling provides an effective and scalable paradigm for integrating LLMs into practical recommender systems. The code is available at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/ClusterRec.
evidence_items.title: ClusterRec: Cluster-Aware Recommendation with Large Language Models for Efficient and Scalable Inference

evidence_items.summary: Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a production-relevant task for modern in-car navigation interfaces. Given a user's current and historical context, the system can suggest the next destination while accounting for both user preference and travel feasibility. However, existing Large Language Models (LLMs) for next POI recommendation (1) overlook real-time traffic conditions and thus fail to account for user-specific trade-offs between POI preferences and travel time, and (2) rely on text embedding-based POI candidate retrieval, which may surface semantically similar yet geographically implausible POIs. To address these limitations, we propose TraPOI, a Traffic-aware LLM for Next POI Recommendation. TraPOI consists of (i) a multimodal embedding alignment module to project POI, GPS, and traffic data into the LLM's latent space, and (ii) a multi-view candidate retrieval module that retrieves distance-based and embedding-based candidates to facilitate spatially feasible and semantically relevant next POI recommendation. We also introduce (iii) multimodal prompting to explicitly incorporate traffic and spatial context into the LLM's reasoning process. We constructed two novel datasets aligning check-in records with real-time traffic data from Seoul and California (CA) to validate our approach. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TraPOI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving accuracy gains up to 11.61%. Our code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/kmw409722-svg/TraPOI.
evidence_items.title: LLM Meets Traffic: Traffic-Aware Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation in Vehicle Navigation Interfaces

evidence_items.summary: The rapid expansion of internet-based health resources and large language models (LLMs) has substantially increased public access to consumer health information. Although this accessibility offers notable benefits, it also raises concerns about the reliability, accuracy, and trustworthiness of information obtained from conventional web-based platforms and AI-generated content. Despite extensive research, no universally accepted definition or standardised framework exists for evaluating the quality of consumer health information. This narrative review examines how consumer health information quality is defined and evaluated across web-based and LLM-generated environments, and assesses the role of search engine ranking mechanisms in shaping the visibility and accessibility of such information. These domains are considered interconnected components of the consumer health information ecosystem: information is provided or generated through different sources, discovered through search and ranking mechanisms, and evaluated using health information quality criteria. The review synthesizes evaluation criteria, assessment instruments, frameworks, and methodological approaches and compares commonly applied dimensions, including accuracy, readability, coherence, reliability, medical adequacy, and completeness. The findings reveal substantial variation in evaluation criteria and methodologies, along with a lack of consensus on appropriate approaches to assessing the quality of consumer health information. The review also identifies limitations in applying traditional evaluation tools to LLM-generated information and highlights the distinction between information quality and information visibility. These findings support the need for a standardized, multidimensional framework for evaluating consumer health information across web-based and AI-generated environments while accounting for information discovery and ranking mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the quality of consumer health information across the web, large language models, and search engines: a review of criteria, instruments, and methods

evidence_items.summary: This proposal outlines the organization of the 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models (EARL), to be co-located with the 35th International ACM Conference on Knowledge and Information Management (CIKM 2026) in Rome, Italy. Following the strong engagement of the first two EARL editions, this third installment aims to solidify the workshop as a premier venue for advancing research at the intersection of large language models (LLMs) and recommender systems (RSs). EARL 2026 will foster discussions on the evaluation and practical deployment of LLM-driven RSs, emphasizing not only methodological soundness and reproducibility, but also the responsible integration of LLMs into real-world systems. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from academia and industry, the workshop will stimulate debate, encourage critical reflection, and shape future research directions in LLM-enhanced RSs.
evidence_items.title: EARL: The 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Some clinical documentations, including surgical antibiotic administration data and hand-written notes, are only captured in non-digitized scanned documents, limiting their accessibility. Commercially available artificial intelligence (AI) tools may offer a means of extracting such data from scanned-in images, however, little is known about their accuracy for this application. Thus, the objective of this study was to evaluate the performance of two commercially available, protected AI tools for extracting antibiotic administration data as part of a larger study evaluating the sustainability of stewardship goals achieved during the Surgical Care Improvement Project mandatory reporting period. Methods: A sample of surgical cases with antibiotic administration data documented only in non-digitized scanned records was manually reviewed and submitted to two commercially available AI tools (Claude Sonnet version 4.6 and OpenAI version 5.0). The AI tools were prompted to extract data about antibiotic name, dose, and administration time. Results: The total accuracy across all three metrics (drug, dose, timing of administration) was limited (3/14, 21.4% for Claude and 2/14, 14.3% for OpenAI), but overall excellent for identifying that an antibiotic had been administered and the type of drug administered (Claude, 100%, OpenAI, 92.8%). AI tools struggled to identify total dose administered (Claude, 50%, OpenAI, 42.9%), primarily due to challenges distinguishing aliquots from administered doses. Accuracy for identifying timing was also variable, particularly when administration time was documented using a graphic scale rather than written text. Conclusions: Potential utility of these commercial tools for extracting antimicrobial use data from scanned-in records depends upon review goals and what level of precision is necessary.
evidence_items.title: The accuracy and utility of large language models for extracting stewardship data from handwritten and scanned-in records

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising technique for applying LLMs to proprietary domains. However, retrieved documents may contain sensitive knowledge, posing risks of privacy leakage in generative results. Thus, effectively erasing private information from retrieved documents is a key challenge for RAG. Unlike traditional text anonymization, RAG should consider: (1) the inherent multi-document reasoning may face de-anonymization attacks; (2) private knowledge varies by scenarios, so users should be allowed to customize which information to erase; (3) preserving sufficient publicly available knowledge for generation tasks. This paper introduces the privacy erasure task for RAG and proposes Eraser4RAG, a private knowledge eraser that effectively removes user-defined private knowledge from documents while preserving sufficient public knowledge for generation. Specifically, we first construct a global knowledge graph to identify potential knowledge across documents, aiming to defend against de-anonymization attacks. Then we randomly split it into private and public sub-graphs, and fine-tune Flan-T5 to rewrite the retrieved documents, excluding private triples. Finally, the PPO algorithm optimizes the rewriting model to minimize private triples and maximize public triples retention. Experiments on four QA datasets demonstrate that Eraser4RAG achieves a strong privacy--utility balance among document-level rewriting methods, outperforming GPT-4o-based rewriting in private knowledge erasure while preserving substantially more public knowledge than aggressive keyword- or entity-suppression baselines.
evidence_items.title: Learning to Erase Private Knowledge from Multi-Documents for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: With the increasing language diversity on the web, the demand for multilingual Question-Answering (QA) has grown significantly. To maximize QA performance, a common way is to equip multilingual large language models (MLLMs) with more parameters, which also incurs significant costs. To improve efficiency without losing performance, we propose a novel task, Homologous Model Routing (HMR). Given a set of homologous MLLMs of varying parameter counts (such as Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B...), HMR tries to select the minimum model that can just correctly answer the current question. Then, we propose a Language-Calibrated Entropy-Aware Dynamic Routing (LEAD-Router) that performs homologous model routing by estimating question difficulty based on response entropy and language-aware calibration. Experiments on the two datasets show that LEAD-Router achieves consistently better routing accuracy and QA performance than baselines.
evidence_items.title: LEAD-Route: An Adaptive Language-Calibrated and Entropy-Aware LLM Selection for Homologous Model Routing

evidence_items.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, but their long chain-of-thought trajectories incur substantial inference latency and computational cost. Small-large model collaborative reasoning mitigates this issue by offloading part of the reasoning steps to a small language model (SLM) while preserving large language model (LLM) computation for more demanding steps. Existing draft-and-verify methods use an external verifier to reject low-scoring SLM steps and regenerate them with the LLM, introducing per-step verification overhead. Moreover, we observe that many LLM rewrites remain semantically close to the rejected SLM drafts, causing unnecessary decoding cost. Further analysis shows that these redundant rewrites often occur on local derivation steps, whose content is largely constrained by recent context. Motivated by these observations, we propose CriticRouter, a verifier-free step-wise routing framework that reduces redundancy based on structural criticality as a routing signal. Specifically, structural criticality measures how sensitive the SLM's next-step generation is to perturbations in earlier reasoning history, and low-criticality steps are viewed as locally stable and delegated to the SLM, whereas high-criticality steps are treated as history-sensitive and routed to the LLM. To reduce probing overhead, CriticRouter further adopts short concurrent probes and progressive mask advancement for better cache reuse. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that CriticRouter achieves comparable accuracy to standard LLM reasoning while significantly reducing latency, demonstrating a better utility-efficiency trade-off.
evidence_items.title: CriticRouter: Criticality-aware Step Router for Small-Large Collaborative Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are increasingly used for multimodal search, open-ended question answering, document understanding, and generated content analysis, yet they still produce claims that are fluent but unsupported by visual evidence. Existing hallucination mitigation methods often rely on external multimodal judges, language-model annotators, or human token labels to localize unsupported content, adding cost and introducing a mismatch with the target model's own failure modes. We propose HIS-Guard, a framework for trustworthy multimodal claim generation that diagnoses unsupported claims using the target LVLM's internal stability signals and routes those signals to selective verification or preference optimization. Its core diagnostic, Hallucination Instability Score (HIS), combines semantic convergence from cross-layer LogitLens entropy reduction with visual grounding coherence from cross-token attention-distribution consistency over image patches. By decomposing HIS into semantic and visual instability, HIS-Guard supports claim-level credibility analysis without external token-level hallucination localizers or auxiliary multimodal judges. We then instantiate a Diagnose-Treat-Prevent preference objective (DTP-DPO): semantic instability treats risky tokens by weighting DPO rewards, while visual and combined instability prevent visual neglect through gated auxiliary regularizers. Across Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B and InternVL2.5-2B, HIS-guided optimization provides downstream evidence that the diagnostic captures useful failure modes. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, HIS-Guard reduces CHAIR_s by 32.2% and CHAIR_i by 45.6% over the baseline, improves over standard DPO trained on identical data, and largely preserves POPE accuracy. Scaling to Qwen2.5-VL-7B keeps HIS-Guard best on both CHAIR and POPE, while InternVL results suggest that the diagnostic signal is useful but the regularization strength is architecture-sensitive. Together, these results position internal stability as a practical signal for trustworthy multimodal information systems, selective verification, and hallucination-aware evaluation. The public implementation is available at https://github.com/20508Z/HIS-DTP-DPO.
evidence_items.title: Internal Stability Signals for Selective Verification and Hallucination Mitigation in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: On multi-hop benchmarks, modern Graph-RAG retrieves the gold answer for 77-90% of questions, yet a budget open-weight 8B model answers only 31-77% correctly. We show that faithfulness (reading the retrieved evidence rather than guessing) and calibration (abstaining when it is insufficient) account for a large, recoverable part of this gap. A leak-controlled decomposition finds that on the hardest, least-contaminated benchmark (MuSiQue), 43% of questions have their supporting facts in the retrieved context yet are answered wrong, and on these the model gives a confident answer 82% of the time rather than abstaining. A grounding-and-calibration prompt makes the model answer from the retrieved context or abstain when it cannot, a more trustworthy operating point at no accuracy cost. A re-ask step then spends some of that calibration for coverage, turning abstentions into correct answers for a gain of +9 pp on KET-RAG and +13 pp on LightRAG (MuSiQue, answer-present slice) that closes about half the gap to a 70B model on KET-RAG and most of it on LightRAG. Few-shot example source moves the model along the same faithfulness-accuracy frontier, better for calibration than accuracy. Unlike structure-exploiting augmentations that degrade on uniform-relevance retrieval, grounding helps most there. For small-model Graph-RAG the target is faithful, calibrated use of retrieved evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/thomouvic/graphrag-faithfulness.
evidence_items.title: The Small-Model Graph-RAG Gap Is a Faithfulness Gap
Schema, values, and priors: understanding LLM-based domain detection for tabular datasets

evidence_items.summary:
PURPOSE
Variability in chest X-ray (CXR) reporting hinders training and evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology report generation. Our previous study showed that Structured Radiology Report Generation (SRRG)-style supervision improves VLM-based CXR reporting over free-text supervision. Here, we examine this finding in a larger multi-institutional setting and address a key preprocessing challenge: reliable free-text-to-structured-report conversion using open-source small language models (SLMs).


METHODS
We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-3B using free-text and SRRG-style structured supervision across 10 institutions covering 97K samples. We then propose RadStructAgent, an agentic framework that converts free-text CXR reports into structured reports using SLMs, combining LLM-based orchestration, judge feedback, and feedback-guided revision. RadStructAgent is evaluated on 1,000 free-text CXR reports using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.


RESULTS
For the report generation task, structured supervision improves Qwen2.5-VL-3B over free-text supervision, increasing GREEN from 0.494 to 0.539, with similar gains across other clinical metrics. For the structuring task, RadStructAgent improves both clinical quality (GREEN) and anatomy-level assignment (RadFAA): for Qwen3-4B, from 0.844 to 0.867 and 0.883 to 0.891; for Qwen3-8B, from 0.863 to 0.881 and 0.889 to 0.902.


CONCLUSION
Structured supervision remains effective for VLM-based CXR report generation when evaluated in a larger multi-institutional setting. RadStructAgent shows that open-source SLMs can be strengthened through agentic verification and refinement, providing a resource-efficient approach for offline and privacy-preserving structured report preparation. Our code, prompt templates, and configuration files are publicly available at: https://github.com/badhon1512/RadStructAgent .
evidence_items.title: RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models.

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (MABSA) aims to identify aspect-level sentiment from user-generated image-text posts. Although visual information can provide useful context for sentiment reasoning, it is not uniformly beneficial for aspect-level prediction. Different image regions may serve distinct roles: some provide content support for post understanding, some offer sentiment-related evidence, while others introduce irrelevant or misleading signals. To address this challenge, we propose VEGA, a MABSA framework that integrates visual evidence construction with evidence-guided region calibration. Specifically, VEGA first leverages a multimodal large language model to construct two complementary types of visual evidence from each image-text pair: content-aware visual evidence and context-aware sentiment evidence. These evidence streams are then used to calibrate region-level visual representations through a dual-support cross-attention mechanism, enabling image regions to contribute according to their roles in content understanding and sentiment inference. Finally, the calibrated visual features are integrated with the original text in a unified encoder-decoder architecture for both multimodal aspect sentiment classification and joint multimodal aspect-sentiment analysis subtasks. Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that VEGA consistently outperforms strong task-specific baselines. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of visual evidence construction and evidence-guided region calibration.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis via Evidence-Guided Region Calibration

evidence_items.summary: Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction (ASTE) aims to extract aspect--opinion--sentiment triplets from review sentences and is a fundamental task in fine-grained sentiment analysis. Recent large language model-based chain-of-thought (CoT) methods improve instruction following and semantic reasoning for ASTE, but their verbose reasoning outputs introduce substantial inference overhead and often lack explicit structural grounding. We propose ReasonGraph, which integrates gold-guided CoT distillation with dependency-graph-based syntactic grounding. The distillation pipeline first trains the model with explicit reasoning chains and final answers, and then shifts to direct answer generation, allowing reasoning ability to be internalized while keeping inference compact. Meanwhile, a GATv2 dependency-graph encoder injects parsed syntactic structures as continuous prefix embeddings, enabling the LLM to adaptively balance syntactic and semantic cues. Experiments on four standard ASTE benchmarks show that ReasonGraph achieves strong performance with significantly faster inference than CoT-based reasoning methods. Further analysis indicates that our method effectively captures complementary semantic and syntactic information and focuses on the most informative cues for triplet extraction. Our code is available at https://github.com/cscsysu/aste-cikm.
evidence_items.title: ReasonGraph: Graph-Enhanced Reasoning Distillation for Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have shown strong potential on complex reasoning tasks, but their scalability is limited by substantial communication overhead and token consumption. Recent methods reduce these costs by pruning redundant agents or edges, but such deletion-based optimization can discard role-specific information and often operates only after activating the full agent pool. To address these limitations, we propose S2R-Merge, a unified routing-and-merging framework that reframes MAS structural optimization from node deletion to information-preserving consolidation. S2R-Merge first uses an uncertainty-aware 2-Stage Soft-Gated Router to select a task-relevant agent subgraph, avoiding unnecessary full-pool activation. It then applies graph-based node merging to identify structurally inefficient agents from policy-gradient-learned communication pathways, absorbing them into strongly related partners while preserving their role-level information through Prompt-level Fusion. Experiments on six reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and GPT-4 show that S2R-Merge achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, reaching 77.22% and 92.37%, respectively. It also reduces average prompt token usage by up to 12.3× compared with full multi-agent collaboration and achieves the lowest token consumption among multi-agent graph-optimization baselines. These results demonstrate that S2R-Merge provides an effective cost-performance trade-off for scalable LLM-based MAS.
evidence_items.title: S2R-Merge: Soft-Gated Routing with Structural Node Merge Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Most of the evidence behind real decisions, contracts, clinical narratives, filings, reports, is text. Increasingly, people want to query it the way they query a database: with selections, joins, and aggregates whose semantics they can defend. Pipelines built on large language models make this feel within reach, but they are best-effort by design: a dropped clause or misread value produces no error, it silently changes the answer. For analytics, that is not good enough. This talk argues that reliability must be engineered into the query processor rather than hoped for from the model, and proposes four principles for doing so: treat the language model as a fallible, inspectable component whose internal states reveal more than its stated confidence; convert those signals into explicit, distribution-free error contracts per operator; make abstention and human review first-class operators whose cost is minimized, not ignored; and treat the user's error allowance as a budget allocated across retrieval, extraction, filtering, and joining, much as an optimizer allocates cost. I will illustrate these principles with recent results, including our own, sketch an architecture in which they compose, and close with open problems: end-to-end guarantees, distribution shift, closed models, and evaluating systems that promise control rather than just accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Reliable by Construction: Query Processing over Unstructured Data with Guarantees

evidence_items.summary: Research collections in the humanities and social sciences describe overlapping subjects under divergent cataloguing practices, so records that belong together stay unconnected across databases. Stable identifiers would make the overlap machine-readable, but assigning them means disambiguating keywords that are short, multilingual, and largely without context. We present Context-Aware Routing for Entity Linking (CAREL), a training-free pipeline that links research metadata keywords to Wikidata QIDs through a four-layer cascade. Its core is Cross-lingual Retrieval Consensus (CRC), a novel signal that turns the agreement of retrieval ranks across language-specific queries into a measure of linking confidence without requiring annotated data. Rule-based layers resolve the clear cases, and only genuinely ambiguous keywords reach a locally deployed open-source large language model (LLM), which bounds inference cost and avoids sending research metadata to external services. On two manually verified benchmarks from multilingual African studies metadata, subject headings anchored in the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) and researcher-supplied tags, CAREL reaches 89.8% and 90.9% accuracy on the headings with Gemma4-31B-it and Qwen3.5-27B, and holds 88.8% and 89.5% on the anchor-free tags. It also detects the keywords for which no Wikidata entity exists, at an F1 of 88 on the tags.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Keywords: Training-Free Entity Linking for Multilingual Research Metadata

evidence_items.summary:
This paper seeks to determine how insights gained from current research on artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare could be used to inform Learning and Development (L&D) and Organization Development (OD) practice around preparing workforces for AI implementation.
 
 
 
 The paper draws on five recent peer-reviewed academic papers identified through a Scopus search on AI and healthcare (2025–2026), professional attitudes to AI in clinical settings, ethical AI governance, large language model adoption and platform-level AI resources, and interprets their findings from an OD/L&D perspective.
 
 
 
 AI adoption is shaped by trust, perceived value and governance; hence, technical competence alone may be insufficient without trust and governance. Attitudes toward AI may vary according to exposure and motivation rather than position alone. Governance can be approached as an organizational competency, while peer communication may complement technical training in supporting trust and adoption.
 
 
 
 This is a secondary analysis of existing healthcare data of patients, clinicians and consumers, and not just one group, and therefore requires additional empirical research beyond healthcare organizations and occupations.
 
 
 
 There are four evidence-informed practice levers to consider in sequence: diagnose, design, combine and evaluate, which means diagnose the attitude along with role; incorporate governance competency learning in the curriculum; combine technical training and peer trust; and evaluate confidence and appropriate use along with competence.
 
 
 
 The paper offers a concise interpretation of recent healthcare AI evidence for workplace learning and OD practice.
evidence_items.title: Healthcare AI adoption: implications for learning and organization development

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge tracing aims to infer a student's evolving mastery from historical learning interactions. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a natural way to encode textualized learning histories, but they are often evaluated primarily as next-step predictors. This leaves open whether the model forms a stable and diagnostically meaningful latent trajectory of student state, or merely exploits shallow statistics such as recent correctness rates. We introduce LCSR-LLM, a longitudinal cognitive state reasoning framework that uses marker-aligned LLM hidden states to estimate a soft latent cognitive-state trajectory at each prediction step. The framework combines state-conditioned prediction with trajectory-level regularization, especially dynamic consistency and entropy control, to encourage smoother and non-collapsed state posteriors. We further propose Longitudinal Aggregation Drift (LAD), a diagnostic protocol that measures sequence-level prediction drift, posterior uncertainty, and trajectory volatility. On ASSIST2012, LCSR-LLM with Qwen2.5-7B reaches 0.7684 AUC, 0.7705 ACC, and 0.8610 F1, achieving the best AUC among our controlled runs and the best F1 among the listed results, while remaining competitive in ACC. Paired trajectory diagnostics show that dynamic consistency and entropy control improve internal trajectory behavior beyond final predictive accuracy.
evidence_items.title: LCSR-LLM: Longitudinal Cognitive State Reasoning for LLM-based Knowledge Tracing

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational contexts, yet their default answer-centric interaction paradigm conflicts with established principles of effective learning. Direct solution delivery can reduce productive struggle and encourage cognitive offloading rather than deep understanding. To address this tension, we present HintLab, a visualization-driven, human-in-the-loop platform for generating, analyzing, and refining LLM-generated pedagogical hints. The system operationalizes five cognitively grounded evaluation dimensions—Convergence, Relevance, Readability, Familiarity, and Leakage Avoidance—and exposes them through interactive visual analytics that support comparative inspection, manual refinement, and scaffolded sequencing of hints. Unlike standard chat interfaces, HintLab enables structured multi-model comparison, answer-space reduction analysis, and convergence-based scaffolding design without requiring domain modeling or programming expertise. A human evaluation involving 901 generated hints demonstrates favorable ratings across multiple pedagogically motivated dimensions, while a hint-assisted question answering study shows that the generated hints substantially improve users' ability to answer previously unsolved questions. The system is publicly available, with source code accessible on GitHub, and a demonstration video online.
evidence_items.title: HintLab: An Interactive Tool for Hint Generation, Analysis and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks that combine textual and visual information. However, final-answer accuracy offers limited insight into whether errors arise from incorrect perception, modality-dependent information extraction, or downstream reasoning. We introduce a perception-aware diagnostic framework for bimodal mathematical reasoning that represents a model's perceived problem understanding as knowledge graph triples and evaluates them using an Auxiliary Perception Set (APS), a human-verified collection of perception-oriented questions grounded in directly observable input information. We apply the framework to Plane Geometry problems from MathVerse, evaluating three MLLMs across two input representations: text and diagram embedded in a single image, and text and diagram provided separately. We also test controlled textual and visual perturbations to examine robustness under modality-specific noise. Results show that perception accuracy and final-answer accuracy often diverge: models that generate more accurate perception triples do not necessarily achieve higher final-answer accuracy, and the same problem content can produce different behavior depending on input representation. Cross-model triple transfer further shows that downstream performance depends on both the quality of extracted perceptual structure and the model's ability to reason over it. These findings suggest that perception-aware evaluation exposes failure modes hidden by answer-only evaluation and provides a finer-grained diagnostic view of bimodal mathematical reasoning.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Answer Accuracy: Diagnosing Perception Failures in Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently improved collaborative filtering (CF) by adding text-derived signals, but often require rich textual data and costly inference. In this work, we revisit RLMRec [11], a representative LLM-enhanced CF framework, and examine whether its gains come from LLM-specific knowledge or from complementary representations. Our analysis suggests that a substantial part of the improvement can be attributed to auxiliary heterogeneous signals, rather than solely to intrinsic LLM knowledge. Motivated by this, we propose HetRec (Heterogeneity-aware Recommender), a text-free, model-agnostic CF framework that replaces LLM-derived textual embeddings with interaction-derived heterogeneous signals. HetRec constructs auxiliary embeddings from heterogeneous-view CF models and enriches them via similarity-aware k-nearest neighbor aggregation, capturing neighborhood-level collaborative patterns. Under the same RLMRec-style alignment framework, HetRec improves over RLMRec variants on the Amazon-book, Yelp, and Steam datasets without textual inputs or LLM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jaeeun-Lim02/HetRec.
evidence_items.title: Revisiting LLM-Enhanced Collaborative Filtering: A Text-Free Alternative with Heterogeneous Interaction Signals

evidence_items.summary: Urban spatiotemporal prediction is crucial for smart city management, yet fragmented data across administrative boundaries significantly impedes effective model training. To overcome data limitations and leverage knowledge from data-rich regions while preserving data privacy, federated transfer learning has emerged as a promising approach for cross-regional urban prediction tasks. However, traditional learning methods encounter the dual challenge: (1) intra-regional knowledge acquisition difficulties due to missing boundaries that weaken spatiotemporal dependencies and cause data sparsity; and (2) cross-regional knowledge transfer bias, where distribution differences between source and target regions trigger negative transfer and reduce model robustness. To address these issues, we propose CRAFT: a novel federated transfer learning framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) for urban spatiotemporal prediction. Leveraging LLMs' powerful semantic understanding and contextual reasoning abilities, CRAFT captures complex spatiotemporal dependencies and uncovers latent regional connections from heterogeneous data sources, thus alleviating boundary-induced data sparsity. Additionally, to address inter-regional data heterogeneity, we employ a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with parameter decoupling, which excels at handling diverse data distributions while minimizing federated communication costs. Experimental results on real-world datasets from multiple cities demonstrate the effectiveness of CRAFT in cross-regional federated transfer learning. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Jasonxx4/CRAFT.
evidence_items.title: CRAFT: Cross-Region Adaptive Federated Transfer Learning for Urban Spatiotemporal Prediction

evidence_items.summary: As large language models advance, news increasingly contains both human-written and LLM-generated content. Existing models tend to exploit linguistic fingerprints in LLM-generated texts rather than deep semantics for veracity inference, leading to shortcut learning and detection bias when classifying both human-written and LLM-generated news. To address this issue, we propose a Semantic Decoupling and Dynamic Enhancement (SDDE) plugin, which can be integrated into fake news detection models as a plug-and-play module to mitigate linguistic fingerprint interference and enhance transferable semantic information. Specifically, SDDE first obtains original text representations from the backbone model and denoises them to extract purified features. Subsequently, based on these features, adversarial training and auxiliary supervision are applied to reduce the influence of linguistic fingerprints while preserving deep semantics. Meanwhile, a cross-attention mechanism supplements semantic details of the purified features to obtain enhanced features. A token-level adaptive gating dynamically fuses enhanced features with the original text representations. Finally, the fused representations are reinjected into the backbone model for training. Experiments show that incorporating the SDDE plugin yields absolute accuracy improvements of 1.19%–6.29% across backbone models on two datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability. The code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/SDDE.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Shortcuts: Semantic Decoupling and Dynamic Enhancement for LLM-Generated Fake News Detection

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant potential in recommendation systems; however, employing Reinforcement Learning (RL) to align them with ranking metrics in the query-generation formulation of large-scale recommendation remains a critical challenge. Current RL-based approaches often suffer from reward sparsity and generating too general queries. In this paper, we propose TAG-Rec, a framework that grounds generative recommendation via Trigger-Anchored Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Built upon a verifiable-anchor training principle, TAG-Rec enforces a ''Trigger-First'' generation strategy in which the model explicitly identifies a salient historical item as a verifiable anchor before generating a search query, structurally transforming open-ended generation into grounded reasoning. TAG-Rec combines three components: (i) Trigger-Grounded Data Curation via reachability verification, which concentrates training supervision on samples that admit a verifiable historical anchor; (ii) the Trigger-First generation strategy that anchors generation in a salient prior interaction; and (iii) a Trigger-aware Reward that supplies dense intermediate feedback to mitigate reward sparsity. On real-world sequential recommendation benchmarks, TAG-Rec achieves up to 23.6% and 13.8% average improvement over strong SFT and RL baselines, with notable gains on long-tail and novelty metrics.
evidence_items.title: TAG-Rec: Grounding LLM-based Recommendation via Trigger-Anchored GRPO

evidence_items.summary: Pre-retrieval query performance prediction methods estimate the effectiveness of a query prior to retrieval and enable control of the search pipeline through tasks such as query routing, selective expansion, and retriever selection. However, because they operate solely on query features without access to retrieved documents, pre-retrieval predictors often struggle to provide accurate predictions. They typically treat query difficulty as a latent statistical property rather than one that can be reasoned about. We propose a new pre-retrieval framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to uncover and encode interpretable reasons of query difficulty. By integrating these reasons with transformer-based neural regressors, our approach allows the predictor to be both aware of and conditioned on reasons that make a query challenging. Our experiments on MS MARCO Dev, TREC DL 2019, TREC DL 2020, and DL-Hard demonstrate that our method consistently achieves reliable and stable correlations across various TREC DL datasets. Our code, models, and difficulty reason annotations are made publicly available at https://github.com/ls3-lab/draq.
evidence_items.title: Reasoning About Query Difficulty to Predict Retrieval Effectiveness

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models offer unprecedented capabilities for sequential recommendation, yet their deployment is fundamentally bottlenecked by the conflict between finite context windows and unbounded interaction histories. Existing methods typically compress multimodal behaviors into textual summaries, inevitably precipitating semantic degradation and interest homogenization. To resolve this, we propose MUSER, a Memory-augmented framework for mUltimodal SEquential Recommendation, built upon a collaborative dual-agent architecture. Specifically, a User Agent maintains a parametric memory via structured input, forget, and rerank operations, guided by a dynamic personality parameter and an Isomorphic Consistency Planning mechanism to ensure long-term preference stability. Concurrently, a Recommendation Agent leverages this stateful memory under a decision-reason bi-objective scheme to jointly optimize recommendation accuracy and high-fidelity textual explanations. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that MUSER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines.
evidence_items.title: MUSER: Memory-Augmented Multimodal Sequential Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: As large language models increasingly support long-context inference, the computation and memory access overhead of attention and KV caches have become critical bottlenecks for inference latency and system scalability. Existing approaches mitigate these costs through KV cache dropping, approximate attention, or system-level optimizations, but often incur non-trivial trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and implementation complexity. In this work, we propose LSH-KV, a coarse-to-fine KV retrieval framework for efficient long-context LLM inference. LSH-KV uses locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) as a lightweight, training-free coarse partitioning layer for similarity-preserving organization of global KV entries. Within each hash bucket, LSH-KV further uses product quantization with offline-precomputed codebooks for efficient approximate similarity estimation, followed by exact re-ranking to preserve attention accuracy. To further improve system efficiency, LSH-KV introduces a score-aware block-level cache management strategy that aligns KV movement between CPU and GPU with retrieval relevance. Experimental results on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that LSH-KV significantly reduces end-to-end inference latency while preserving generation quality, even when selective attention is performed using only a fraction of the input tokens. These results show that LSH-KV enables scalable, robust, and accurate inference under long-context settings. The code is available at https://github.com/HarryFunn/lsh-kv.
evidence_items.title: LSH-KV: Efficient KV Cache Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Inference via Locality-Sensitive Hashing

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been explored for generative recommendation, where item tokenization plays a critical role. Existing studies design item identifiers such as discrete Semantic IDs, single-token identifiers, and multi-token or set identifiers. However, in many identifier-based methods, the item-level grounding of these introduced identifiers is not established during general-domain pre-training and must instead be learned during recommendation-specific adaptation. Consequently, LLMs may treat them as opaque prediction symbols rather than stable item representations. To address this issue, we propose MISTRec, a masked item-slot modeling framework for learning structured continuous item representations. MISTRec introduces three key designs. First, MISTRec decomposes each item into continuous CF-aware and latent semantic slots, reducing the entanglement between collaborative signals and metadata-derived item semantics. Second, it trains these slots with Masked Slot Autoencoding (MSA) by reconstructing corrupted historical slots and completing a fully masked future item. Third, it introduces False Negative Reweighting (FNR), which downweights semantically conflicting negatives during target alignment and improves the stability of full-catalog ranking. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that MISTRec consistently improves next-item recommendation over strong sequential and generative baselines, while yielding more stable item neighborhoods across random seeds.
evidence_items.title: MISTRec: Masked Item-Slot Token Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are fundamental for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in factually consistent reasoning across diverse data-mining tasks. However, when reasoning over complex graph topologies, LLMs can be brittle in maintaining structural consistency and may rely on spurious correlations. We propose SKILL (Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning), a novel paradigm that transforms relational rules from passive symbolic patterns into explicit, generation-time symbolic guidance for LLM-based reasoning. Unlike existing methods that isolate symbolic mining from neural inference, SKILL introduces a semantically aligned rule synthesis framework that filters spurious patterns and enables LLMs to leverage relational regularities during inference. By grounding generation in pruned, query-specific subgraph structures together with rule–path evidence, SKILL improves inductive generalization while preserving generative flexibility. Extensive experiments on three inductive benchmarks demonstrate that SKILL achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to a 5% absolute improvement in Hits@1, highlighting a new and effective way to integrate symbolic structure into LLM reasoning over knowledge graphs. Source code is available at https://github.com/luilui97/SKILL.
evidence_items.title: Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning for LLM Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, with long or short variants, has become a central paradigm for enhancing the reasoning ability of large language models. Long CoT aims at achieving high accuracy in complex multi-step reasoning at the cost of high inference overhead, while short CoT focus on offering a more efficient but less capable alternative. To balance reasoning accuracy and reasoning efficiency, collaborative approaches combining long and short CoT have been widely explored. However, existing collaborative approaches either operate token-level pruning, risking disruption to reasoning coherence, or rely on instance-level routing, which over-look the excessive self-verification within long CoT reasoning. To address these limitations, a semantic step-level reasoning optimization approach for collaborative CoTs, named SemCoT, is investigated in this paper. Technically, verification redundancy and trigger mechanisms in long CoT reasoning are first analyzed. Specifically, a dynamic trigger leveraging lexical cues and logit uncertainty is designed to detect the onset of self-verification in long CoT reasoning. A finetuned short CoT model is subsequently employed to filter trivial verification, with redundant cases truncated through context steering. Confident phrases are finally embedded to ensure contextual coherence. Experimental results demonstrate that SemCoT reduces average reasoning length by 48% across several benchmarks while maintaining similar accuracy, highlighting its practical effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: SemCoT: A Semantic Step-level Reasoning Optimization Approach for Collaborative Chain-of-Thoughts

evidence_items.summary: Sequential recommender systems commonly learn item representations from interaction data. This paradigm works well for frequent items, but becomes unreliable for long-tail items whose ID embeddings receive limited updates. Offline semantic embeddings derived from large language models provide useful item-side knowledge beyond interaction logs. They can therefore compensate for the insufficient interaction supervision of long-tail items. However, directly optimizing such semantic priors for recommendation may distort their original semantic structure. Moreover, semantic information should not be injected uniformly across all items, since head items are already well supported by interactions while long-tail items require semantic compensation more urgently. In this paper, we propose DART, a constrained semantic enhancement framework that couples Residual Trust Semantic Adaptation with Tail-Aware Dual-View Alignment for sequential recommendation. DART treats offline LLM-derived item embeddings as frozen semantic anchors and injects collaborative signals through a trust-region-constrained residual pathway. This design allows item representations to absorb useful collaborative information while limiting semantic drift. To further improve long-tail recommendation, DART introduces a tail-aware dual-view alignment mechanism that concentrates cross-view transfer on long-tail items instead of aligning all items uniformly. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that DART achieves strong overall performance and consistent gains in long-tail settings. Further ablation and representation analyses verify the effectiveness of residual-trust adaptation and tail-aware semantic transfer.
evidence_items.title: DART: Residual Trust and Tail-Aware Dual-View Alignment for Sequential Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for time series anomaly detection (TSAD), yet their direct use often remains inferior to methods designed specifically for TSAD. In this work, we study whether this limitation arises primarily from weak forecasting or from insufficient exploitation of forecast residuals. Across LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, we find that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can improve forecasting accuracy, but does not consistently improve anomaly detection under fixed residual thresholding. The primary driver of detection performance is not forecasting quality, but how the resulting residuals are analyzed and refined in subsequent stages. Motivated by this finding, we propose a Forecaster–Detector–Imputer pipeline that restricts the LLM to forecasting normal temporal behavior, applies classical detectors to the resulting residuals using adaptive windowing and contamination-aware thresholding, and refines candidate detections through imputation via a time-series foundation model followed by a second detection pass. The proposed framework reaches F1 = 0.789 with LLaMA and F1 = 0.785 with Mistral, roughly doubling the zero-shot baselines, with results confirmed on an independent NAB benchmark. These results suggest that LLMs are most effective for TSAD when used as forecasting components within a hybrid residual-analysis pipeline, and that the primary bottleneck lies in post-hoc residual exploitation rather than forecasting quality alone.
evidence_items.title: A Hybrid Framework for Time Series Anomaly Detection with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in question answering, recommendation, and conversational decision support. In many such settings, the user asks for a single answer even though the prompt does not specify the criterion needed to justify a unique choice. We study this setting as semantic underdetermination: multiple answers remain compatible with the prompt unless an additional ranking criterion is supplied. Rather than claiming a formal impossibility result, we study an empirical tension among three properties: premise-entailment correctness, criterion neutrality, and single-turn decisiveness. We evaluate 140 manually curated underdetermined prompts across seven categories on six LLMs, from 4B to frontier scale, under four response policies that handle under-specification differently. Forcing a direct answer makes models far more decisive (decisive rate 32%?93%) but lowers judged utility (4.06?3.53 out of 5, a large effect), because a confident answer must commit to a criterion the user never gave. Asking for the missing criterion instead gives the highest judged utility (4.53/5) and LLM-predicted satisfaction (4.48/5) but is rarely decisive in one turn (5.4%). A criterion-sensitivity score supports the mechanism: differences are small in size, but every one of the six models is most criterion-sensitive when forced to answer and least when it asks for the criterion. These findings suggest that asking for the missing criterion is a practical and transparent strategy for LLM systems facing under-specified user requests.
evidence_items.title: Direct Answers, Hidden Criteria: Empirical Trade-offs in LLM Responses to Underdetermined Prompts

evidence_items.summary: Memes, widely shared on the internet as a form of cultural expression, present a challenge in identifying harmful content due to their compact format and subtle meanings. Current detection methods employ pre-trained models to extract image and text features from memes, subsequently combining these features through deep neural networks for classification. However, these approaches often overlook the underlying meanings embedded in memes, focusing solely on shallow semantics and surface-level harmful signals. This makes it difficult to capture the cultural connotations and subtle expressions inherent in memes. Moreover, they lack explanations for their judgments. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework for explainable harmful meme detection. This framework combines the advantages of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and fine-grained heterogeneous semantic graphs. By leveraging multi-hop reasoning, we utilize MLLMs' extensive knowledge to provide comprehensive meme analyses, addressing meme literacy gaps. We extract key objects, relationships, and attributes from images to produce detailed scene graphs, which support a deeper understanding of the meme. The fine-grained heterogeneous semantic graphs filter and integrate multiple information sources to uncover hidden harmful elements. Additionally, through multi-hop reasoning and scene graphs, our approach generates reliable explanations via MLLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on widely used datasets.
evidence_items.title: Deconstructing Harmful Memes: Fine-Grained Analysis of Subtle Semantics

evidence_items.summary: In modern recommender systems, the ''filter bubble'' effect remains a formidable challenge as models tend to over-exploit historical interactions at the expense of potential interest discovery. Although various exploration strategies have been proposed, effectively balancing prediction precision with serendipity within the ranking layer remains an open problem. To address this challenge, this paper introduces T-MSDF, a novel T-shaped convolutional Multi-stream Sequential Discovery Framework. T-MSDF leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct a category affinity table that quantifies semantic complementarity between product categories, enabling the generation of augmented behavior sequences along exploration paths grounded in real-world common-sense logic. The framework consists of four synergistic components: (1) an LLM-constrained Sequence Expansion module that generates knowledge-augmented behavior streams; (2) a T-shaped Convolutional Fusion Network that harmonizes temporal evolution with spatial complementarity across behavior streams; (3) an Interest Decoupling and Alignment scheme, which disentangles convergent preferences from divergent exploration signals via residual extraction and discovery-aware contrastive learning; and (4) an Adaptive Gated Fusion Network, which dynamically weights the decoupled interest representations to prioritize serendipitous recommendations without compromising ranking precision. Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests on a large-scale industrial platform demonstrate that T-MSDF significantly improves key discovery metrics, achieving a +5.92% increase in Discovery Rate (DR) and a +6.15% lift in Discovery-CTR, alongside notable growth in CTR (+1.18%) and GMV (+2.30%).
evidence_items.title: T-MSDF: T-shaped Convolutional Multi-stream Discovery Framework with LLM-Driven Compatibility Priors

evidence_items.summary: Two-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) offers an attractive path to deploying Large Language Models under strict memory budgets, yet scalar quantization suffers from catastrophic performance collapse at this extreme bit-width. While Vector Quantization (VQ) methods resolve the accuracy issue, existing approaches suffer from practical inefficiencies: complex optimization pipelines result in hours-long quantization, and some methods exhibit severely limited inference throughput. We propose EPTQ, a 2-bit PTQ framework available in two complementary variants (E8 and FE8), achieving high accuracy and practical efficiency through three contributions: (1) Factored E8 (FE8) lattice quantization, which decomposes the E8 codebook into a compact 4, KB structure that fits in the GPU L1 cache, enabling fast codebook lookup at inference time; (2) Lightweight scale normalization via row/column scaling vectors (g, h), which aligns weight distributions to maximize E8 quantization efficiency, requiring only element-wise per-token scaling at inference; and (3) Adaptive critical weight preservation via knee-point threshold detection, which more accurately identifies Hessian-sensitive weights than approaches relying on fixed global criteria, consistently improving perplexity across models, with zero bit-overhead by encoding the preservation mask into the existing codebook index space. Evaluated across multiple LLMs including Llama-2 and Llama-3 families, EPTQ (E8) achieves accuracy competitive with or surpassing QTIP on Llama-2 models, while EPTQ (FE8) surpasses competing VQ methods in decode throughput on most models, achieving up to 38% faster inference than FP16, with both variants reducing quantization time by over 80% compared to competing approaches.
evidence_items.title: EPTQ: Fast and Accurate 2-bit Post-Training Quantization via Factored E8 Lattice

evidence_items.summary: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) mitigates data sparsity and cold-start issues by transferring user preferences across domains. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) effectively capture collaborative signals, they struggle with the inherent structural sparsity present in individual domains. Specifically, users or items with few interactions become ''isolated nodes''. Traditional cross-domain methods fail to rescue these nodes because they rely on explicit, overlapping interaction topologies that are often missing, severely hindering message passing. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich semantic knowledge yet lack the inherent ability to interpret collaborative graph structures. To address this limitation, we propose SGLP (Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors), a framework that leverages LLM knowledge as a structural prior to reconstruct sparse interaction graphs. Specifically, SGLP employs LLMs to generate Item Semantic Embeddings and User Global Semantic Profiles, establishing a robust semantic foundation. Distinct from traditional Graph Structure Learning (GSL) methods that rely solely on intrinsic node features, SGLP introduces a Semantic-Guided Graph Modeling module. This module applies differentiable structure learning to dynamically construct a task-adaptive hybrid graph, transforming unstructured semantic similarities into structured collaborative connections. To resolve distribution discrepancies between the reconstructed structural and semantic views, we enforce a Semantic-Behavioral Alignment constraint via contrastive learning. Furthermore, a Bi-Level Sequence Prediction strategy is introduced to alleviate negative transfer arising from domain shifts. Extensive experiments on three real-world Amazon datasets demonstrate that SGLP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the efficacy of integrating semantic priors into graph structure learning for cross-domain recommendation.
evidence_items.title: SGLP: Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly moving from experimental prototypes into operational peer review workflows, where they are used to polish, rewrite, synthesize, and generate reviews. This shift creates an urgent challenge for organizations that depend on expert assessment. Rather than asking only whether AI can improve peer review, this talk confronts a more fundamental question: can we reliably measure what makes a review useful, fair, and decision-relevant? The talk examines this question through the lens of AI-assisted peer review and shows that commonly used signals and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation often fail to capture substantive review quality. Drawing on real-world deployment experience at Reviewerly, we present case studies in which evaluation metrics reward surface-level improvements like polish and fluency while overlooking evidentiary content, correctness, and editorial usefulness. We then discuss practical lessons for building reliable evaluation systems in real peer review workflows. Although peer review is the central case study, the broader message applies to many industry and organizational settings where AI is being introduced into expert judgment workflows. Responsible automation requires more than stronger generation models. It requires evaluation methods that measure the qualities we actually want AI systems to improve.
evidence_items.title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Assisted Peer Review

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge-grounded assessment of procedural compliance is a growing challenge in healthcare informatics. Such assessment benefits from explicit grounding in authoritative clinical references. Hand hygiene assessment offers a canonical instance, since hand hygiene is the single most critical defense against healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). Existing automated solutions often provide only coarse-grained compliance signals, while fine-grained technique analysis can incur substantial computational cost. Direct application of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) introduces additional challenges because processing long-form clinical videos is expensive and generic MLLMs lack grounded procedural references. We propose HH-Track, a knowledge-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for fine-grained hand hygiene assessment. A skeleton-guided encoder first extracts structured clinical metrics and produces compact visual digests via boundary-progressive sampling. A prototype-anchored dual-stream RAG mechanism then retrieves step-aligned textual WHO guidelines and visual prototypes from curated reference resources. The MLLM uses these references for structured frame-level comparison during compliance assessment. To support this work, we construct Clinical-HHA, a hand hygiene dataset of 270 full-session recordings segmented into 1,408 step-level clips with template-guided expert compliance reports, paired with a curated visual prototype library. Release of both resources is subject to ongoing institutional review. Across five MLLM backbones, HH-Track improves compliance accuracy by an average of 36.1 percentage points over the Direct configurations, and the full dual-stream configuration further outperforms text-only grounding. Generated reports also show stronger agreement with expert-written references on average. These results support prototype-anchored multimodal retrieval for knowledge-grounded procedural assessment.
evidence_items.title: HH-Track: Skeleton-Guided Visual Understanding with Prototype-Anchored RAG for Hand Hygiene Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in Information Retrieval (IR) evaluation to annotate query-document pairs for relevance, enabling significant cost reductions compared to the traditional human-only assessment process. However, LLM-generated human judgements are not error-free and, compared to humans, are more prone to introducing systematic latent biases and producing spurious results. Therefore, since the evaluation target remains the human, it is necessary to understand how to align observations derived from LLM-generated annotations with those that would have been made using human relevance judgments. This work introduces a novel framework for estimating the performance we would observe if relevance judgements were human-made, using a large amount of LLM-generated judgments with a limited pool of human-annotated queries. The proposed approach exploits hierarchical Bayesian modeling and calibration to build Credible Intervals (CrIs) providing statistical guarantees on the estimated performance. The obtained results show how the computed CrIs allow (a) over 95% coverage while exploiting a limited number of human annotations and (b) to jointly take into account the LLM error and the variance due to topics, enabling future use of the computed CrIs for statistical hypothesis testing.
evidence_items.title: Modeling Uncertainty in LLM-Based Information Retrieval Evaluation via Hierarchical Bayesian Models

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise as embedding generators for sequential recommendation. Effective adaptation typically involves two stages: collaborative signal injection and discriminative representation learning. However, optimization objective and item semantic misalignments arise between these two stages, resulting in catastrophic forgetting of collaborative relationships learned in the first stage. To address these issues, we propose a novel LLM-based embedding method called GCTP, which obtains both collaborative and discriminative embeddings. Specifically, we maintain a generative training objective throughout the training process, thereby alleviating potential optimization conflicts. Moreover, we preserve local semantics to ensure semantic consistency during training, and capture global semantics with minimal modifications when extracting item embeddings. Experiments on real-world datasets show that GCTP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based embedding methods.
evidence_items.title: Learning Collaborative and Discriminative Embeddings with LLMs for Sequential Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a practical way to improve the reasoning and decision-making abilities of large language models, but its training signal is often sparse. When a policy faces prompts beyond its current ability, every sampled trajectory in a group may fail the verifier, resulting in an all-zero group. In this case, group-relative policy optimization gives little useful gradient even when the prompt contains valuable learning content. This capacity-difficulty mismatch is especially costly for smaller models used in knowledge-intensive and web-interaction tasks. We present POLAR, a difficulty-aware training framework that augments on-policy RL with conditional guidance from a larger reasoner. POLAR uses the standard GRPO branch when at least one sampled response succeeds, and switches to a supervised objective over verified teacher trajectories only when the whole student group receives zero reward. The method can turn otherwise wasted all-zero groups into targeted learning opportunities while keeping policy exploration on prompts the student can handle. We formalize the switching criterion, teacher selection objective, mixed RL/supervised loss, and compute overhead. We evaluate POLAR on WebShop, GAIA, and WebWalkerQA using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B policies. The results show consistent gains over matched GRPO baselines, with large improvements on hard web traversal questions for the two smaller policies. Ablations and diagnostics further show that the gains come from the proposed all-zero recovery mechanism.
evidence_items.title: POLAR: Policy Optimization through Larger Reasoners

evidence_items.summary: Social simulation plays an important role in domains where human studies face practical constraints, such as sociology, psychology, medicine, and education. Conventional social simulations often rely on rule-based, statistical, or mechanistic models with predefined assumptions, which can oversimplify the complexity, diversity, and context dependence of real-world human behavior. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising opportunity by enabling agents to interpret contextual information, perform flexible reasoning, and adapt their behaviors to evolving environments, opening new frontiers for modeling human behavior, social interactions, and collective dynamics[1, 2, 6, 7]. Despite these opportunities, LLM-agent-based social simulations raise significant challenges, including persona and domain-knowledge modeling [4, 5], behavioral evaluation and analysis [3, 12], safety, ethics, accountability in error-sensitive domains, and scalable infrastructure [8, 10, 11] for large-scale and long-horizon simulations. To answer these questions, the second LLM Agents for Social Simulation workshop (LASS), themed Fundamental Challenges and Real-World Applications, aims to bring together researchers and practitioners from diverse disciplines and backgrounds to explore how LLM agents can be more faithfully modeled, rigorously evaluated, safely governed, and effectively applied to address real-world problems in vertical domains, with careful consideration of their unique requirements, challenges, and practical limitations, thereby promoting human well-being and broader societal benefit.
evidence_items.title: The 2nd Workshop on LLM Agents for Social Simulation

evidence_items.summary: State-of-the-art Information Retrieval (IR) pipelines often rely on dense neural models to index and retrieve large document collections. After an initial retrieval stage, precision-oriented re-ranking approaches can further refine the ranked list. However, re-ranking quality strongly depends on the availability of reliable relevance signals. Recent work has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate relevance judgments that can serve as such signals. However, achieving strong alignment with human gold labels generally requires either very large and complex LLMs or extensive human supervision. In this work, we investigate whether relatively small LLMs, despite producing limited and often noisy relevance assessments, can still be leveraged to improve the ranking of documents retrieved by dense bi-encoder models. Specifically, we introduce new approaches based on the recently proposed Dimension IMportance Estimators (DIMEs), incorporating LLM-generated relevance judgments into the re-ranking process. Our study assumes a practical setting: we consider access only to relatively small LLMs and to very small sets of relevance judgments generated for the top-retrieved documents of each query by dense retrieval models, and we investigate how to leverage these sparse, often noisy signals to refine the ranking of the entire retrieved set. Our method leads to substantial improvements in document ranking, boosting nDCG@10 and AP by up to 9% and 15%, respectively, across different datasets, LLMs, and bi-encoder backbone retrieval models. These results show that even a few noisy relevance judgments from small LLMs can provide a powerful signal to improve the effectiveness of IR systems.
evidence_items.title: Effective Re-Ranking with DIMEs using Few Noisy LLM-Generated Relevance Judgments

evidence_items.summary: Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). Attention-based Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) have been widely adopted to capture long-range spatial dependencies, but their node-level attention incurs quadratic complexity and limits scalability in large-scale traffic networks. Although sparse and hierarchical attention mechanisms reduce this cost by restricting node pairs, they still rely on node-level modeling. Through empirical analysis on a 2,352-node benchmark, we find that removing node-level attention from representative baselines does not consistently degrade performance, suggesting that its additional predictive benefit may be marginal in large-scale settings. In contrast, region-level attention appears useful for modeling traffic propagation, which is also consistent with classical traffic engineering models that represent traffic dynamics over aggregated spatial units. Motivated by these observations, we propose STAAR, a Spatio-Temporal Attention over Adaptive Regions framework that dynamically constructs soft traffic regions and models dependencies among them. Specifically, adaptive region assignment assigns each node to multiple regions with normalized weights, while spatio-temporal attention captures time-lagged dependencies by flattening region tokens across time steps into a unified sequence. Extensive experiments on large-scale traffic benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves competitive accuracy with substantial efficiency gains, reducing training time by 3.5×–29× and inference time by 2.8×–28× compared with existing attention-based STGNNs.
