The source code of STAAR is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/STAAR.
evidence_items.title: STAAR: Spatio-Temporal Attention over Adaptive Regions for Traffic Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Entity resolution solutions based on deep learning have been gaining more attention due to their improved performance in linking records of the same entity. However, due to the complexity of models (especially state-of-art language models) used for entity resolution, it is challenging to provide privacy-preserving variants of deep entity resolution models to comply with data privacy constraints in applications like medical data analysis. In this paper, we propose Hide-And-Seek-Pair (HASP), an efficient privacy-preserving deep entity resolution protocol that utilizes and optimizes homomorphic encryption with deep models in a two-stage computation fashion that provides a practical balance between robust privacy guarantees and computational efficiency. Additionally, by employing Synthetic Ranging, Polynomial Degree Optimization and Differential Loss Term, HASP ensures accurate non-linear function approximation in encrypted neural networks. Overall, the framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various benchmarks while offering a secure and efficient method for privacy-preserving entity resolution.
evidence_items.title: Hide-And-Seek-Pair: Efficient Two-Stage Privacy-Preserving Deep Entity Resolution

evidence_items.summary: Terrestrial carbon flux prediction is critical for quantifying ecosystem carbon sources and sinks. However, current deep learning models still struggle with cross-ecosystem generalisation across the heterogeneous biomes covered by global eddy-covariance networks. A fundamental reason is that different ecosystems are shaped by past climate over very different timescales: climate may continue to influence ecosystem processes for only weeks in tropical savannas but for months in temperate forests, while existing models apply a single uniform temporal context window to all ecosystems. To address this challenge, we propose MemPerceiver, a multimodal framework that augments the EcoPerceiver backbone with six ecologically motivated memory scales (-180 to -7 days) and a per-scale gating network, allowing the model to learn which of the predefined temporal horizons are most informative for each prediction, without requiring biome-specific lag labels. On the CarbonSense benchmark of 385 eddy-covariance sites across 15 IGBP classes, MemPerceiver achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) and Gross Primary Production (GPP), with particularly large gains in data-scarce settings: relative to EcoPerceiver, it reduces RMSE by 23.0% on the one-shot WAT class and improves NSE by 24.0% on the zero-shot SNO class. Averaging the learned gate activations within each biome yields an interpretable temporal fingerprint, and within-biome consistency analysis shows that these fingerprints provide a stable, model-derived view of biome-specific ecological memory. The code is available at https://github.com/gaoshan-bi/MemPerceiver.
evidence_items.title: MemPerceiver: Adaptive Multi-Scale Memory Reveals Biome-Specific Temporal Fingerprints in Carbon Flux Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Cross-session HD-sEMG gesture recognition is a zero-shot domain generalization problem central to deployable myoelectric interfaces. Existing approaches typically treat the session gap as a generic distribution mismatch and address it through larger models, uniform normalization, or latent feature alignment. We argue that, in HD-sEMG, part of this gap arises before representation learning: electrode reattachment perturbs the sensing interface, producing structured drift that is frequency-selective in amplitude and non-uniform across electrodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose a calibration-before-recognition paradigm for cross-session HD-sEMG generalization and instantiate it as Frequency–Electrode Calibration (FEC), a lightweight plug-in framework that recalibrates band-wise spectral magnitudes and down-weights unreliable electrodes before backbone feature extraction, without target-session labels or model updates. On the Hyser cross-session benchmark (20 subjects, 2 recording days separated by 3-25 days), FEC with a MobileNet3D-SE backbone achieves 70.96% zero-shot accuracy using only 99.2K parameters, improving the naive backbone by 9.33% and the strongest normalization-style calibration baseline by 4.99%. These results suggest that explicitly modeling sensor-level drift can shift cross-session generalization from purely model-centric compensation toward pre-recognition calibration, offering an interpretable view of cross-session HD-sEMG degradation and enabling a parameter-efficient framework for resource-constrained edge deployment in real-world wearable myoelectric systems.
evidence_items.title: Calibration before Recognition: Sensor-Level Domain Generalization for Cross-Session HD-sEMG Gesture Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Unlike web-search, enterprise search queries are more contextual, documents are private and heterogeneous, and ground-truth relevance labels are scarce. Production systems at this scale have long relied on gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) models such as LightGBM with hand-engineered features, given their speed, interpretability, and robustness on numeric features. However, high-quality semantic embeddings from large, pre-trained language models open new possibilities for neural learning-to-rank models that can jointly learn from sparse hand-crafted features (e.g., personalization signals such as user activity, document recency, and lexical matching features like BM25) and dense semantic representations. In this paper, we present our work on using wide & deep neural networks for search relevance over the enterprise files data. Due to privacy constraints on customer data, which limits direct inspection, and the lack of publicly available enterprise search datasets, we complement our private data experiments by adapting the H&M fashion recommendation dataset for experimentation. Our results show consistent and significant improvements when embedding is added as input to the ranking systems.
evidence_items.title: Files Search Relevance using Wide and Deep Networks

evidence_items.summary: Training large Transformer language models is dominated by the cost of synchronous parameter updates: every block of weights is moved at every step using a gradient computed before any block has moved. The resulting trajectory is wasteful, because per-block updates are evaluated on a frozen snapshot of the rest of the network that the next step will already invalidate. Second-order methods such as Shampoo and K-FAC address this spatially through preconditioning, and sharpness-aware methods such as SAM trade compute for sharper minima, but both leave the temporal coupling between blocks untouched. We introduce Gradient Interaction Graph Optimization (GIGO), a meta-optimizer that estimates a sparse directed graph of cross-block gradient dependencies online, partitions each step into contiguous sequential stages along this graph, and refreshes downstream gradients using a stale-activation approximation. The framework wraps any base optimizer, adds one cached boundary activation per stage (~32 MB at Tseq= 1024, scaling linearly with sequence length), and is compatible with mixed precision and data parallelism. On GPT-2 Small through XL (124M-1.5B), GIGO-Adam reaches the same OpenWebText/C4 perplexity in 32.0-34.0% fewer optimizer steps than synchronous AdamW --- a lead of 8-22 percentage points over the strongest 2024-vintage baselines (SOAP, Muon, Sophia, Lion, GaLore) on the Small comparison cohort --- with a per-step overhead of 32-38% and a net wall-clock benefit ranging from +5.2% (Small) to +16.2% (XL) across the four sizes tested. The benefit vanishes or reverses where the method's preconditions do not hold: a synthetic block-diagonal control (SRR=0.0%), the overhead-dominated Penn Treebank stress test (-18.5% wall-clock), and a weak-coupling small-vision-Transformer diagnostic (-12.4% wall-clock on CIFAR-100). Ablations decompose the mechanism: the partial-re-forward refresh primitive alone (random partition) accounts for 9.4% SRR, the interaction-graph schedule contributes a further ~22pp, and the layer-contiguity constraint controls overhead. Our convergence theorem matches the standard Adam O(T-1/4) rate uniformly in graph-estimation quality, providing a safety guarantee; the empirical step-reduction is reported as an empirical regularity not formally predicted by the theory.
evidence_items.title: Gradient Interaction Graph Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Misinformation diffusion at scale on social media poses serious societal risks, as it can distort collective decision-making, undermine public health interventions, bias political discourse, and trigger large-scale behavioral cascades during emergencies. Most existing approaches rely heavily on observable content signals or user-level features, primarily capturing surface-level correlations while overlooking the latent causal mechanisms governing diffusion dynamics. To bridge this gap, we formulate misinformation diffusion prediction from a causal perspective and propose MisTran, a mechanism-aware framework that models diffusion through causal mediation. Specifically, MisTran introduces a structured mediator to represent propagation mechanisms that connect persuasive content to cascade growth, enabling the model to move beyond correlation-based inference toward mechanism-oriented prediction. To further improve robustness, we incorporate LLM-based counterfactual reasoning to encourage causal consistency during training. By constructing hypothetical variations of posts, the model learns invariant propagation patterns that reflect stable causal structure rather than spurious correlations. Extensive experiments on a real-world misinformation diffusion benchmark demonstrate that MisTran consistently outperforms strong baselines. Ablation and interpretability analyses further validate the effectiveness of mechanism-constrained modeling and provide interpretable insights into the dynamics of misinformation diffusion.
evidence_items.title: Causal Modeling of Misinformation Diffusion via LLM-based Counterfactual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Traditional Federated Learning (FL) relies on iterative parameter exchange, which limits architectural flexibility and introduces high communication overhead for large foundation models. To address these issues, Data-Driven Federated Learning (DD-FL) has recently emerged as a scalable alternative. Instead of exchanging model parameters, DD-FL adopts a one-shot data-centric pipeline, where heterogeneous clients collaboratively annotate a shared unlabeled public dataset and the server performs knowledge distillation through soft-label aggregation. While DD-FL improves scalability and supports heterogeneous architectures, it also introduces a new attack surface on the shared public dataset. These public datasets are often collected from web crawlers or collaborative platforms with limited integrity validation, making data poisoning feasible. Moreover, since DD-FL removes parameter-level interactions and relies on soft-label aggregation across heterogeneous models, traditional FL backdoor attacks designed for individual models are easily diluted and exhibit poor cross-architecture transferability. In this paper, we propose a semantic backdoor attack for DD-FL. Our method generates poisoned samples by aligning image perturbations with target semantic directions in a shared vision-language space. This enables poisoned samples to induce semantically aligned target predictions across heterogeneous client models, making the backdoor more transferable during soft-label aggregation. We also study how biased aggregation weights further strengthen the attack effect. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show that our method achieves higher attack success rates and robustness than existing baselines, while maintaining high clean accuracy and strong visual stealthiness.
evidence_items.title: Cross-Architecture Semantic Backdoor Attack in Data-Driven Federated Learning

evidence_items.summary: Predicting single-cell molecular state from routine histology could make spatial profiling more scalable, but existing histology-to- expression methods are mostly limited to spot-level targets, re- stricted gene panels, or organ-specific settings. This leaves three gaps for practical single-cell deployment: a lack of large aligned- cell resources, limited support for direct multi-organ prediction, and incomplete full-gene expression recovery from whole-slide images. We address these gaps by curating CellST-24M, a 23.94M- cell histology–transcriptomics resource spanning 66 studies, 25 organ categories, Visium HD, and Xenium, and by introducing STMoE, a WSI-only organ-routed prediction framework for full- gene single-cell expression inference. STMoE detects cells from H&E slides, encodes cell-centered and tissue-context crops with a frozen UNI2-h pathology foundation model, aligns image and expression embeddings with soft contrastive learning, and predicts full-gene profiles through organ-routed retrieval from training-only reference banks. On matched human lung benchmarks, STMoE achieves state-of-the-art cell-level performance, outperforming cell- adapted BLEEP, sCellST and GHIST under both in-domain and cross-patient settings. Across 22 organs, STMoE supports direct multi-organ prediction and achieves gene-wise Pearson up to 0.6451 and cell-wise Pearson up to 0.8379, while retaining approximately 60% predictive capability under cross-patient transfer. In down- stream marker-derived analysis, predicted profiles recover coarse cell-state structure with 0.5935 accuracy and 0.5922 balanced accu- racy. Together, CellST-24M and STMoE establish a benchmark and modeling framework for WSI-only, multi-organ, full-gene single- cell histology-to-expression prediction.
evidence_items.title: STMoE: Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts for Single-Cell Gene Expression Prediction from Histology

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale search and recommendation systems routinely run online experiments for ranking models, feed policies, user-interface treatments, and ad/recommendation blending strategies. These launches are rarely single-metric decisions: teams often need to improve click-through rate, conversion, dwell time, retention, or revenue while controlling negative feedback and latency. We propose AV-MO-SOPTIMA++, an anytime-valid framework for multi-objective online experimentation under adaptive traffic allocation and optional stopping. Instead of relying only on marginal arm-objective confidence sequences, AV-MO-SOPTIMA++ uses prospective two-sample contrast confidence sequences for decision-relevant arm pairs; these contrasts may be pre-activated for a fixed decision mode or activated online when new bottleneck constraints appear. The method derives Pareto and guardrail certificates from these contrasts and propagates certified dominance through a dominance graph. The framework further uses decision-specific stopping rules for full Pareto, relaxed Pareto, and guardrail launch decisions, together with a bottleneck-aware allocation policy that prioritizes comparisons currently blocking a valid decision. Experiments show that the anytime-valid controller maintains calibration under optional stopping, exposes false certificates from nominal multi-objective peeking, and supports safe guardrail launch decisions with fewer samples than fixed-horizon A/B or full-Pareto PSI in a launch benchmark. Component ablations show that contrast certificates reduce guardrail stopping time and bottleneck allocation sharply reduces bad-arm exposure. In full Pareto identification, contrast variants reduce samples on separated instances, while near-boundary instances remain challenging for all validity-first methods.
evidence_items.title: Anytime-Valid Multi-Objective Online Experimentation with Contrast Certificates

evidence_items.summary: Pre-trained 2D graph encoders have achieved strong performance in molecular representation learning by capturing transferable topological patterns from large-scale unlabeled molecular graphs. However, downstream molecular applications often involve rich chemical and geometric information associated with atoms and bonds, which is not explicitly modeled by conventional 2D graph pre-training approaches. Existing molecular pre-training methods typically incorporate such knowledge during large-scale pre-training, requiring specialized architectures and substantial computational cost. In this paper, we investigate how to enhance pre-trained 2D graph encoders through lightweight downstream prompt adaptation with molecular knowledge. We propose a molecular prompting framework that integrates heterogeneous molecular information into downstream graph learning without modifying the pre-trained encoder parameters. Specifically, molecular knowledge is first projected into the latent space of pre-trained topological representations to reduce the discrepancy between topology and molecular semantics. Based on the aligned representations, we further employ knowledge-conditioned prompt generators to produce adaptive prompts for different molecular components, enabling fine-grained and instance-aware downstream adaptation. The proposed framework can be flexibly incorporated into existing 2D graph pre-training methods while maintaining strong parameter efficiency. Extensive experiments on molecular classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over representative graph pre-training and molecular representation learning baselines, particularly under low-resource settings.
evidence_items.title: Molecular Knowledge Guided Prompt Adaptation for Pre-trained 2D Graph Encoders

evidence_items.summary: Understanding how semantics are processed at the lexical level has been a key aim for the cognitive sciences, with large-scale semantic rating studies in different languages playing a crucial role in facilitating the advancement and development of theories of lexical processing, as well as providing valuable methodological resources that can be used in empirical investigations. In this paper, we present the CzeLex database, a megastudy of 9601 Czech words that have been normed along five psycholinguistic dimensions from a large sample of 4405 Czech-speaking participants. We provide individual rating data at the item and participant levels, as well as aggregated data from both mean ratings and latent means derived using cumulative-link mixed modeling, along with a comprehensive analysis comparing aggregation methods. We demonstrate that the dataset has good reliability and that specific dimensions predict lexical processing measures in a lexical decision task, regardless of the aggregation method used. These norms are the largest available subjective rating resource for Czech and further contribute to the growing body of languages with openly available data on these dimensions. We hope that the dataset will be a valuable resource for researchers working on Czech, in addition to opening up new opportunities for cross-linguistic semantic investigations. All data, code, and analyses are available at https://osf.io/tqxfm.
evidence_items.title: CzeLex: A megastudy dataset of concreteness, imageability, age of acquisition, valence, and gender ratings for 9601 Czech words

evidence_items.summary: Concept bottleneck models are only as useful as the concept space they expose. Existing concept-annotation-free CBMs often treat this space as text-pool retrieval: an image is explained by whichever prompt words score highly, so visual evidence that is fine-grained, compositional, or hard to name can be missed. We introduce SAND-CBM, which shifts the bottleneck from prompt retrieval to image-side basis reconstruction in a frozen vision–language space. Text-similarity channels are retained as named anchors, but they are complemented by learned visual-factor channels that can surface candidate evidence beyond the vocabulary. The core design is a signed–nonnegative–calibrated–shared (SNCS) representation contract: signed dictionary rows preserve CLIP-space directions, nonnegative activations give additive channel strengths, training-set calibration makes channels rankable, and a class-conditional selector reuses one shared dictionary across classes. SAND-CBM is concept-annotation-free rather than label-free: it uses no concept names, concept annotations, or concept-level targets for the learned image-side basis, while task labels train the final readout and an explicit low-bandwidth class gate. This design provides a more diagnostic interface: important channels should be removable, low-contribution or random removals should have weaker effects, discovered activations should align above null controls, and class gates should reuse rather than duplicate evidence. Across four visual benchmarks, SAND-CBM remains competitive in accuracy while showing a more concentrated and intervention-consistent concept-candidate interface than matched controls. Core code is available at https://github.com/LMBTough/SAND.
evidence_items.title: SAND-CBM: Image-Side Basis Reconstruction for Concept Bottleneck Models

evidence_items.summary: Cross-modal retrieval systems enable searching content in one modality using queries from another. Recently, retrieving images using natural language queries -- text-to-image retrieval -- has received a lot of attention due to advances in deep learning vision models and interest in multi-modal processing in general. While several modeling approaches exist, ranging from simple keyword matching to joint embedding models and neural rerankers, there is limited understanding of how candidate generation, reranking, and fusion interact across retrieval pipelines. In this paper, we present an analysis of retrieval-stage interactions in text-to-image retrieval pipelines, spanning a comprehensive set of categories drawn from recent advances in information retrieval: single index pipelines, multi-stage retrieve and rerank pipelines, and ensemble pipelines. We compare the effectiveness of these pipelines on the MS-COCO and Flickr30K benchmarks revealing several retrieval-stage phenomena governing reranking effectiveness, candidate-set expansion, and ensemble behavior.
evidence_items.title: Retrieval-Stage Interactions in Cross-Modal Text-to-Image Retrieval Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: Characterising individual differences in behaviour and predicting future behaviour are central goals of psychological science. However, behavioural data are difficult to obtain, and most research relies on nomothetic approaches that aggregate them into summary statistics. This aggregation obscures person-specific patterns that would afford an idiographic understanding of individual behaviour. Pervasive digital technologies (e.g., smartphones, wearables, and computer-mediated systems) now generate fine-grained, temporally ordered records of everyday behaviour, creating unprecedented opportunities to study both systematic inter-individual differences and patterns of intra-individual variation in digital behaviour. Here, we introduce Natural Behaviour Processing (NBP) as a framework for analysing digital behavioural data using sequence modelling approaches adapted from natural language processing. We argue that behaviour shares structural properties with language: both involve a repository of possible actions (vocabulary), systematic patterns governing how elements typically combine (grammar), and context-dependent meaning (semantics). These structural parallels motivate applying sequence-based models, which have revolutionised language processing, to the study of behaviour more broadly. We provide a brief illustrative review of pioneering studies demonstrating that sequential approaches capture person-specific patterns that aggregation loses, across topics including life outcomes, decision making, social media use, consumer behaviour, digital education, and health. We discuss the challenges facing NBP adoption, including the tension between predictive modelling and theoretical understanding, the need for large-scale curated behaviour datasets, and methodological training requirements. By modelling the order and context of everyday actions rather than aggregates, NBP could enable person-specific representations of behaviour that support both individual-level prediction and systematic comparison of individual differences across people.
evidence_items.title: Towards natural behaviour processing for the representation and prediction of digital behaviour.

evidence_items.summary: Generative question answering and knowledge access systems increasingly use reasoning language models to synthesize retrieved or domain-specific information, but verbose rationales can raise latency and serving cost. We study whether policy entropy can serve as a training-time signal for uncertainty-aware compute allocation in such information access settings, rather than only as an online stopping heuristic. Our method estimates token-level entropy from repeated samples, assigns each question to a reasoning-budget tier, compresses traces for lower-uncertainty cases, and trains compact student models with mixed-granularity supervision and optional reinforcement learning. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two knowledge-intensive QA settings in healthcare and finance, the method reduces reasoning length while preserving or improving accuracy. These results suggest that uncertainty estimates can shape supervision for resource-efficient generative AI and help models learn adaptive reasoning behavior without adding an inference-time controller.
evidence_items.title: Training Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Reasoning Budgets with Policy Entropy

evidence_items.summary: Schema matching, or aligning semantically related elements across schemas, is a foundational task in data integration and interoperability. In this talk, we report on a year-long effort to align attributes in XML documents to a fine-grained concept vocabulary. This problem is especially important in insurance, where organizations exchange policy and claims data through legacy, proprietary, and product-specific XML schemas that must be reconciled for interoperability. This setting is understudied and differs from existing schema-matching benchmarks: source schemas contain local conventions and custom business logic, while the target vocabulary has been built over decades by many contributors, leading to inconsistencies. Building on recent work that combines smaller fine-tuned language models with larger frontier models, we propose an agent-based architecture for schema matching. The talk discusses the industrial constraints that shaped the system, failure modes of retrieval-and-re-ranking systems, and practical lessons for schema matching in the wild.
evidence_items.title: Aligning Real-World Document Schemas to Fine-Grained Concept Vocabularies

evidence_items.summary: Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.
evidence_items.title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control

evidence_items.summary: Generative recommendation has attracted widespread attention as a new paradigm in recommender systems. Its core idea is to discretize item semantic representations into semantic IDs and leverage the generative model's sequence modeling capability to predict the next item the user may prefer. Early approaches mainly focused on textual semantics, and recent multimodal generative recommendation methods incorporate additional modalities to provide richer semantics. However, existing methods typically handle modalities independently during both tokenization and generation, leading to insufficient modality fusion in semantic ID construction and inadequate cross-modal integration during recommendation. Moreover, the modality tokenizers are optimized with representation-level reconstruction or alignment objectives and lack recommendation-aware supervision, resulting in sub-optimal performance. To address these issues, we propose Accumulative Modality Tokenization for Multimodal Generative Recommendation, namely AMTGR. Specifically, we harness the Multimodal Large Language Model as the unified tokenizer to progressively accumulate and tokenize multimodal information, and design a collaborative-aware reconstruction task as the tokenizer's optimization objective to achieve recommendation-oriented multimodal semantic IDs, which will be jointly fed into the generative model to achieve effective cross-modal integration during recommendation. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that AMTGR significantly outperforms baselines, and further analyses verify the effectiveness of high-quality multimodal semantic IDs and the unified modality integration.
evidence_items.title: Accumulative Modality Tokenization for Multimodal Generative Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Deep neural networks increasingly suffer from progressive information geometry degeneration as network depth scales, manifested as gradient attenuation, representation collapse, and feature homogenization across layers. Existing connection mechanisms, including residual routing and manifold-constrained hyper-connections, primarily focus on numerical stabilization but fail to preserve the intrinsic geometric structure of feature propagation. To address this issue, we propose SOHC (Special Orthogonal Hyper-Connections), a geometry-preserving routing framework that formulates inter-layer information propagation as exact manifold transformation on the special orthogonal group. Specifically, SOHC parameterizes routing matrices through the Cayley transform, ensuring analytically exact isometric propagation along the geometry-preserving routing stream throughout network depth. This exact orthogonal residual path preserves signal energy and spectral geometry along the isometric stream, providing a stable backbone for deep information propagation. Moreover, we design a gated dual-stream architecture that combines globally stable isometric propagation with locally adaptive semantic refinement, balancing structural stability and representation expressiveness. Extensive experiments on deep language modeling and sequential recommendation benchmarks demonstrate that SOHC consistently improves optimization stability, representation diversity, and downstream performance over existing hyper-connection methods. Further analyses show that SOHC effectively mitigates representation rank degeneration and preserves stable feature geometry throughout deep signal propagation, validating the importance of geometry-preserving routing for deep neural architectures.
evidence_items.title: Special Orthogonal Hyper-Connections for Geometry-Preserving Deep Routing

evidence_items.summary: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) enables the fabrication of metallic components with complex geometries and high performance. However, achieving coordinated control of formability including defect suppression and cracking resistance together with mechanical properties such as strength, ductility, and fatigue life remains a critical challenge for LPBF alloys. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted for process optimization, defect prediction, and performance evaluation, conventional AI models often lack physical metallurgical interpretability, leading to limited generalization and unreliable extrapolation beyond training domains. This review focuses on the role of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in addressing the formability–performance trade-off in LPBF alloys. We first introduce four knowledge domains that establish physical interpretability in metallic materials: physical metallurgy principles, cross-scale numerical information, microstructure image analysis, and causal physical mechanisms. Subsequently, we systematically examine XAI applications across representative LPBF alloy systems. In performance-oriented alloys such as steels and titanium alloys, XAI facilitates mechanism–aware control of non-equilibrium phase transformations, microstructural anisotropy, and defect-sensitive fatigue behavior. In formability-oriented alloys including aluminum alloys and nickel-based superalloys, XAI supports cracking susceptibility prediction, process–window identification, and printable alloy design. Despite these advances, most current studies remain task-specific and single-objective, with limited integration of formability and performance optimization. To overcome this limitation, we propose a unified multi-objective optimization framework incorporating physically constrained modeling, standardized multimodal databases, and causal reasoning. This review provides guidance for the intelligent, reliable, and collaborative design of LPBF alloys with both high formability and excellent mechanical performance.
evidence_items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence for laser powder bed fusion alloys: breaking the formability–performance trade-off via collaborative control

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning methods are increasingly discussed in relation to robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, robotic assistance, computer navigation, and AI-based prediction represent distinct functions that are often conflated under the single label “AI-assisted robotic TKA,” obscuring the state of evidence for each. This review clarifies these distinctions and maps the current evidence for AI-related functions across the TKA pathway, keeping AI prediction evidence analytically separate from robotic execution evidence at the level of each clinical function. We performed a critical narrative review and evidence map of peer-reviewed literature relevant to robotic-assisted TKA, navigation-assisted TKA, AI/ML prediction models, digital planning, implant sizing, intraoperative decision support, postoperative monitoring, implementation, and economic evaluation. Evidence was interpreted according to clinical function, comparator structure, validation status, and translational maturity. Because the available literature is methodologically and conceptually heterogeneous, quantitative pooling and formal comparative-effectiveness claims were not attempted. Robotic-assisted and navigation-assisted TKA have the most mature evidence base for improving technical precision, particularly implant positioning and radiographic alignment. In contrast, AI/ML evidence is concentrated mainly in adjacent pathway functions, including radiographic interpretation, implant-sizing prediction, patient-selection support, dissatisfaction prediction, outcome modelling, perioperative risk stratification, and postoperative monitoring. Direct clinical evidence demonstrating that AI-enabled robotic TKA provides incremental patient-level benefit beyond conventional robotic assistance remains limited. Current studies are constrained by inconsistent terminology, short follow-up, limited external validation, incomplete reporting of AI components, heterogeneous outcomes, cost uncertainty, and uncertain generalizability across patient populations and healthcare settings. AI should not currently be treated as a single validated surgical intervention in TKA. Rather, it represents a family of emerging pathway-level functions that may support preoperative planning, intraoperative decision support, patient selection, risk communication, and longitudinal recovery monitoring. Future studies should explicitly define the AI component being evaluated, distinguish AI functionality from robotic or navigation assistance, use standardized comparators, and assess long-term patient-reported outcomes, implant survivorship, safety, cost-effectiveness, and equity across multicenter prospective cohorts or randomized trials.
evidence_items.title: Distinguishing artificial intelligence from robotic execution in total knee arthroplasty: a narrative review and evidence map

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVES
To critically evaluate the current role of artificial intelligence (AI) in dental diagnosis across multiple dental disciplines, assessing diagnostic performance, methodological quality, risk of bias, validation, explainability, and clinical applicability.


DATA AND SOURCES
This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025639340). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to December-2025. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Risk of bias in diagnostic accuracy studies was assessed using QUADAS-2-tool, evaluating the domains of patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing whilst randomised studies were assessed using Cochrane RoB 2-tool. Reporting quality and transparency of AI-model development and validation were assessed using the selected items from TRIPOD-AI reporting guideline. Methodological quality and risk of bias in AI model development and evaluation were additionally assessed using PROBAST+AI.


STUDY SELECTION
Ninety-six studies met the inclusion criteria, of which 90.6% were retrospective. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) were the most frequently used architecture (82.3%). Sixteen studies failed to specify the CNN architecture used. Reported diagnostic accuracy ranged from 81% to 99% across dental specialties, with high performance in implantology (92-99%), orthodontics (88-99%), endodontics (87-99%). Panoramic radiographs and cone-beam computed tomography were the most used imaging modalities. QUADAS-2 analysis indicated that high-risk of bias in 55.2% of studies and most lacked external validation, whilst Assessment using selected TRIPOD+AI items identified important gaps in reporting completeness and transparency, particularly in sample-size justification, missing-data handling, protocol availability, study registration, and data or code availability.


CONCLUSIONS
AI demonstrates substantial technical capability to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, the predominance of retrospective designs, limited external validation, and methodological weaknesses constrain the strength of current evidence.


CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE
The use of AI is potentially considered as a decision-support tool rather than replacement for clinical judgement.
evidence_items.title: A Systematic Review of Bias, Validation, and Explainability in Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for Dental Diagnostics.

organizations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey
evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can produce highly realistic dermatological images, raising concerns about clinicians’ ability to distinguish authentic pathology from synthetic representations. To assess whether dermatological expertise influences the detection of AI-generated vitiligo images, and to evaluate the self-detection capabilities of the algorithm, we conducted a participant-blinded cross-sectional study in which 31 dermatologists, stratified by experience, classified one AI-generated vitiligo image alongside three real controls while blinded to the number and identity of the synthetic images. Interrater agreement was assessed using Fleiss’ kappa statistic, and the synthetic image was additionally evaluated using three large multimodal models. Residents detected the AI-generated image more frequently than senior dermatologists and key opinion leaders. After disclosure of the correct classifications, the experts identified specific biological inconsistencies, whereas residents relied primarily on intuitive impressions, and the performance of the AI models varied across the detection and post-disclosure artifact-recognition tasks. This study is limited by its evaluation of a single AI-generated image depicting a single disease (vitiligo), and the findings may therefore not be generalizable to other dermatological morphologies, image-generation prompts, or multi-image scenarios. In this exploratory study, greater clinical experience was associated with reduced detection of the evaluated synthetic image; whether this reflects a general effect of expertise requires further study. These findings highlight the emerging risks associated with medical AI and support the integration of AI-focused visual analysis into dermatology education.
evidence_items.title: When expertise fails: detection of artificial intelligence - generated vitiligo imagery across the spectrum of dermatological experience; a cross-sectional exploratory study

evidence_items.summary: The GREEN-AI workshop addresses the growing need for environmentally sustainable Artificial Intelligence (AI). As AI models continue to scale in size and complexity, their energy consumption, carbon footprint, and resource demands raise urgent questions about the long-term ecological and social consequences of deploying large-scale AI systems at an ever-increasing pace. Distinct from workshops that apply AI to environmental or climate-related problems, GREEN-AI focuses specifically on the sustainability of AI itself—spanning its computational, methodological, and infrastructural dimensions. It offers a dedicated forum for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to explore energy-efficient algorithms, sustainable data management and infrastructure practices, and novel evaluation metrics that explicitly incorporate environmental impact alongside traditional performance measures. By bridging academia and industry, GREEN-AI aims to catalyze actionable change and foster innovation that reconciles rapid technical advancement with global sustainability objectives. The workshop encourages contributions from diverse perspectives, including hardware-aware optimization, green computing, and responsible model development. Structured as a focused half-day event, it will feature invited talks, peer-reviewed paper presentations, and interactive panel discussions designed to shape a more responsible, resource-conscious, and ecologically aware AI ecosystem.
evidence_items.title: GREEN-AI: Grounding Research on Energy- and Resource-Efficient Networks for Sustainable AI

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly being adopted across the behavioral sciences, reshaping how researchers generate ideas, design studies, collect data, and analyze results. While GenAI offers substantial benefits such as increasing productivity, enabling more sophisticated methods, and lowering technical barriers, these gains come with potential costs in the form of errors. This article discusses the risks of errors as a foundation to decide when and how to use GenAI in behavioral research. We distinguish between two types of errors of shifting relative threat, depending on how narrowly a research task is specified. Open-ended tasks (e.g., ideation, literature review) leave a large space of plausible outputs and make researchers relatively more liable to errors of omission. In constrained, well-specified tasks (e.g., running a specified analysis, writing code to a stated scheme), the narrow solution space limits the scope for omission, raising the relative threat of errors of commission. We argue that commission errors are potentially easier to detect. Omission errors, by contrast, are harder to detect and pose greater risks to the diversity and scope of scientific inquiry. We propose that GenAI usage should be guided by a comparative assessment of error detectability. We offer practical recommendations for evaluating GenAI applications and for preserving the methodological diversity that sustains cumulative science.
evidence_items.title: Risks of omission and commission errors when using generative AI in behavioral science research.

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet limited research has examined how GenAI-supported learning operates alongside geographically distributed peer collaboration. This qualitative study explores student experiences in an AI-enhanced cross-campus cybersecurity learning environment connecting university campuses in California, United States, and Ontario, Canada. Anonymous reflections were collected from 19 students (nine in California and ten in Ontario) about their experiences with GenAI-supported learning, cross-campus interaction, associated challenges, and recommendations for improving the learning experience. The findings indicate that students perceived GenAI as supporting concept clarification, greater perceived learning efficiency, idea development, and problem-solving, while also emphasizing the importance of critically evaluating GenAI-generated information. Cross-campus interaction was perceived as exposing students to diverse perspectives, experiences, and approaches to cybersecurity, which participants described as broadening their understanding of collaborative problem-solving across contexts. Students nevertheless identified challenges involving scheduling, technology, differences in experience, GenAI accuracy, and responsible use. They recommended more structured cross-campus projects, hands-on activities, clearer guidance on ethical GenAI use, and greater engagement with industry professionals. The study contributes to research on technology-enhanced learning in higher education by suggesting how GenAI-supported learning and geographically distributed peer interaction can provide complementary educational resources: GenAI offers immediate cognitive and informational support, while cross-campus interaction provides access to situated human perspectives. Together, these experiences highlight the importance of verification, contextual judgment, critical AI literacy, and intentional pedagogical design in GenAI-enhanced learning environments.
evidence_items.title: Learning with GenAI across campuses: student experiences of GenAI-enhanced cybersecurity education

evidence_items.summary: Background: Lung function is a key indicator of respiratory health and is known to be influenced by lifestyle practices such as yoga. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled non-invasive, scalable, and real-time assessment of physiological parameters. Swaasa is an AI-based novel technique designed to assess lung function through cough analysis, offering a potential alternative to conventional spirometry. Objective: The present study aimed to evaluate lung function using Swaasa among yoga practitioners and compare the findings with age- and sex-matched non-yoga practitioners in a cross-sectional design. Methods: A cross-sectional comparative study was conducted on adult participants divided into two groups: regular yoga practitioners ([≥]1 year of practice) and non-yoga practitioners. Lung function parameters, including Forced Vital Capacity (FVC), Forced Expiratory Volume in one second (FEV), and cough pattern indices, were assessed using the Swaasa AI-based system. Results: Yoga practitioners demonstrated significantly higher AI-derived lung function indices, including FVC and FEV, compared to non-yoga practitioners (p < 0.05). Improved respiratory health and reduced respiratory variability were also observed in the yoga group, indicating enhanced respiratory efficiency. Conclusion: The findings suggest that regular yoga practice is associated with better lung function as assessed by Swaasa.
evidence_items.title: Swaasa an AI-Based Novel Technique to Assess Lung Function in Yoga Practitioners in Comparison to Non-Yoga Practitioners: A Cross-Sectional study

evidence_items.summary: With the rapidly evolving digital technology landscape, characterized by cutting-edge technologies, such as artificial intelligence, big data, and machine learning, data privacy is increasingly becoming a topic of global urgency in both policy and technical domains. It, therefore, calls for practical and context-sensitive anonymization strategies that enable researchers to protect sensitive information while preserving data utility for analysis and sharing. Despite the availability of numerous anonymization techniques, their practical adoption remains limited, because existing tools often require advanced programming skills, are commercially restricted, or provide little guidance for selecting appropriate methods. Consequently, many researchers and institutions, particularly in resource-constrained settings, face difficulties implementing privacy-preserving data sharing. Existing anonymization software tends to be either prohibitively complex, commercially restricted, or not sensitive to resource-constrained research settings. In this paper, we introduce a novel Data Anonymization Platform designed to implement ethical data stewardship that is both usable and scalable while adhering to high privacy standards. The platform integrates several anonymization methods, including suppression, masking, bucketing, pseudonymization, tokenization, and k-anonymity, among others, on a Shiny-based dashboard. It enables users to upload datasets and apply anonymization techniques through an intuitive point-and-click interface. It adapts the results based on the dataset’s structure and produces code in R, Stata, and Python to support reproducibility, transparency, and accountability. The platform then allows users to download the anonymized dataset upon completion. Unlike many existing anonymization tools that require advanced programming expertise or provide limited support for reproducible workflows, the platform combines an intuitive low-code interface, integrated disclosure-risk assessment, and automatic generation of reproducible R, Stata, and Python code within a single environment. By lowering technical barriers to advanced anonymization, it enables institutions in resource-constrained settings to implement privacy-preserving data sharing while aligning with international data governance standards. This platform is informed by the principles of data justice and equitable data governance, which emphasize fairness, inclusion, transparency, and the protection of individuals and communities throughout the data lifecycle. By lowering technical barriers to privacy-preserving data sharing, the platform seeks to reduce inequities in access to advanced anonymization technologies and promote context-sensitive anonymization practices, particularly for sensitive health, education, and community data in Africa. In doing so, it contributes to more trustworthy, accountable, and equitable data ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: A Low-Code Data Anonymization Platform for Achieving Data Privacy for Research Data

evidence_items.summary:
This study examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) personalisation depth and algorithmic transparency relate to continued engagement with streaming platforms through consumers’ psychological ownership of the recommendation stream, and over what range of privacy concern the transparency route holds.
 
 
 
 A 14-day, two-wave panel of streaming subscribers in Türkiye (N = 450) was analysed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and re-estimated with covariance-based SEM. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment (N = 236) manipulated both features.
 
 
 
 Personalisation depth showed an indirect-only mediation pattern through ownership in the estimated model, with a direct path practically equivalent to zero within a pre-specified bound; the pattern replicated under random assignment. Ownership carried 45 per cent of the association between transparency and engagement, and a direct path accounted for the rest. The transparency–ownership link was no longer significant above a privacy-concern level of about 4.5 (7-point scale), a region holding roughly two in five respondents. Platform involvement strengthened the personalisation route; no group difference was detected for transparency.
 
 
 
 Participants were subscribers aged 18–35 in three Turkish cities, engagement was self-reported and ownership and engagement were measured on the same occasion.
 
 
 
 Ownership measures can complement viewing and churn metrics when personalisation is evaluated, and layered explanations let users choose how much detail they see.
 
 
 
 For interactive marketing, the study recasts the AI feed as a possession consumers co-produce, not exposure firms deliver. It tests, and does not assume, whether design features keep a direct relationship with engagement once ownership is modelled.
evidence_items.title: When the algorithm feels like mine: personalisation depth, algorithmic transparency and psychological ownership in continued streaming engagement

evidence_items.summary: Clinical decision-making increasingly depends on heterogeneous and distributed information sources, including medical images, radiology and pathology reports, electronic health records, laboratory measurements, biosignals, temporal patient trajectories, and clinical guidelines. Recent advances in multimodal learning, foundation models, and retrieval-augmented generation have opened new opportunities for Artificial Intelligence (AI) in clinical scenarios. However, current systems still struggle to support effective information access and knowledge integration across these sources, as retrieving, aligning, fusing, and reasoning over heterogeneous clinical evidence remains challenging in reliable, interpretable, and workflow-aware settings.The workshop Clinical-MIRF: Multimodal Information Retrieval and Fusion in Clinical Workflows aims to explore innovative methodologies and applications in multimodal information retrieval, cross-modal fusion, knowledge-grounded reasoning, and trustworthy information access in clinical workflows. Clinical-MIRF will bring together researchers from information retrieval, knowledge management, biomedical AI, medical imaging, natural language processing, clinical informatics, and human-centered AI. Topics include multimodal indexing and search, cross-modal representation learning, clinical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval, fusion of imaging and textual evidence, evaluation protocols for multimodal clinical systems, robustness, fairness, privacy, and human-in-the-loop clinical decision support. Accepted workshop papers will be published in post-proceedings by Springer in the Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS) series.
evidence_items.title: Clinical-MIRF: Multimodal Information Retrieval and Fusion in Clinical Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in the UK. Early detection and removal of adenomatous polyps are essential to improving outcomes. Artificial intelligence-assisted colonoscopy tools, such as GI Genius (GIG), may enhance adenoma detection rates (ADR) and reduce the likelihood of missed lesions. A patient-level simulation cost-effectiveness model was developed to estimate the economic and clinical impact of GIG-assisted colonoscopy compared with standard colonoscopy alone in a symptomatic for suspected CRC population in England. The model adopted a National Health Service and Personal Social Services perspective, with a lifetime time horizon. Key model inputs were informed by the NAIAD trial, which evaluated the impact of GIG-assisted colonoscopy on ADR, compared with standard colonoscopy. Base case and probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) were conducted to estimate the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio and the probability of cost effectiveness. Base case results suggest that GIG is a cost-effective intervention, associated with per-person cost savings of £69 and quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gains of 0.046. This was primarily due to increased ADR and subsequent reduced CRC incidence. Scenario analyses testing uncertainty around the sensitivity of colonoscopy, clinical outcomes for those initially undiagnosed, differences in outcomes across experienced and non-experienced endoscopists, and the total costs of GIG produced findings that were consistent with the base case and did not materially change the estimated costs or QALYs. PSA results indicate that GIG is cost effective in 53% of simulations at the £20,000 per QALY gained threshold. This uncertainty is attributable to the marginal change in QALY outcomes between arms of the model, meaning that minor fluctuations in QALY outcomes between PSA iterations lead to large variations in the ICER. The results highlight that GIG is a cost-saving intervention that can improve health outcomes by increasing ADRs. Scenario analyses broadly support the base case findings, suggesting that the conclusions were generally consistent across the alternative assumptions explored. PSA results highlighted considerable decision uncertainty, driven by the small incremental differences in QALYs. PSA results highlight considerable decision uncertainty, driven by the small incremental differences in QALYs.
evidence_items.title: The economic and clinical impact of an AI-assisted tool for colonoscopy to support diagnosis of colorectal cancer in symptomatic patients in England

evidence_items.summary: The year 1948 gave birth to two transformative pillars of modern computing: Claude Shannon's information theory, which gave rise to data compression, and Alan Turing's writings on intelligent machinery, which ignited the field of artificial intelligence. Today, nearly eight decades later, we are witnessing a profound hybridization of these once-distinct fields. As we push to efficiently store, process, and retrieve massive datasets across diverse data types, users, devices, and systems — from vector and graph databases to cutting-edge agentic memories — AI and compression can no longer operate in silos. In this talk, we investigate how Learning is fundamentally reshaping the fields of Indexing and Compression. We will focus on two challenging research directions: designing Learned Data Structures that fuse classical indexing with machine learning to achieve unprecedented efficiency, and developing next-generation Data Compressors driven by powerful autoregressive and diffusion neural models to reach new frontiers of efficacy. We will also examine the reverse direction — how Compression can reshape Learning through model compaction and comprehension. By unpacking the distinct computational advantages and current practical pitfalls of these lines of investigation, we will outline a roadmap for these research frontiers and hopefully inspire new cross-disciplinary collaborations.
evidence_items.title: Learn to Compress or Compress to Learn? Shannon and Turing meet again in the LLM era

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) enables real-time microscopic assessment of tissue during brain tumor surgery and has been investigated as an adjunct to intraoperative diagnosis and fluorescence-guided resection. Previous reviews have largely focused on the technical characteristics and clinical applications of CLE. This study aimed to provide a quantitative overview of the development of the field, its collaborative structure, intellectual foundations, and major research themes.


METHODS
The Web of Science Core Collection was searched on May 30, 2026. After title and abstract screening, 114 publications from 2010 to 2026 were included. Bibliographic data were analyzed using VOSviewer version 1.6.20. Co-authorship, citation, co-citation, author-keyword co-occurrence, and bibliographic coupling analyses were performed. Publications with zero citations were additionally examined according to publication year, document type, and research topic.


RESULTS
The 114 publications received 1801 citations and had a dataset H-index of 25. Publication output increased after 2018 and reached its highest annual level in 2024. The United States, Germany, and Italy were the leading contributing countries, while Mark C. Preul, Jennifer M. Eschbacher, and Evgenii Belykh were among the leading contributors. The main thematic core included CLE, brain tumors, fluorescein sodium, glioma, and fluorescence-guided surgery, with recent work extending toward telepathology and artificial intelligence-assisted image interpretation. Thirty-two publications (28.1%) were uncited; 16 (50.0%) were meeting abstracts, and 19 (59.4%) were published between 2024 and 2026.


CONCLUSION
CLE research in brain tumor surgery has expanded since 2010, with published studies increasingly addressing potential clinical applications, telepathology, and computer-assisted image interpretation rather than demonstrating established adoption in routine clinical practice. Uncited publications included both publication types with lower citation visibility and recent studies with limited time to accumulate citations. These bibliometric patterns should not be interpreted as evidence of the clinical effectiveness of CLE. Further multicenter studies using standardized imaging and interpretation protocols and clinically relevant outcomes are needed to clarify the role of CLE in routine neurosurgical practice.
evidence_items.title: Global research trends in confocal laser endomicroscopy for brain tumor surgery, 2010-2026: A bibliometric review.

evidence_items.summary:
Background
The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) holds transformative potential for clinical nursing practice, yet its integration also brings significant risks and uncertainties. Despite growing discourse on AI in health care, frontline nurses' firsthand experiences, perceptions, and practical needs regarding GenAI remain largely under-synthesized in the existing literature.


Objective
This systematic review aimed to synthesize qualitative evidence to clarify the core themes related to clinical nurses' perceptions, experiences, obstacles, and requirements when using GenAI in real-world clinical settings.


Methods
A systematic search was conducted across 10 electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP Information, SinoMed, and Wanfang) for records published between January 2018 and June 2026. Eligible studies included qualitative and mixed methods studies involving registered nurses that explored their perceptions and experiences of GenAI in clinical practice. Two independent reviewers (MMW and CYZ) performed study selection, quality appraisal, and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Extracted data encompassed study characteristics, participant demographics, and GenAI-related contextual factors. Data synthesis followed Thomas and Harden's 3-phase thematic synthesis: initial inductive coding generated descriptive themes, which were subsequently integrated with the Technology Acceptance Model for Artificial Intelligence in Nursing (TAM-AIN) framework to develop higher-order analytical themes. Certainty in the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE-CERQual (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation-Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research).


Results
Of the 4350 initially identified records, 13 studies from 6 countries (China: n=6; Saudi Arabia: n=3; United States, Singapore, Australia, and South Korea: n=1 each) met the inclusion criteria, encompassing qualitative data from 234 registered nurses. Three main themes emerged: patterns of nurses' engagement with GenAI (ranging from passive observation to proactive integration), multidimensional perceived threats to adoption (functional, professional, and accountability-related), and the moderating role of organizational readiness, which influenced whether these threats hindered or facilitated GenAI uptake in practice. The GRADE-CERQual assessment showed moderate to high confidence in all findings.


Conclusions
Nurses' engagement with GenAI ranges from passive observation to proactive integration, accompanied by legitimate concerns about functional reliability, professional role displacement, and accountability ambiguity. The moderating role of organizational readiness further highlights that training, tool optimization, and institutional governance remain critical yet often unmet. These findings necessitate coordinated efforts across workforce development, technological design, and regulatory frameworks. Future research should prioritize the development of clinically validated, context-aware GenAI systems that incorporate human-in-the-loop oversight, ensuring that efficiency gains do not compromise the delivery of compassionate, person-centered care.
evidence_items.title: Nurses' Attitudes and Experiences With Generative AI in Clinical Practice: Qualitative Systematic Review.

evidence_items.summary:
This study investigates how investor overconfidence shapes trading behavior and realized performance in cryptocurrency markets. Specifically, it examines whether overconfident trading leads to systematic return penalties, and whether these effects intensify under high-volatility conditions and for less experienced investors.
 
 
 
 Using 77 million transaction records from 405,000 investors across four major cryptocurrency exchanges over 2014–2024, this paper proxies overconfidence by trading frequency and portfolio concentration (HHI). To strengthen causal interpretation, it exploits quasi-exogenous variation in trading frictions – exchange outages and fee-tier resets – as instruments for trading intensity, supplemented by extensive robustness checks and alternative concentration measures distinguishing benchmark (BTC/ETH) holdings from altcoin-dominant portfolios.
 
 
 
 Both overconfidence proxies are robustly associated with significantly lower realized and risk-adjusted returns, indicating economically meaningful welfare losses for retail investors. The penalty is strongly state-dependent, becoming substantially larger during high-volatility regimes and among novice traders. Instrumental-variable results confirm that intensified trading causally contributes to performance deterioration rather than merely reflecting unobserved investor heterogeneity.
 
 
 
 This study contributes transaction-level evidence to behavioral finance by quantifying volatility-sensitive overconfidence costs in an emerging digital-asset setting. It also provides managerial and regulatory implications by highlighting trading frictions as a market-design margin: exchange fee policies, operational resilience and consumer-facing risk disclosures can serve as practical levers to mitigate avoidable retail losses and improve market quality.
evidence_items.title: Behavioral overtrading, bot filtering and retail performance in centralized cryptocurrency markets: transaction-level evidence from anonymized exchange data

evidence_items.summary: We present an index lake for Anserini: a remote index representation of all inverted indexes from Anserini's reproducibility suite. Each index is represented as a set of Parquet files on remote object storage, and retrieval is performed through SQL with DuckDB. Through an extensive benchmark of 239 experiments across 50 collections, we empirically confirm our results are consistent with Anserini's. We analyze query latencies over the index lake and conclude that (1) most experiments can be run relatively efficiently, requiring only a couple of seconds per query; and (2) for large collections and learned sparse indexes, queries suffer from increased latency due to high overhead. We are also able to reduce total network transfer, since (1) index lakes are smaller than the corresponding prebuilt Lucene indexes; and (2) up to 90% of the index can be skipped by pushing filters on the postings table to the data lake. The index lake increases reproducibility and makes it easier to run new experiments on standard test collections and prebuilt indexes.
evidence_items.title: Geese Belong in (Data) Lakes: An Index Lake for Anserini

evidence_items.summary: Time series data is highly valuable yet sharing-sensitive across nodes, making federated learning a promising paradigm to leverage distributed temporal data. However, varying sampling standards lead to heterogeneous data structures across nodes, with diverse time granularities and inconsistent variable sets being particularly prominent, posing significant challenges for conventional federated learning frameworks. In this paper, we propose PiXTime, a novel Transformer-based time series forecasting model designed to tolerate and exploit such structurally heterogeneous distributed data. Specifically, we redesign the internal modules and adopt the parameter-decoupling philosophy by carefully designating each module as either local or shared to handle the unique challenges of the federated scenario. To address granularity misalignments, PiXTime retains a personalized set of local modules for each node, acting as a crucial bridge between the node-specific raw temporal granularities and the unified feature dimension of the federated network. To tackle variable inconsistencies, we design a shared VE Table that explicitly injects globally unified variable categorical identities into specific auxiliary tokens, enhancing PiXTime's capability to collaboratively train under highly diverse auxiliary variable distributions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PiXTime not only establishes state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in handling structurally heterogeneous distributed data but also achieves superiority in conventional benchmarks. We open-source our code at https://github.com/WearTheClo/PiXTime.
evidence_items.title: Towards Efficient Federated Time Series Forecasting under Structural Data Heterogeneity across Nodes

evidence_items.summary: Collaborative applications increasingly manage interconnected data as property graphs whose data and schema both evolve at runtime. Under concurrent updates, schema migration either incurs high latency or risks data divergence, and concurrent schema changes must be merged correctly and reflected onto the data. We present REFRACT,, a coordination-free middleware built on conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs). It combines a graph schema CRDT that deterministically merges concurrent Schema Modification Operators (SMOs), such as renames, property and label changes, and type splits and joins, into a single schema; a property-graph lens engine that lazily translates raw data into the current schema at query time, and a graph data CRDT that stores and merges schemaless data. To the best of our knowledge, REFRACT, is the first system to treat property graph schema evolution itself as a replicated convergent object. Preliminary experiments on the LDBC Social Network Benchmark show that REFRACT, matches the overhead of Cambria, the state-of-the-art document-level baseline, while adding graph-native schema merging, and cuts schema-change downtime by over two orders of magnitude compared to eager migration.
evidence_items.title: Coordination-Free Schema Evolution for Replicated Property Graphs

The file “cdf2003-12singles.txt” developed using ATUS data, that contains tab-separated values for the starting times and cumulative probabilities plotted in Fig. 2 in supporting design report. There are 101 rows in the file. The first entry in each row is the cumulative probability (0 to 1.0) and the second entry is the corresponding starting time (0.0 to 24.0 hours). The second file (“two events 2003-12.txt”) was developed that contains data for all 36,652 ATUS respondents who reported two grooming events in 2003 to 2012. Results in this file are used in TEVA-SPOT to generate random starting time for individuals who take two showers per day. The file has 36,652 rows and five tab-separated columns. The first column contains the year the data were collected and the second column contains the ATUS identifiers used for the respondents. The third column contains the starting times in hours local time for the first event and the fourth column contains the starting time in hours local time for the second event. The fifth column provides the ATUS weights for the respondents. Weights are needed to compensate for the manner in which sampling and data collection were carried out in ATUS. The Report (EPA/600/R-15/271) documents the design for incorporating the capability for estimating inhalation doses in TEVA-SPOT. This dataset is associated with the following publication: Davis, M., R. Janke , and T. Taxon. Assessing Inhalation Exposures Associated with Contamination Events in Water Distribution Systems.
